Spread Love & Acceptance: The whole book, the short version.
By Christian. Published by Spread Love & Acceptance.

This edition: October 2026. Made from the chapters at spreadloveandacceptance.com/book, where they are kept up to date.

Free to read and share. You may print, copy and share this book for personal use and for non-commercial teaching, as long as you credit “Spread Love & Acceptance, spreadloveandacceptance.com” and don’t change it or sell it.

Not therapy. This book is general education about people and relationships. It is not a diagnosis, treatment or a replacement for help from a doctor, counsellor or other trained professional, and it can’t know your situation.

If you are not safe. If you feel afraid of someone you live with, or someone controls your money, phone or movements, that is not a problem to fix with a worksheet. spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety lists free, private help. If you are in danger now, call your local emergency number.

The examples are made up. The people in the scenes and examples are invented, built from common patterns. None of them is a real person or a testimonial.

Research mentioned in the chapters is listed, with links, in the research notes at the back and at spreadloveandacceptance.com/research.

If you need help now

If you might act on thoughts of ending your life, or someone is in danger right now, call your local emergency number: 999 in the UK, 112 or 999 in Ireland, 911 in the US and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand.

If you are struggling, or worried about someone else, you can talk to a trained person now. These lines are free, private and open day and night. You don’t have to be sure it is a crisis to call or text.

Where you areCall or text
United StatesCall or text 988 (the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), or chat at 988lifeline.org. You can also text HOME to 741741 (Crisis Text Line).
United KingdomCall Samaritans free on 116 123. Or text SHOUT to 85258 (Shout, a free text line).
IrelandCall Samaritans free on 116 123.
CanadaCall or text 9-8-8 (the Suicide Crisis Helpline), in English or French.
AustraliaCall Lifeline on 13 11 14, or text 0477 13 11 14.
New ZealandCall or text 1737 (Need to talk?).
Anywhere elsefindahelpline.com lists free helplines in many countries, by phone, text and chat.

For children and young people

UKChildline, 0800 1111 (free, for anyone under 19)
IrelandChildline, 1800 66 66 66 (free, for anyone up to 18)
CanadaKids Help Phone, 1-800-668-6868, or text CONNECT to 686868
AustraliaKids Helpline, 1800 55 1800 (ages 5 to 25)
New ZealandYouthline, 0800 376 633, or text 234
US988 is for every age.

If you’re worried about someone

Ask them plainly: “Are you thinking about ending your life?” Studies have found that asking does not put the idea in someone’s head, and talking about it may even ease it. Listen, stay with them if you can, and call or text one of the lines above together. Part Three, Chapter 12, page 305 says more about helping someone in a crisis, and Chapter 16, page 371 about worry, low mood and when to get help.

This book is general education, not a crisis service. The website’s tools keep what you type on your own device, so nobody there can see it or reply to it. The numbers were checked in October 2026. Numbers can change; findahelpline.com keeps an up-to-date list.

How to use this book

This is a book about seeing what is really going on, in yourself and between people, without blaming anyone, and then changing one small thing. This copy holds 26 chapters in three parts, in the short version. There is no wrong way in.

The parts

  • Part One: Self-discovery. Where you came from, who you are now and who you are becoming. You can read all of it on your own.
  • Part Two: Between us. One idea per chapter about sharing a life, a home or work with someone, each with a worksheet that puts it to use.
  • Part Three: Understanding people. How feelings, stress, trust, change, grief, groups and love work, for anyone, in any kind of relationship.

Two sizes of every chapter

Every chapter comes in a short version (about 10 to 15 minutes) and a full version with the research, more examples and more to try. This is the short version. The full version is free at spreadloveandacceptance.com/book.

Read in order, or by need

Read it front to back like any book, or start with the chapter that fits what is going on. Each chapter ends with What to remember, This connects to (the chapters that explain it or put it to use, with page numbers) and Put it to use, with codes you can scan for the matching tool.

In every chapter

  • A short scene: a made-up moment from everyday life.
  • Words you could use: sentences to say out loud.
  • Try this: one small thing to do this week.
  • Common mix-ups: easy mistakes, and what is closer to true.

The site, the program and Professor Puddles

The book has a free website with the workpapers (pages you fill in) and tools (helpers you use) that the chapters mention; the next page explains both. Nothing you type there leaves your device, and there is no account. The six-week program (spreadloveandacceptance.com/prog-01) puts Part Two to work a week at a time, and the self path does the same for Part One. Professor Puddles, the site’s friendly guide, answers questions about the book’s ideas.

Go gently

Some chapters touch hard things: grief, shame, anger, worry, trauma. Skip anything that isn’t right for today. Nothing here is a test, and nothing needs to be done all at once.

Workpapers, tools and three friends

Workpaper WP-03 Workpapers: pages you fill in

A workpaper is a page you fill in, on your own or together: a one-week log, a list of who owns which job, a short check. Each one has a number, like WP-03, and it is always called a workpaper, for example “Workpaper WP-03: One owner per job”. The blank workpapers are also at the back of this book, one page each, to copy.

Tool Tools: helpers you use on the site

A tool is an interactive helper on the website: a quiz, a calm-down timer, a card maker, or the Chat analyzer that reads a message with you. You use it and it gives you something back. It is always called a tool, for example “Tool: Chat analyzer”.

The book keeps the two apart: a workpaper and a tool never share a list. Both are free, need no account, and what you type stays on your device.

Three friends who give hints

  • Professor Puddles, the site’s cheerful raindrop professor, gives most of the hints: a thought to take with you, and the workpaper or tool that fits.
  • Tidbit, the quick, curious pup with the big smile and the collar, bounds in now and then with a playful tip.
  • Sugarfoot, the steady, gentle pup with the long soft ears and the best hugs, turns up with a calm, slow tip.

They keep to the lighter pages. Where a chapter talks about crisis, deep grief or being hurt, the pages stay quiet and plain.

zqhandedqz

If someone handed you this book

Maybe it was left on your side of the bed with a page turned down. Maybe someone said, “Could you just read this bit?” Either way, you didn’t choose it. Fair enough. Here is the short version, written for you.

This isn’t a case against you

The book starts from something researchers have found again and again: when two people each estimate their share of the housework, the two answers usually add up to more than 100%. Nobody is lying. You see every minute of your own effort and only some of theirs, and so do they (Chapter II, page 88). So the book never asks who the bad guy is. Its numbers score the setup, never a person.

What’s in it for you

  • Fewer repeat arguments about the same jobs.
  • Jobs that are clearly yours, so nobody needs to remind you about them.
  • Credit for what you already do. Your jobs go on the list too: the car, the bins, the late-night lifts, the things you fix.
  • A say in what “fair” means in your house. It isn’t always 50/50 (Chapter IV, page 120).

It doesn’t ask for therapy talk, and you never fill anything in about the other person. You can say no.

A first week: three small things

  1. Log your own week. Rough minutes on “Who did what”, including the thinking part: booking, remembering, planning. Ten minutes in all. Only yours, never theirs.
  2. Ask one question, and just listen. “What’s the one job you’d most like to stop thinking about?” Don’t defend or count. Write the answer down.
  3. Take over that job, the whole of it, including the noticing (below).

Words to open the talk

“I read the bit you gave me. I don’t agree with all of it, but I get the point about the stuff nobody sees.”
“I’d rather own a couple of things properly than ‘help’ with everything. Which one would you most like off your mind?”
“Give me a week to see what I actually do. Then let’s look together.”

Best left out, for now: “Just tell me what to do” (it hands the thinking straight back), “You should have asked” and, in the first five minutes, “I do loads too.” That may be true. Save it for when you both have your logs.

Taking over a whole job, noticing included

Every job has a part you can see (doing it) and parts you can’t: noticing it needs doing, remembering, planning and checking it got done (the Preface, page 62). Taking a job over means all of it.

  1. Pick one job that repeats: the children’s clothes and shoes, the bins, the car, school forms, the dentist.
  2. Get the handover once. What it involves, when it’s due, where things are, who to call. Ask your questions now, not every week.
  3. Move the remembering out of their head. A phone reminder, the calendar, a list on the fridge: anywhere but the other person.
  4. Do it start to finish for a month without being reminded. If you need reminding, fix your reminder, not the relationship.
  5. Do it your way. If the result is fine, the method is yours. Their part is to let it be done differently.
  6. Ask for a backstop if you like: someone who notices a slip and says so once, kindly. A backstop isn’t a supervisor (Chapter II, page 88).

A made-up example. Hester has always looked after the children’s clothes: spotting toes at the end of shoes, school sizes, swimming kit, passing on what’s outgrown. Wilf takes it over. Hester writes the handover note: sizes, the shop, which drawer holds the next size up. Wilf sets a reminder for the first Sunday of each month: “Shoes, uniform, kit.” In week two he misses the PE kit for a school trip. Hester says once, “The trip kit is Thursday,” and he adds “school letters” to his Sunday check. A month in, Hester says the biggest change is that she no longer thinks about shoes at eleven at night.

If you think it’s already fair

Log your week anyway. If it comes out even, that is useful to know, and the book will say so: a fair score doesn’t silence anyone, and a low one doesn’t blame anyone. And if this book feels like the wrong place to start, Find it fast, page 9 lists other ways in.

Then

Part One · Then

Know yourself: then, where your lens came from

Why you expect what you expect, and how the rules you picked up growing up still make small decisions for you today.

In this chapter

  1. You’re not one thing
  2. Your lens came from somewhere
  3. Each stage of growing up asks its own question
  4. When something happened matters
  5. Some old answers were learned without all the facts
  6. An old rule can read other people for you
  7. Write down the rulebook from home
  8. You get to choose which rules to keep
  9. What you carry forward is yours
  10. You, in all your relationships
  11. Common mix-ups

This is where the book begins. Part One (Then, Now and Next) is about you. Part Two (a Preface and Chapters I to V) is about the people you share a life with. Part Three (Chapters 1 to 17) is about how people work. Some printed copies hold only one or two of the parts; every chapter is free to read at spreadloveandacceptance.com/book, and the book at a glance (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/topic-start-here) there gives a one-minute tour of the whole thing.

Sunday, 10:15am

Last night’s pan is soaking on the hob, there’s a tin of tomatoes open by the kettle, and one of the three mugs has grown something. Your partner is asleep. You haven’t had a single thought yet, not one, and already there’s a voice going of course it’s you, it’s always you.

Nobody said that. Nobody’s even awake.

Across town Ray is drying a plate that nobody will ever see. His wife died two years ago, and he still can’t sit down with the paper until the last fork is back in the drawer. His mother couldn’t either.

  1. You’re not one thing.

    Dot is seventy-one and her son is forty minutes late for Sunday lunch. When he finally comes in, cold air and apologies and a bunch of garage-forecourt carnations, she says, “Well, the beef’s ruined,” in a voice she will regret by pudding.

    Three things went into that sentence. She has liked things on time since she was a girl; that’s wiring, and it isn’t going anywhere. Her father treated lateness as a kind of insult, and she picked that up without ever deciding to. And she was awake at four listening to the wind rattle the side gate. A strong reaction is usually all three at once, and it helps to know which one is shouting loudest. This chapter is about the middle one, what life taught you. Now (page 35) deals with the other two.

    Dot doesn’t say any of this. She says, “Sit down, then,” and gives him the end bit, which he likes. It’s a start.

    Dig deeper: the three layers

  2. Your lens came from somewhere.

    You learned what to expect from people long before you had words for it, at home mostly, but also at school and from whatever was on the telly at teatime. By the time you’re grown up the lens doesn’t feel like a lens any more. It just feels like seeing.

    Birthdays give it away. Imogen grew up with a party every year, a sheet cake, and cousins driving down from Glasgow with a balloon tied to the wing mirror. Stuart got a card propped against the cornflakes and a slightly better tea. So when Stuart books a quiet table for two on her thirtieth, he thinks he has nailed it. She spends the starter trying not to look at the door.

    It took them two more birthdays to say it out loud. “In my family this was a big deal,” she said in the end. “What was it like in yours?” He thought about it. “Mum did a trifle.” Where your lens came from (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up) walks through the idea slowly, and you can read one section and stop.

    Dig deeper: the lens idea

    Tidbit

    The rules from home aren’t good or bad. They’re just yours, and worth a proper look. How you like to talk is a good first one to look at.

    Tool: How you connect: the 2-minute style quiz spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength

  3. Each stage of growing up asks its own question.

    A small child is working out whether the world is safe. A bit older and the questions change. Am I any good at this? Where do I fit? Can I be close to someone without disappearing? Later, grown-ups wonder whether any of it has meant anything. What sticks is the answer you landed on at each stop, because you can go on using it for decades without noticing you’re using it.

    Jago moved schools four times between eleven and sixteen. He’s forty-four now, a site manager, and on the first morning of every new contract he still stands by the portakabin feeling like the new kid with the wrong shoes. He only clocked why last year. Which of those questions still feels loud for you?

    Dig deeper: the stages

  4. When something happened matters.

    An experience goes deeper when it lands on the question you were busy with at the time. Moving house at four is mostly about a new bedroom. Moving at fourteen, in the thick of working out where you belong, can leave you feeling on the outside for years.

    Two sisters were six and fifteen when their parents split up. The younger one remembers glow-in-the-dark stars on her new ceiling and a different bus to school,, and remembers it fondly, which drives her sister up the wall. The older one remembers every other Friday, standing in the hall with a holdall, being torn in two. They are both right, which is why that year still comes up at Christmas (see Family rifts, spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts). Deeper doesn’t mean permanent, mind. People go on learning all their lives.

    Dig deeper: why timing matters

  5. Some old answers were learned without all the facts.

    Plenty of adults carry a sentence about themselves that they picked up before they were old enough to check it. I’m only all right when I’m useful. My needs are a nuisance. If I get it wrong, I’m bad. A child can’t see what is going on for the grown-ups. They only know how the room felt.

    Sheila has fostered for eleven years and she’s very good at it. She also can’t ask for respite, the planned weekend when someone else has the children, not even in the week she put the cereal in the fridge and the milk in the cupboard. “They’ve got enough on,” she told her link worker, who had rung specifically to offer it.

    Looking again as an adult doesn’t mean deciding it was all fine back then. It means you’re allowed the full picture now. Try writing down one old belief about yourself, then underneath it what you’d say to a friend who believed the same thing about themselves. It reads very differently in someone else’s mouth.

    Dig deeper: old answers and fairer readings

  6. An old rule can read other people for you.

    If silence at home meant someone was angry, then a partner’s quiet evening can feel like weather coming in. And a rule nobody has ever said out loud can’t be agreed to, so the other person can only break it. If you loved me you’d just know. Whoever notices, does it. Each is somebody’s family rule, enforced on someone from a different family.

    Gemma’s housemate goes out at ten past seven without saying goodbye. Gemma, who grew up in a house where the door going without a word meant a row was coming, spends the whole morning at work going over what she might have done. The housemate was on the 7.14 to a shift she’d nearly slept through.

    If you catch yourself reading a silence, you can just ask. “You went off quick this morning. Everything all right?” Nine times out of ten it’s a train.

    Dig deeper: rules that read others

    Professor Puddles

    When an old rule jumps in before you’ve had a chance to think, you don’t have to argue with it. Write it down, and look at it again on a calm day.

    Tool: Old rules, new choices spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up

  7. zqaxselfx1xthenxxpxrulebookqz

    Write down the rulebook from home.

    If you only do one exercise in this book, I’d make it this one. Finish these six lines the way the home you grew up in would have finished them.

    “In my family, love looked like…” “When someone was upset, we…” “The jobs were split like this…” “Resting was okay when…” “Asking for help meant…” “The unforgivable thing was…”

    The last one is usually the interesting one. The rulebook page (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up#home) has room to write them, and nothing is saved anywhere except on your own device.

    Amira and Daniel did it one December, after Daniel’s mum had asked about Christmas again and Amira had gone very quiet. Somewhere on each of their pages, in different words, was the same rule. Holidays belong to my family. It explained four years of tug of war in one go, and they laughed, a bit, before the actual negotiating started (see Two faiths, one family, spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths). One line today is plenty. If you show it to someone, you might say, “This is a rule I grew up with. I’m not saying it’s right. I just want you to know it’s there.”

    Dig deeper: the six rulebook lines

  8. You get to choose which rules to keep.

    Go back over your lines and ask of each one whether you still want it. Some you’ll keep. Some you’ll look at and think, well, that one can go.

    When a reaction feels too big for the moment, wait till you’ve settled and give it a minute’s questioning. Where did I learn this? How old does it feel? Is it true here, with this person, today?

    Bev runs a team at a building society and realised, eventually, that she hid problems from her manager until they’re too big to hide, because at home a mistake meant a mood that lasted days. She wrote a new rule on a yellow sticky note and stuck it to the bottom of her monitor. Mistakes are information. We fix them together. Three years on it has gone curly, and she won’t take it down.

    Pick one of your rules and write the version you’d rather live by. “I used to think ___. Now I’m choosing ___.” Later, if you like, swap rulebooks with someone you trust and pick some shared rules on purpose.

    Dig deeper: the lens check, and choosing together

  9. What you carry forward is yours.

    You didn’t choose the home you grew up in, or what anyone else did, or what you concluded at seven about how things work. What’s in your hands now is smaller than that and a good deal sturdier. You decide which rules you keep. You decide how you talk to yourself about them, and where your energy goes, and that includes people. Give your care where it’s met with care. Where it’s all one way, let it shrink back to something that feels fair, so you have some left.

    Marcia has organised every meet-up with an old school friend for nine years. The friend always comes and has never once suggested a date. Last spring Marcia stopped chasing. She sent one message (“I’d love to see you, let me know when works”) and then nothing, which was harder than it sounds. The friend didn’t reply for five weeks. In those five weeks Marcia went to a quiz, twice, with people who did reply (see Always the one reaching out? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends)).

    Is there somewhere you give far more than comes back? You could give a little less there this month and see what happens. (If you are afraid of someone, this isn’t about managing them. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has people to talk to.)

    Dig deeper: your part, then and now

Tuesday, half past eleven

Two people get the same text from the same friend. Can we talk tonight? Fern is pleased. She likes a plan. Callum feels his stomach go, because in his house “we need to talk” never once meant anything good, and he spends his lunch hour in the car park outside Greggs rehearsing answers to accusations nobody has made.

The friend wanted to know if they were still up for splitting a cottage in Pembrokeshire in August. Callum said yes too quickly and then had to ring back about the dates.

You, in all your relationships

Your old rules come with you everywhere, starting with the voice you use on yourself after a mistake. At home they decide who notices, who plans and what a quiet evening means. Two housemates can share a fridge for a year before finding out they’ve been living by different rulebooks about mess. In families, the old roles switch back on before you’ve got your coat off (the helper, the peacemaker, the one who makes it funny). At work, someone praised mainly for being useful says yes to everything and then quietly seethes, and seeing the rule is often enough to buy them a pause before the next yes. After a breakup old rules can get louder, which makes it a good time to look at them kindly (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). How you connect (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength) is a two-minute quiz on the talking rules you brought with you. Help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) lists pages for many more situations.

Common mix-ups

The worry people bring to this chapter most often is that looking back means blaming their family. It doesn’t have to. Many of the adults who raised us had lenses of their own, and if that doesn’t fit your story, you don’t have to make it fit. Then there’s the fear that anything which started in childhood is fixed for good. Many old patterns soften once you can see them and feel safe enough to try something else, and some leave a lasting sensitivity that you learn to carry and explain. Not every big reaction is an old wound, either. Quite often it’s just a full tank (Chapter III, page 105, helps you tell leftover stress from this-moment stress). And some people decide there’s no point looking at their own rules if the other person won’t look at theirs. I don’t agree with that one at all. Knowing your own rules changes how you react whether or not anyone else reads a word of this.

A note on care: This part looks back at growing up. It is general education, not a diagnosis or therapy, and it can’t tell you what anyone has. Not every home felt calm or kind, so take only what is useful. If looking back feels heavy, you can stop and come back another day, or explore it with a qualified professional, if and when you want that. Nothing here is required, and nothing you write needs to be shared.

If you want to go on, notice one “always” or “never” that went through your head this week. Whose voice was it in? How old did you feel? Where your lens came from, Roots & Wings (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up#roots) and Know your own wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself) go further.

What to remember

  • You’re not one thing.
  • Each stage of growing up asks its own question.
  • Some old answers were learned without all the facts.
  • Write down the rulebook from home.
  • What you carry forward is yours.

zqselfx2xnowqz

Now

Part One · Now

Know yourself: now, your wiring, your weather and your words

Why the same words can land differently on different days and in different people, and how to understand today’s you well enough to say what helps.

In this chapter

  1. Today is made of two layers you can work with
  2. Know how you like to be spoken to
  3. Check your weather before you speak
  4. Ask where this feeling is coming from
  5. Plan what settles you on a calm day
  6. Your needs and limits are information, not demands
  7. Being wired differently is not being wrong
  8. Explain yourself without over-sharing
  9. Do your part, and only your part
  10. You, in all your relationships
  11. Common mix-ups

Sunday, 7:50pm

Your friend pauses the film. “You all right? You’ve been quiet all day.”

“Fine.”

Which isn’t a lie, exactly. You genuinely don’t know if you’re fine, or tired, or still chewing on something somebody said on Thursday. You couldn’t explain it to yourself, never mind to her. You reach for the remote and she lets you.

  1. Today is made of two layers you can work with.

    Your wiring is the lasting part. Temperament, pace, senses, the way words go in. You work with that, by building a life that suits it. Today’s conditions are the passing part (sleep, hunger, the hour) and you work around those, usually by eating something or sleeping on it. Most of the frustration here comes from mixing the two up. (Then, page 22, covers the third layer, the patterns life taught you.)

    Dean works nights at a distribution centre. For months the school-run chatter at ten past eight was unbearable to him, all of it, the who-sat-next-to-who and the who-said-what in PE, and he started quietly wondering whether he was any good at being a dad. Then his partner swapped with him. He does the half-three pick-up now, after he’s slept, and the same chatter is funny again (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours). His daughter says he’s “got nicer”. He’s chosen not to take that personally.

    Write down one thing that always bothers you. That one’s probably wiring. Then one that only bothers you when you’re tired.

    Dig deeper: wiring and conditions

    Professor Puddles

    Your wiring stays the same from day to day. Your weather doesn’t. A one-minute check in the morning helps you tell the two apart.

    Tool: My weather today spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

  2. Know how you like to be spoken to.

    Pace, tone, how much needs spelling out, what a silence means. All of it changes how words land. How you connect (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength) gives you words for it, and a four-letter Wave Code that’s meant to be light-hearted, so please don’t put it on your CV. The “How to talk to me” card (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card) fits the same thing onto one page you can hand over before a hard talk.

    Agnes is seventy-two and loves a phone call. Her grandson Liam loves a text and regards the phone ringing as a kind of emergency. For about a year each of them privately decided the other had gone a bit cool. It took a cousin, over the trifle at Christmas, to say, “Nan, he’s not ignoring you, he just doesn’t answer the phone. To anyone. Ever.” There’s a Sunday call at six now, with texts in between, and Liam mostly picks up.

    If you want somewhere to start, finish this. “I take things in best when…”

    Dig deeper: your wiring and your Wave Code

  3. Check your weather before you speak.

    Everything you hear goes through your own state on the way in. Part Two, Chapter III (page 105) looks closely at the stress tank in a shared home. This chapter only adds the self side, which is a one-minute reading on your own before you decide what a hard moment means. My weather today (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) is the quick check. How much are you carrying? is a fuller one on a short worksheet.

    A couple living five hours apart worked out, eventually, that every bad call they’d had came at the end of her late shift, around midnight her time. Every single one. They moved anything serious to Saturday mornings, with coffee, and found they mostly agreed with each other (see Long distance, spreadloveandacceptance.com/long-distance).

    Words you could use “I’m running on empty tonight. Can we pick this up tomorrow morning?”

    zqaxselfx2xnowxxstatexwordsqz

    One state, many words. The chapters and tools use a few everyday pictures for one thing, how much room you have today.

    • The three states (Chapter 2, page 166, calls them the ladder) are calm and connected, revved up, and running on empty.
    • My weather today uses sky words for the same three. Clear is calm and connected, gusty is revved up, and fogged in is running on empty. Its pressure is how much you were already carrying.
    • The stress tank is the score from How much are you carrying?, from 0 to 1, where higher means fuller.
    • The battery is the other side of the tank, the energy you have left, so a full tank means a low battery.

    “Gusty”, “revved up”, “a fairly full tank” and “a low battery” can all describe the same Tuesday afternoon. I’d pick one set and stick with it.

    Dig deeper: reading your state before you speak

  4. Ask where this feeling is coming from.

    It’s 4.45 on a Friday and a colleague leans over the partition. “Quick question?”

    Your heart goes. Why? If you stop and look, there’s a fair bit in there. A jumpiness that belongs to a manager you had six years ago, who never once had a quick question. A long week. And nothing to eat since a biscuit at eleven. What it needs is five minutes and a sandwich, and then you can answer him like a normal person.

    That’s the whole check, really. Name the feeling, roughly. Ask whether it fits the size of the moment or feels older. Ask what it needs. The answer is usually more ordinary than you’d think, and it works best once the first wave has gone past.

    zqaxselfx2xnowxxhardxtoxnameqzWhen feelings are hard to name. For some people “What are you feeling?” is a hard question most days and nearly impossible on bad ones. They notice a racing heart or a heavy stomach and can’t tell if it’s worry or hunger or something else. Psychologists call this alexithymia, which means “no words for feelings”. It’s a trait that runs from a little to a lot. It’s common, especially among autistic people, and it isn’t an illness. The feelings are there. The words come slowly. Start with the body (“tight chest, skipped lunch”). Pick between two words instead of hunting for one (“more tired or more annoyed?”). Use the sky words if feeling words won’t come. “I’ll tell you tomorrow” is a real answer.

    Dig deeper: a four-step self-check
  5. zqaxselfx2xnowxxpxsettleqz

    Plan what settles you on a calm day.

    Halfway through being wound up is a terrible time to work out what calms you down. The Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11) is a plan you make beforehand. What tends to set you off, two things that help, and one sentence for stepping away that says when you’ll be back. It’s for you. It is never a list of instructions for anyone else.

    Elsie is fourteen and she and her mum have the same row about her phone roughly twice a week. She made a kit, grudgingly, mostly to get her mum off her back. The next time it kicked off she said, “I need ten minutes, I’ll come back,” and went upstairs and lay on her bed with her headphones in, furious. Twelve minutes later she came down. Her mum had put the kettle on. Neither of them mentioned the phone, which wasn’t exactly a resolution, and was a great deal better than the usual.

    You could say “I need ten minutes. I’ll be back at quarter past.”

    Dig deeper: deciding ahead

    Sugarfoot

    Make your calm-down plan on a slow, quiet day, with a cup of tea if you like. It’s far easier than making one in the middle of a storm.

    Workpaper WP-11: The Calm-Down Kit spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11

  6. Your needs and limits are information, not demands.

    What helps you and what you’ve got left are facts about you. Said kindly, they let other people plan around you. “A heads-up helps me.” “I can do this one. Not that one.” “I’m low today, can it wait till tomorrow?” You don’t have to justify a need. A reason is a kindness you can add if you want to.

    Quinn lives with his two partners in a terrace with one bathroom and an alarming number of shoes in the hall. He needs an hour on his own after work. Before he said so, that hour looked like sulking. Once he’d said it, plainly, it turned into part of the week, like bin day, and one of the others now does his tea on Thursdays.

    Two workpapers from other chapters help with the words. Who did what, from the Preface (page 62), has ready-made kind ways to say no. Say it so it lands, from Part Two, Chapter IV (page 120), turns a raw reaction into a plain request. Or try this. Write one need you’ve never said out loud, and say it to the bathroom mirror without the apology on the front.

    Dig deeper: saying your needs kindly
  7. zqaxselfx2xnowxxpxdifferentqz

    Being wired differently is not being wrong.

    Some people take in words, noise, change and feelings differently from the way most social customs were built. That’s wiring. You can understand it, plan round it and get support for it if you want. Shona has ADHD and spent years calling herself hopeless because she kept missing plans with friends. Now she just tells people the one thing that works, a text the day before, and she turns up. Mostly on time (see Neurodivergent relationships, spreadloveandacceptance.com/neurodivergent-relationships).

    zqaxselfx2xnowxxdoublexempathyqzA mix-up runs both ways. When an autistic and a non-autistic person misread each other, the autistic person usually gets the blame. The double empathy problem, named by the autistic researcher Damian Milton, is the idea that the gap runs both ways. Each person reads the other through their own way of communicating, and each finds the other hard to read. In one study, a story passed along a chain of autistic people kept as much detail as one passed along non-autistic people, while mixed chains lost detail faster. I find that study quietly cheering. Wired Differently (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wired-differently) shows how two differently wired people can each misread the other, and “Where did we lose each other?” lets both of you adjust a little.

    Dig deeper: wiring is not a flaw

  8. Explain yourself without over-sharing.

    Most moments need one short sentence, and there are really only three. “This is how I’m wired, it won’t change, but this helps.” “This is an old alarm going off, I’m working on it.” “Low-battery day, sorry.” You never owe anyone your history. Give them the bit that helps them help you.

    Rob has a long-term illness and a new friend from the climbing wall who keeps suggesting things. “Some days I’ve got less in the tank,” he told him, on the bench, unlacing his shoes. “If I cancel, it isn’t you.” The friend said “Fair enough” and asked if he wanted a lift on Thursday. That was it. No medical notes required (see When one of you is ill, spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill).

    Dig deeper: scripts, and how much to share

  9. Do your part, and only your part.

    Today you control your own words, your effort, your rest, your limits and what you ask for. You don’t control anyone else’s mood or pace, and trying to will flatten you quicker than almost anything. It helps, too, to match energy with energy. Meet warmth with warmth, and give a little less where you keep giving far more than comes back.

    Lorna is thirty-eight and her dad still worries about her driving. She has tried reassurance, statistics, and once, unwisely, sarcasm. None of it worked. What she does now is text “Home safe x” after any long run up the M6, and then she lets his worry be his (see For grown-up children, spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children). He still worries. She sleeps better.

    (If you are afraid of someone, this isn’t about managing them. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has people to talk to.)

    Dig deeper: your circle of control, and matching energy

Friday, 6:40pm

“Surprise! I’ve booked us dinner with my cousins tonight. Half seven, the Turkish place.”

They meant it as a present. Your chest went tight and you heard yourself say “Great” in a voice so flat you could have ironed on it. Later, at the sink, you try to work out which bit that was. The plan changing. Something older. Or just Friday. Probably some of each. You still haven’t said anything, and the taxi’s booked for ten past.

You, in all your relationships

Your wiring and your weather come with you everywhere, starting with how you treat yourself on a bad day. Noticing that you’re low ought to come before deciding that you’re failing. Partners can give each other a heads-up or a quiet hour, and every partner has wiring of their own. With friends and family, the question is usually how you like to keep in touch and how much you can give this month. At work it might be an agenda the day before, or a minute before you answer. Housemates mostly negotiate noise, and the bathroom. If you live on your own, you get to build a week that fits how you’re built (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Common mix-ups

Knowing yourself is mostly about what helps. A label can come later, or never, and the three layers and a Wave Code are everyday words with no diagnosis in them. “That’s just how I am” may well be true, especially about wiring, but it works much better as the start of a conversation than the end of one. Telling people how you’re wired doesn’t make them your managers either. It helps your words land. You still do your part, and they still have needs of their own.

And “I’m fine” does sometimes mean fine. Sometimes it means you’ve been tired for so long you’ve stopped noticing. A quick reading once a week shows you the baseline you’ve got used to, which can be a bit of a shock.

A note on care: This part is general education. It isn’t a diagnosis, a test or treatment, and it can’t tell you whether you’re autistic, have ADHD or anything else, or what anyone else has. If you’d like to understand yourself more deeply, a qualified professional can help, if and when you want that. Nothing here is required, and nothing you try needs to be shared. If talking about any of this with someone ever feels unsafe, or you feel you can’t say no, stop and talk with a trained counselor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counseling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? lists free, private hotlines.

To put this to use, take one reaction you had this week and give it a line for each layer. The wiring bit, the older bit, today’s bit. Take a one-minute reading of your weather. Then write one sentence about what helps you, and keep it to yourself for a few days before trying it on someone. Know your own wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself), the “How to talk to me” card and How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying) are free on the site.

What to remember

  • Today is made of two layers you can work with.
  • Check your weather before you speak.
  • Plan what settles you on a calm day.
  • Being wired differently is not being wrong.
  • Do your part, and only your part.

zqselfx3xnextqz

Next

Part One · Next

Know yourself: next, shaping who you are becoming

You aren’t finished, and some of who you become is up to you. This chapter is about choosing a direction and building small steps that still work on a tired day.

In this chapter

  1. Start with what matters to you
  2. Pick one small goal, in plain words
  3. Name what gets in the way
  4. Make the step tiny, and repeatable
  5. Decide ahead with a simple if-then
  6. Ask for support, as information
  7. Look back kindly once a month
  8. Kindness to yourself is part of the plan
  9. Set goals inside your circle, and spend energy where it comes back
  10. You, in all your relationships
  11. Common mix-ups

Wednesday, 9:10pm

The trainers have been by the front door since Sunday, laces tucked in, pointing outwards like a promise. You were going to walk after dinner. Dinner was two hours ago. Monday, you think. Monday has a nice clean feel to it.

  1. zqaxselfx3xnextxxpxmattersqz

    Start with what matters to you.

    A goal built on somebody else’s idea of a good life is very hard to keep going with. So before you pick one, ask what you want your days to feel like, and write two or three plain words. Calm, say. Or close to family, or steady, or making things. They give you a direction to face instead of a score to hit. If you’re not sure what fills you up and what drains you, How you connect (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength) can help you notice.

    The week their youngest went off to Sheffield, Marion and Keith each wrote two words on the back of a gas bill. Hers said “useful, outdoors”. His said “calm, curious”. Keith looked at hers for a while and said, “That’s why you keep going on about the bird hut.” She had been eyeing the volunteers’ hut at the nature reserve since February. He had been spending a suspicious amount of time staring at the vegetable patch (see Kids grown and gone, spreadloveandacceptance.com/empty-nest). Write yours in pencil. You’re allowed to change them.

    Dig deeper: values first

  2. Pick one small goal, in plain words.

    Just one, and say it as something you’ll do. “Walk for ten minutes after dinner” can go in a diary. “Get healthier” is a hope. Hopes are lovely and you can’t do anything with them on a Tuesday. Your own actions are up to you. How people respond, and how it all turns out, aren’t.

    A student in a shared room in halls wanted to be “less messy”, which her roommate had heard before. As an action it became “clothes in the basket before bed”. She managed it about four nights in seven, and her roommate said that was four more than last term (see Sharing a room, spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room). Try rewriting one wish so it starts “I will…”

    Dig deeper: one goal, in plain words

  3. Name what gets in the way.

    This is where Then (page 22) and Now (page 35) earn their keep. The obstacle might be your wiring, and a plan that ignores how you’re built was made for somebody else. It might be an old rule (“rest has to be earned” is a popular one). Or it might simply be a tired Tuesday. Whichever it is, change the arrangement and leave yourself alone.

    Kofi kept missing his evening run and had more or less concluded he was lazy. He works in a warehouse on a rota that changes every week, so “evenings” meant something different every Monday. Once he tied the run to his first day off, whenever it fell, he stopped missing it. He’s still slightly annoyed it took him a year to see (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours).

    Dig deeper: what gets in the way
  4. zqaxselfx3xnextxxpxtinyqz

    Make the step tiny, and repeatable.

    Small enough to survive your worst week. “Put my shoes on” counts. I mean that. Tie it to something you already do, and do it often. The 90-second daily check-in in Part Two, Chapter I (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-1-in-depth) runs on the same idea, that small and often outlasts big and rare, and Ten-minute start (spreadloveandacceptance.com/start-in-10-minutes) shows how small a whole path can be.

    Six months after the breakup, Ade wanted to “get back out there”. Far too big for a Sunday night. What he actually did was send one message to one friend every Sunday, usually from the sofa during the weather forecast, usually something feeble like “you watching this?” Two of the friends started replying with whole paragraphs (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). If you like a game for this sort of thing, the Re-check Drive (spreadloveandacceptance.com/recheck-drive) turns small steps into calm football. If your step takes more than two minutes, shrink it again.

    Dig deeper: tiny, repeatable steps

    Tidbit

    Tiny steps count, wobbly ones included. If you like a game, there’s one where each small kind act moves the ball up the field.

    Tool: Gentle games: the Re-check Drive (calm football) spreadloveandacceptance.com/recheck-drive

  5. Decide ahead with a simple if-then.

    “If it’s after dinner, I put my shoes on.” Deciding ahead means one decision fewer on a tired day. It’s the same thinking as the Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11), made while you’re calm.

    Handovers with her ex had been going badly for a year, so Kerry made a rule for the car. When she pulls up outside his house she turns the engine off and takes three slow breaths before she opens the door. It doesn’t make him less irritating. It does mean she gets out of the car as herself (see Co-parenting, spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting).

    Pick a cue that happens every day anyway, like the kettle or brushing your teeth. If the if-then doesn’t work, change it.

    Dig deeper: if-then plans
  6. zqaxselfx3xnextxxpxsupportqz

    Ask for support, as information.

    Tell one person what you’re trying and what would help. “I’m trying to walk after dinner. Would you ask me how it’s going on Sunday?” They can say no. You don’t need anybody’s permission to start.

    Since her husband’s stroke, Glenys has done nearly all of his care. For months she said “I’m fine” whenever her brother asked. In the end she asked him something so specific it was hard to refuse. “Could you sit with him Thursdays, two till four, so I can swim?” He said yes before she’d finished. He brings Bourbons. She’s swum eleven Thursdays out of fourteen, which she thinks is pretty good.

    Some goals are better shared with a qualified professional, and asking for one is a sensible step whenever you want it. (If someone uses your goals to check up on you or control you, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has people to talk to.)

    Dig deeper: asking for support

  7. Look back kindly once a month.

    This is the monthly look-back from Part Two, Chapter V (page 136), pointed at yourself instead of a household. Ten minutes, once a month. What went well? What kept slipping? Was the gap in the plan, in what you had to give that month, or in one strange week? You don’t add up old misses. The only question is what to try next month. Its workpaper, What keeps coming back? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-04-what-keeps-coming-back), is written for a shared home, but the two questions work fine on your own.

    Pauline is raising her two grandchildren. On the first of March she sat down with a pot of tea and a biro and saw that bedtime was working and homework very much wasn’t. So in March, homework moved to the kitchen table straight after a snack, before the telly went on. It worked for one child. The other one, she says, is “a work in progress, like me”.

    Dig deeper: a monthly look at yourself

    Professor Puddles

    Your monthly look is the solo version of the monthly look-back for people who share a home. Borrow its two questions if you like: what kept slipping, and what would have made it easier?

    Workpaper WP-04: What keeps coming back? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-04

  8. Kindness to yourself is part of the plan.

    There’s an old image of the second arrow that I find useful here. The first arrow is the slip itself. The second is the telling-off you give yourself afterwards, which hurts more and helps less. A plan that needs you to be harsh with yourself is mostly second arrows. Rest belongs inside the plan, and you can shrink a goal or drop it whenever you like.

    Harvey is sixteen. He planned to revise every night, missed three in a row, and announced at breakfast that he was useless and might as well not bother. His nan went on buttering toast. “What would you tell Kian?” she said. Harvey rolled his eyes so hard it looked painful. That evening he did twenty minutes before tea, and said nothing about it to anyone.

    Dig deeper: kindness as part of the plan

  9. Set goals inside your circle, and spend energy where it comes back.

    A goal that needs someone else to change is really a wish. You might wish your sister rang more. That’s outside your circle. Ringing her on the first Sunday of the month, and telling her you’d love her to ring too, is inside it. Then treat your energy like the limited thing it is. Put more into the people and plans that give something back, and less into the ones that only take, so you’ve still got some left when you get near the goal.

    Dig deeper: planning inside your circle

The first of the month

You open your notes app. Of the four small things you tried, two have stuck and two quietly stopped somewhere in the second week. You still don’t know why the Saturday swim fell away. You liked the Saturday swim. You put a question mark next to it and close the app.

You, in all your relationships

A goal for yourself nearly always brushes against other people, and small steps work everywhere. With a partner, offer one small habit instead of demanding one. With friends, one message a week can keep a friendship warm for years. In a family it might be a regular call, a visit you can actually keep up, or a first step after a long silence (see Reaching out, spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts). At work, one comment per meeting. With money, one small saving habit that’s yours alone.

Common mix-ups

The commonest, and the least true, is that a goal has to be big to count. Small and repeatable is what survives a bad week, and most big goals turn out to be a lot of small ones in a trench coat. Some people think that once they understand themselves they should be able to change anything. Wiring stays, though, so the aim is a goal that fits how you’re built. Asking for support doesn’t mean you couldn’t manage. It gives people what they need to help. And “I’ll start on Monday” isn’t always a dodge. A fresh start can genuinely help. Today’s tiny version still counts.

A note on care: This part is general education. It isn’t therapy, coaching or medical advice, and it can’t promise any result. Goals about your health, money, work or a hard stretch in life may deserve a qualified professional, and there’s no shame in asking for one. Nothing here is required, and nothing you write needs to be shared. If a goal ever starts to feel like a weight, you can shrink it or put it down.

If you want to start tonight, write your two words, one goal as something you’ll do, the smallest first step you can think of and one if-then. Then put ten minutes in the calendar for a month from now. Your self-discovery path (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) and Ten-minute start are free on the site.

What to remember

  • Start with what matters to you.
  • Name what gets in the way.
  • Decide ahead with a simple if-then.
  • Look back kindly once a month.
  • Set goals inside your circle, and spend energy where it comes back.

zqprefaceqz

Preface

Preface to Part Two

The work nobody sees: invisible labour at home

Part Two of the book is about the people you share a life or a home with, and it opens here. Running a life takes a lot of work that nobody sees. This preface helps you make that work visible, to yourself and to anyone you share it with, so you can talk about it fairly and kindly.

In this chapter

  1. Unseen work quietly adds up
  2. A lot of it is thinking, not doing
  3. The other person usually just hasn’t seen it
  4. Writing it down isn’t keeping score
  5. Each of you writes only your own side
  6. The borrowed words are there to take the blame away
  7. One small step at a time
  8. It can help in many kinds of shared life
  9. The mental load: what the research says
  10. On your own: your own unseen work
  11. One household, followed for a month
  12. Your situation, chapter by chapter
  13. Common mix-ups
  14. Limits and cautions

In short

  • Running a home takes unseen work, the noticing, remembering and planning that many people call the mental load.
  • The other person usually just hasn’t seen it. This work hides by nature, and missing it says little about how much someone cares.
  • Each of you writes only your own side of one ordinary week, and you read the two lists together.
  • The list is for seeing. Thank each other for the past, and plan next week.

Sunday, 9pm

Someone notices that the laundry has been sitting in the washer since Saturday morning and will need doing again, that the school trip form is due on Tuesday, and that the birthday card for Auntie Jean is still in its cellophane on the hall table. They also notice that nobody else has noticed. From the hallway the house looks fine. That’s exactly the trouble.

  1. Unseen work quietly adds up.

    Remembering appointments, noticing that the milk is low and calming a tense moment never show up on a calendar, so they rarely get a thank-you, and over months they pile up. This book calls the pile unbilled debt, because nobody ever sends a bill for it. (It’s a ledger word, and I make no apology for it. I spent my career as a government auditor, and work that only gets done because the same person quietly catches it every time has a name there: a control that was never there to begin with.) You can thank someone for what they carried before, and you leave the past unbilled. Marcus remembers every school form, dentist visit and bit of lunch money for their two children. His husband, Theo, sees two children who always seem to have what they need, PE kit included, and genuinely doesn’t know how. He isn’t careless. The work is out of his sight.

    Tonight you could write down three things you did today that nobody saw, and leave the list alone for now. If you show it to someone later, something like “I’m not asking you to pay anything back. I just want you to see them” sets the right tone.

    Dig deeper: the work that goes unseen

    Professor Puddles

    The easiest way to see unseen work is to write it down for one ordinary week. Each of you logs only your own jobs, and the thinking counts too.

    Workpaper WP-01: Who did what spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-01

  2. A lot of it is thinking, not doing.

    Before a job gets done, someone has to notice it, remember it, plan it and check that it happened. That thinking takes real time and energy even though nobody can see it. In a shared flat above a launderette, Yasmin notices that the broadband deal ends in three weeks, compares six plans, picks one, sets it up and checks it went through. Paying took two minutes. The thinking took most of a Thursday evening, and nobody else in the flat knows it happened.

    Pick one job at home and split it into its steps, noticing, planning, doing and checking, and then ask who usually does each step.

    Dig deeper: the kinds of unseen work

  3. The other person usually just hasn’t seen it.

    When this work is done well, nothing seems to happen, so the other person is rarely ignoring it. From where they stand, things appear to take care of themselves. Edna minds her grandchildren three afternoons a week and quietly moves her own doctor’s appointments to fit, while her daughter believes it all slots in easily. A gentle question often opens it up (“What’s something you do that you think I don’t see?”), followed by listening without explaining.

    Sometimes it only becomes visible when the person who carried it has gone. A widower finds out, slowly, over his first winter alone, how many jobs his wife quietly held: the birthday cards, the boiler service, knowing who to ring when someone was ill. He never saw them until they stopped getting done. If that’s where you are, the section for people on their own, further on in this chapter, was written with you in mind.

    Dig deeper: why it stays hidden

  4. Writing it down isn’t keeping score.

    The point is for both of you to see the same picture, in the same words, at the same time, so that the talk starts from facts you share. This book calls that shared record a ledger, a plain list of who did what, kept for seeing. Two colleagues who job-share each list a week of tasks and find that every difficult client call has landed on the same one of them. They leave last year alone and agree to take turns with the Friday calls. Before you show anyone a list, ask yourself honestly whether it’s to plan next week or to prove a point. If it’s the second, keep it in the drawer for now.

    Dig deeper: why a ledger isn’t a grudge

  5. Each of you writes only your own side.

    Nobody fills in anything for the other person. You each note what you did and then read the two lists together, which keeps it fair and keeps it kind. Each of you also adds the context only you have, such as a long week at work or children off school with colds, so that you both understand what you read. Arran, Dani and Sol are three partners sharing a rented house, and each writes only their own list. Reading them together at the kitchen table, Sol learns for the first time that Arran has been ringing the landlord about the damp every single month since February.

    Dig deeper: your side, their side

  6. The borrowed words are there to take the blame away.

    The book uses a few terms from accounting and science because they describe what is happening without saying whose fault it is. Each one is explained in plain words, and you never need them to use anything here. Two brothers share their mum’s care, and one of them swaps “You never help” for “There’s some unseen work here we haven’t looked at.” His brother finds it much easier to hear. If words like “ledger” or “debt” feel heavy, use your own. “Our list” and “the stuff nobody sees” do the same job.

    Dig deeper: why the book borrows these words

  7. One small step at a time.

    Each chapter adds one idea and one tool, and one week of notes is enough to start. Later come a 90-second daily check-in about how much you were carrying that day, and a monthly look-back that needs only a few lines a week. A nurse on nights and a partner on days hardly see each other awake, so they start with one week of notes stuck to the fridge with a magnet from Whitby, and change nothing yet. Your first step can be as small as picking a start day and setting one reminder.

    Dig deeper: how the book fits together

    Tidbit

    Counting jobs isn’t keeping score. It’s looking for the work nobody noticed, and the quick split check is a good place to start.

    Tool: Who does what? Quick look spreadloveandacceptance.com/lemonade-stand

  8. It can help in many kinds of shared life.

    Partners, families, housemates, co-parents and coworkers all share unseen work. The examples often use a couple at home, and the ideas fit anyone who shares a load. In a foster home, the carer keeps track of family visits and social worker calls, while a teenager in the home quietly cooks for the younger ones twice a week, and both kinds of work deserve to be counted.

    Dig deeper: who this book is for

Your part, and only your part. You can’t make anyone see the unseen work, and you can’t write their side of the ledger. You can write your own side honestly, say it once, kindly, and then match what you take on to what comes back. If you keep carrying more than your share with nothing in return, stepping back towards your share isn’t a punishment. It protects the energy you need to stay kind. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

Friday, after work

“You didn’t have to do all that,” they say, and they mean it kindly. You think: someone did have to. The list only ever lived in your head, so to them it looked as if it took care of itself, the way a house seems to clean itself if you’re never in it on a Saturday morning.

zqaxprefacexxmentalxloadqzThe mental load: what the research says

Many people call the thinking side of home life the mental load, meaning the noticing and planning that come before a job gets done and the checking after. It includes knowing the baby needs the next size of clothes, and remembering the form and the party present. It is real work, even when it doesn’t look like any.

Studies of couples find some patterns, on average. In couples of a man and a woman, women tend to do more of the noticing and checking (Allison Daminger, 2019). After a first baby a gap often opens, and in one study of working couples, mothers took on most of the new childcare while keeping their paid hours (Jill Yavorsky and colleagues, 2015). Arlie Hochschild called the home work that starts after paid work ends “the second shift.”

There is a fair point on the other side too. Sometimes the parent who knows how things are done holds on to that, without meaning to, which researchers call gatekeeping. When a parent openly invites the other in and lets them do it their own way, the other parent tends to do more of the care (Sarah Allen and Alan Hawkins, 1999; Sarah Schoppe-Sullivan and colleagues, 2008).

These are averages across many homes, and they say nothing certain about yours. In your home it may be the other way round, or already even, or shared between two men or two women, which is why the book asks you to look at your own week on paper instead of guessing.

Hollie and Gareth have a toddler and a baby, and Gareth works shifts. Their week’s minutes come out nearly even, yet Hollie did almost three-quarters of the jobs nobody asked anyone to do. Their week is in Chapter II (page 99).

You could say “You do lots of the doing. It’s the remembering I’d love you to take some of, whole jobs, start to finish.” Or the other way round, “Show me once how you like it done, then let me do it my way.”

Dig deeper: the mental load, fairly

On your own: your own unseen work

You don’t need anyone else to start seeing the unseen. For one week, notice the jobs only you remember (the appointments, the smoothing-over) and write them down for yourself. Count it without charging for it, since the point is to see your real load so that you can plan your energy. Notice which jobs are yours by choice and which simply landed on you, and pick one you could hand back or do less often. Nicola, divorced, has the children every other week, and on paper she sees that she is still buying the birthday presents for both sides of the family, four years after the divorce. She hands his side back in one friendly message, and he replies with a thumbs-up and, to her surprise, “fair enough”. More for people living alone or after a breakup is on On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

One household, followed for a month

Three adult siblings share the care of their father, who lives alone in the house they grew up in. On paper the visits are split evenly, two days each. When each of them writes a week of their own side, the picture changes. The eldest, Ffion, also holds the prescriptions, the hospital letters and the calls to the GP, none of which counts as a visit. Their brother is surprised and a little defensive, and the first conversation ends early. A month later they try again, and he takes over the prescriptions completely, with the reminders on his own phone. Their sister still finds the hospital letters too much to face, so Ffion keeps them for now, and they agree to look again in the spring. The ideas in this chapter fit friendships, teams and shared houses in the same way, and Help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) has a page for many kinds of shared life.

Your situation, chapter by chapter

Some situations get their own section:

  • Faith, culture, elders and in-laws. Chapter I (page 85)
  • Small children or a new baby. Chapter II (page 99)
  • Two homes after a split, and step-parents. Chapter III (page 117)
  • Money between you, and a couple with a housemate. Chapter IV (page 133)
  • New together, or grandparents raising a grandchild. Chapter V (page 147)

Common mix-ups

“If it mattered, they’d have asked for help” misses how hidden this work is, often from the person doing it, until it’s written down. Nobody needs exactly 50/50 either; what you’re after is a split you can both see and both agree to. Please don’t start by going over the last ten years. Start with one ordinary week, and thank each other for the past without trying to settle it. And the one doing less usually isn’t the one who cares less. Usually they just can’t see it yet, and once you’ve both seen it, what happens next is a choice you make together.

To start, each of you can list the things you did this week that nobody saw, then swap lists, read the other one slowly and say one thing on it you hadn’t noticed before. Pick one item from their list and say thank you for it in a specific way. If writing things down isn’t your style, a ten-minute talk over a cup of coffee with the same questions works too. Fixing comes later, once you have both seen the same picture. Who did what (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-01) turns this into a gentle week-long log, and How to say a specific thank-you (spreadloveandacceptance.com/turning-toward) has more ideas.

Limits and cautions

These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If talking about the split ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private hotlines.

A list should never be demanded, checked over your shoulder, or used to keep track of where you go or what you spend. If that is happening, it isn’t a ledger. It’s control, and it’s not your fault. Signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#signs). If you are a counsellor or group leader using this book with others, see For counsellors (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors).
