I

Part Two · Chapter I

Why we get out of tune: communication at home

Why two kind, reasonable people can end up in a tangle neither of them started, and how to get back in step.

In this chapter

  1. The tangle often isn’t about the words
  2. Nearly in step is the noisy part
  3. Three things knock you out of tune
  4. Stress changes your station
  5. Nobody has to be wrong
  6. Get back in tune before you carry on
  7. Go back in with a clear sentence
  8. Small daily check-ins keep you in tune
  9. Faith, culture and family voices
  10. On your own: your side of the tuning
  11. One example, followed through
  12. Common mix-ups

In short

  • A clash is often about how things were said. Pace, tone and urgency can be out of step even when both of you mean well.
  • Nobody has to be wrong. Say that you are out of tune, pause with a time to come back, and slow down.
  • Go back in with one clear sentence that says what happened, how you feel and what you would like.
  • A 90-second daily check-in keeps small drifts small.

Tuesday, 6:40pm

“I said I’d do it.”

“I know, I’m just asking when.”

Four sentences later nobody is talking about the bins any more. Somebody has mentioned last Christmas. Neither of you could point to the moment it turned.

The radio picture in this chapter is my own. The About page on the website describes how, for years, my closest relationships “filled up with static”, with the same misunderstanding arriving again and again, and how what was missing was never care, on either side. It was timing, and a shared way of putting things. This chapter is the shared way.

  1. The tangle often isn’t about the words.

    Two people can each say something perfectly reasonable and still clash, because the tone underneath doesn’t match. Think of two radios slightly out of tune with each other. Together they make a crackle that neither of them was making alone.

    One housemate asks, “Is anyone using the oven tonight?” The other says, “Why, did I leave a mess?” A plain question about a lasagne has been heard as a complaint about a baking tray. After your next small clash, ask yourself whether it was the words or the way they came out. It’s usually the way.

    You could say “I think the words were fine. Something in how we said them got crossed.”

    Dig deeper: the radio static

  2. Nearly in step is the noisy part.

    Radios on very different stations don’t whistle at each other. The whistle comes when they are close but not quite matched, which is why people who know each other well can still clash. Research suggests we check our meaning less with people we’re close to, because we assume they already understand us.

    Two sisters who talk on the phone every day argue about holiday plans far more often than either of them does with the cousins they see once a year at a christening or a funeral. The cousins get spelled out; the sisters get shorthand. With someone close to you, check one meaning today: “Just so I’ve got it right, you mean…?”

    Words you could use “I think I assumed you knew what I meant. Let me say it more clearly.”

    Dig deeper: why close can be noisy

    Tidbit

    Compare your daily rhythms: whose engine runs fast in the morning, and whose at night? Different speeds aren’t wrong, they’re just different.

    Tool: Rhythms side by side spreadloveandacceptance.com/tools/frequency-calibration

  3. Three things knock you out of tune.

    How fast you’re talking is one. Tone is another, as when a simple update is heard as a complaint. The third is how urgent something feels, since “when you get a chance” can mean tonight to one person and some time next week to another. Texts lose most of their tone, which makes urgency especially easy to misread.

    One of two business partners texts “Need to talk” between meetings. The other reads it as a crisis and lies awake until two in the morning running through every possible disaster, including the bank. It turns out to be about the printer. Add a time to your next request, so “at some point” becomes “by Friday”, and an update can say it’s an update.

    Ways to say it “By when would be good?” “Is this an update, or a worry?”

    Dig deeper: pace, tone and urgency

  4. Stress changes your station.

    When you are tense, you may talk faster and be more likely to hear a pause as a snub. When you are tired and flat, your replies get slower and shorter. The Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks), a thirty-second self-check, gives you a best guess at which state you are in.

    A dad gets home from a night shift at the depot and answers his teenage son in single words. “Fine.” “Yep.” “Later.” His son decides he doesn’t care. He’s simply running on empty, and he’d tell you so if he had the words left.

    Words to try “I’m running low right now, and it isn’t about you. Can we talk after I’ve slept?”

    Dig deeper: how stress shifts your tune

  5. Nobody has to be wrong.

    Two radios that both work perfectly will still crackle if they are slightly off, and arguing about whose fault the static is won’t clear it. Retuning will, which just means getting back in step.

    A grandmother tells her grown-up son, at the door, that he looks tired. She means it as care. He hears “you’re not coping”. Both of them are right about what they meant and what they heard, which is exactly why arguing about it goes nowhere. In your next clash, try “we” instead of “you”: “We got crossed there.”

    You could say “I don’t think either of us meant it that way. Can we try that again?”

    Dig deeper: taking the blame out

  6. Get back in tune before you carry on.

    Say out loud that you think you’re out of sync, and check how tense you feel. Either of you can call a pause, and whoever pauses names a time to come back. Slow down, take shorter turns, and only then go back to the actual topic.

    Two roommates in halls agree on a pause word on a calm Sunday, and they pick “static” because it makes them laugh. Three weeks later, in the middle of a row about someone’s music at one in the morning, one of them says it. They stop. They come back at nine the next evening, as agreed, and sort it out in ten minutes. Agree a pause word with someone today, while you’re both calm.

    Words you could use “I need ten minutes. I’ll come back at half past.”

    Dig deeper: the four steps to retune

  7. Go back in with a clear sentence.

    When you return to the topic, say what happened, how you feel and what you’d like, in that order and in one go. “The bins go out early on Wednesday morning. I get anxious when they’re late. Could you put them out tonight?” Or, from one co-parent to another: “The swim kit wasn’t in the bag and I felt stressed at drop-off. Could you pack it on Sunday nights?” It’s worth writing one of these about something small before you need it, so the shape is in your hand when you do.

    Dig deeper: going back in

    Professor Puddles

    When you go back in, one clear sentence beats a speech. This workpaper helps you shape it before you say it.

    Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

  8. Small daily check-ins keep you in tune.

    A short chat each day, like the 90-second daily check-in (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-13-daily-check-in), makes tiny corrections before small things drift into a big argument. Habit research suggests small routines at a regular time are easier to keep than big ones done rarely. The quiet, easy stretches are the ones that drift most, so keep it going even when nothing seems wrong (see Complacency, spreadloveandacceptance.com/complacency).

    A long-distance couple, one in Leeds and one in Toronto, send each other one 90-second voice note every morning. On the weeks they forget, they notice the difference by Thursday, usually as a slightly odd phone call about nothing much.

    Ways to say it “Today I was carrying quite a lot. One thing I liked today was…”

    Pick a time and a cue (straight after dinner works for a lot of people) and try it for three days.

    Dig deeper: staying in tune

Your part, and only your part. You control what you send, whether you check how it landed, and whether you step out to retune. You don’t control how it’s heard or how fast the other person settles. Matching energy here means matching care and effort, never volume: if someone gets louder, you don’t have to follow. Stay at your level, and give the conversation the energy it gives back. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

Saturday, 10am

One of you says the spare room needs clearing out at some point. She meant this month, and he heard today and has already cancelled his plans in his head. By lunchtime you are both upset about a room nobody has touched, and when you stop to ask what “at some point” meant, you find you are still not sure you agree.

zqaxchapterx1xxfaithxcultureqzFaith, culture and family voices

For many couples, faith is where they turn first, and a shared faith can be one of the strongest tools for staying in tune. Praying together, or a quiet moment after worship, can serve as a daily check-in. Some couples each pray on their own before they come back to a hard talk, with the pause still ending at a named time. A pastor, imam, rabbi, priest or trusted elder can be a good first person to talk to, and many can suggest a trained counsellor who shares your faith.

Emeka and Ngozi, married for twenty-six years, do their monthly look-back on a Sunday after church, over lunch. When a talk gets heated, either of them can say, “Let’s pray on it and come back at eight,” and they do.

Culture shapes how you talk too. In many families, respect for elders decides who can speak plainly to whom, and one habit helps a great deal, which is that each of you speaks to your own parents and relatives once you have agreed the message together.

Words to try “Can we pray about this and talk again tonight?” “Mum, we love you, and we’ve thought about it carefully. This year we’ll visit in August instead of at Easter.”

From two faiths or cultures? See Two faiths or cultures, one family (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths). Dig deeper: faith, elders and family far away

On your own: your side of the tuning

Getting out of tune takes two, but retuning can start with one. You can learn your own pace and your own sense of urgency, so you notice when you are the one running fast or slow. Learn your early signs of drifting. A clipped reply is a common one, and so is a sudden need to win. Learn how you take words in best and say it once, as in “I hear things better in writing.” When you drift, step out, settle and come back, which you can do without anyone’s permission. Hamid lives alone and has noticed that his texts to friends come out short when he is tired, so now he waits until morning to answer anything that matters (more in On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

One example, followed through

Cerys, Marisol and Dougie share a house and a car, and two of them talk fast while the third, Dougie, talks slowly. At house meetings Dougie kept getting talked over, and for a while the other two read his silence as agreement. It came out in March, when he said he had never actually agreed to the new car rota. They tried a simple change, a round in which each person speaks once before anyone answers. It felt stilted at first, and Cerys kept wanting to jump in. By the third meeting Dougie was saying more, and the rota he suggested is the one they now use. They still have the occasional evening when the meeting turns into two fast talkers and one quiet one, and someone usually says “round” to reset it. Help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) has pages for many other kinds of shared life.

Common mix-ups

Retuning isn’t giving in. You still come back to the topic, at a time when you can hear each other. Being out of sync doesn’t mean one of you is wrong, either; two fair points in two different tones will still clash. And a pause never means the topic is dropped. A pause always comes with a time to come back, or it isn’t a pause.

To try it, agree on a shared phrase while things are calm, such as “I think we’re out of tune”, so that it works as a signal when you need it. For one week, each of you can note one moment you felt out of step, and at the end you can compare whether it was mostly pace, tone or urgency. Rewind the talk (spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder), Say it so it lands (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-09-say-it-so-it-lands) and the 90-second daily check-in are free on the site.

A limit to keep in mind: These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If talking things through ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private hotlines.

A pause is for both of you. If one person is never allowed to pause, or a “pause” is used to punish with days of silence, that isn’t retuning. Signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#signs).

II

Part Two · Chapter II

Is the split working? A fair look at chores at home

One gentle question: can the way you share the work keep going, or is one of you quietly running on empty?

In this chapter

  1. Look at the month, not last night
  2. Three things go in
  3. Balance: how the hours split
  4. Ownership: does each job have a name?
  5. Stress: how full each stress tank is
  6. One number comes out, from 0 to 1
  7. Start with the biggest shortfall
  8. It judges the setup, never a person
  9. Words this chapter uses
  10. On your own: is your own load working?
  11. One setup, looked at twice
  12. Common mix-ups
  13. Small children and a new baby
  14. If only one of you wants to try this
  15. More for your situation

In short

  • Look at the month, not last night, using what you both wrote down.
  • Three things go in, which are how the hours split, whether each job has a name, and how full each person’s stress tank is.
  • One number comes out, from 0 to 1. Start with whichever part pulled it down most.
  • It judges the setup, never a person, and it is where a talk starts.

Any given week

One of you is quietly doing eleven small things a day that the other has never had to think about: the bin rota, the fish food, the reply to the school, the dentist reminder, the bit of the shopping list that says “bulbs?”. When the other says it feels even, they mean it. From inside their own week, it does.

  1. Look at the month, not last night.

    When people ask whether the split is working, the answer usually comes from whatever happened most recently. This chapter asks a calmer question, using what you both wrote down. Ask it again every few months, even when things seem fine, because a split that worked once can quietly go stale.

    Two housemates had one truly awful week of dishes in May, the kind where you wash a fork to eat with it. The whole month, written down, showed three ordinary weeks and one exam week, which changes the conversation completely. Put a short check in your calendar for about a month from now.

    Dig deeper: what the check is for

    Sugarfoot

    One bad evening isn’t the whole story. Give it a month, then run the check together, slowly, with something to eat.

    Tool: Fair split check: this week spreadloveandacceptance.com/is-the-setup-working

  2. Three things go in.

    The first is how evenly the hours are shared. The second is whether every regular job has a clear owner, from the job list in One owner per job (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-03-one-owner-per-job). The third is how stressed each of you already is from everything else going on. A workpaper is one of the site’s free fill-in worksheets. You don’t need any of them to start; rough notes on the back of an envelope work too.

    You could say “Let’s each bring our own numbers, so neither of us has to guess.”

    Dig deeper: where each number comes from

  3. Balance: how the hours split.

    From your week-long logs, work out each person’s share of the hours. An even split scores 1 and one person doing everything scores 0, whichever person it is. If you have agreed an uneven split that suits you, perhaps because one of you works longer hours outside the home, compare against that split instead. With three or more of you, compare each person’s share with an even share (100 divided by the number of people) or with the split you agreed. Three partners who log 30 hours of home jobs between them, at 15, 9 and 6, would each have 10 as an even share. The “Who does what?” page (spreadloveandacceptance.com/lemonade-stand), where each person lists their hours, does the arithmetic for you.

    Log one week each, and include the small jobs that take under ten minutes. Those are the ones that go missing.

    Dig deeper: the balance score

  4. Ownership: does each job have a name?

    Each job gets two names. The owner does the job from start to finish, and the backstop notices if it slipped and checks in gently, which is very different from supervising. It can be the same person, though a second name gives the job a gentle check. Count the jobs that have an owner and divide by all the jobs on the list, and leave the jobs nobody owns on the list, because they matter most. A decision you make together, such as which school, can be marked “Both (decide together)” and counts as owned, while a job that needs doing gets one name.

    This one comes almost straight from my old job. In audit work, most of the failures I saw weren’t incompetence. They were unclear ownership: work that belongs to everyone belongs to no one, and it quietly lands on whoever notices first. Two sisters care for their dad, and nobody owned his repeat prescription, so for a fortnight each of them thought the other had ordered it. He ran out on a Sunday.

    Words you could use “Can we put a name next to this one, so it doesn’t fall between us?”

    Dig deeper: the ownership score

    Professor Puddles

    A job without a name tends to land on whoever notices first. Write one owner next to each job, and the guessing stops.

    Workpaper WP-03: One owner per job spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-03

  5. Stress: how full each stress tank is.

    Each of you rates how full your own stress tank is with How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying), where a higher score means more stress. Under 0.30 is light, 0.30 up to 0.60 is medium, and 0.60 or more is high. The score uses the average of your two scores, but if either of you is at 0.60 or more, talk about that first, even when the overall result looks fine. A setup that only works when you are both well rested can’t last, so more stress lowers the result. A grandmother raising two grandchildren scores 0.70 while her son, who helps at weekends, scores 0.35. Her 0.70 is the headline, whatever the average says. Each of you scores your own tank on the same day, before looking at the other’s.

    Dig deeper: the stress score

  6. One number comes out, from 0 to 1.

    A result of 0.70 or above reads as working well, meaning the setup is holding. From 0.40 up to 0.70 it reads as needs a look, because something is drifting, often who owns what, and below 0.40 it reads as needs a rethink, together. The result is called the setup score. It is a simple weighted sum, in which the hours count most, then the owners, then stress, and although it looks like a probability it isn’t one. Two friends who run a café together score 0.55, which tells them nothing is broken and something is drifting; it turns out to be the Monday ordering, which both of them assumed the other did. Write the date next to your number, so you can compare next month.

    Dig deeper: the formula and what each range means

  7. Start with the biggest shortfall.

    The single number matters less than which of the three parts pulled it down most. The shortfall is how far one part fell below the most it could add, and in the middle band it is often ownership, which is why the calculator suggests One owner per job first. Separated parents score 0.62 and find that their biggest gap is that nobody owns the school forms, so that is the only thing they change this month.

    Ways to say it “Which part pulled the number down most? Let’s start there.”

    Dig deeper: reading your result

  8. It judges the setup, never a person.

    The number isn’t a verdict on who’s better or whether the relationship works. It’s where a conversation starts, never how one ends. These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If talking about the split ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private hotlines.

    One partner sees 0.35 and says, “So I’m the problem.” The other says no, the bathroom has no owner and he works nights, and they start there. Before you begin, agree that either of you can say “pause” and come back later.

    Dig deeper: what the number is not

Your part, and only your part. The score describes the setup you share, but your levers are your own: your jobs, your hours and what you agree to take on. You can propose a fix; you can’t make the other person accept it. If the balance stays one-sided, step your load back towards your share on purpose, and say so kindly. Matching effort with effort protects your stress tank, and your tank is part of the score too. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

Sunday evening

Two week-long logs and two cups of tea on the table. One list has 31 rows. The other has 18. For a moment nobody says anything, and the fridge hums. Then one of you says, “I honestly didn’t know about half of these.”

Words this chapter uses

A log is a simple list of the jobs you did this week and roughly how long each took. The owner does a job from start to finish, including remembering it, and the backstop notices if a job slipped and checks in gently. Your stress tank is how much stress you are already carrying from the rest of life. The setup is the way you share the work right now, which can always be changed, and the setup score is the one number from 0 to 1 that sums up the three readings. Invisible jobs count too. Planning meals, remembering birthdays, booking the vet and noticing that the soap is running low all belong in your log.

On your own: is your own load working?

You can ask the same question about your own week, which is whether you are spending more energy than comes back. Add up what you carry, jobs and worries both, and set it beside what refills you. If it runs in the red, change your side by dropping, delaying, asking or saying no kindly. A limit describes your supply, and it says nothing about your worth. After a breakup, Leanne has her children every other week and fills the quiet weeks with favours for friends, including one memorable flat-pack wardrobe. Writing it down shows her she never rests (more in On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Words to try “I’d love to help, and I can’t this week. Can I let you know next week?”

One setup, looked at twice

Three people share a flat above a bakery, and everyone agrees that cleaning matters while nobody owns the bathroom. Their first check scores 0.67, and the biggest shortfall is ownership: eight of the twelve jobs have a name, and the bathroom, the bins, the recycling and the hallway don’t. They give each of those four jobs an owner and a backstop. A month later, with the hours and their stress tanks about the same as before, the score is 0.79. Ownership went from 0.67 to 1.00, and that part counts for 0.35 of the score, so it adds 0.12. The bathroom is better and the recycling is still a sore point, because the one who owns it works late on collection night, and that is the job they talk about next. Shift work, illness and caring can all make hours look even while sleep or energy is not, and an uneven split agreed on purpose can be the fair one (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours, and When one of you is ill, spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill).

Common mix-ups

A low number doesn’t mean the relationship is failing. It means the current setup needs changing, and setups change all the time. Please don’t guess the numbers; a guessed number is a feeling with a decimal point, so use your written logs. One of you can’t fill it in for both, either. Each person writes their own log and scores their own stress tank. And fair doesn’t have to mean exactly 50/50. Fair is what you both agree to with your eyes open, and an uneven split you chose together can be the fair one. Two kinds of fair (page 120) looks at this.

zqaxchapterx2xxsmallxchildrenqzSmall children and a new baby

Small children bring a flood of new jobs, and most of them are thinking jobs, such as the nursery bag, the jabs, the party invitations, the next size of clothes and the night wakings. That is why the mental load (see the work nobody sees, page 71) often grows after a baby arrives, usually without anyone deciding it. Log the children’s jobs too, with the thinking time, and count the nights. Hand over whole jobs, such as the clothes and sizes or the GP and the jabs, so that the new owner does the noticing too, in their own way. If a baby is on the way, write your first job list together before the birth, plan the nights and agree to look again at six weeks, at three months and before either of you goes back to work. In the first weeks, share by energy more than by hours, so that whoever was up in the night gets the rest.

Hollie and Gareth have Alfie, who is three, and Poppy, who is eight months old, and Gareth is a paramedic on shifts. Their logged minutes come out nearly even, yet Hollie did almost three-quarters of the jobs nobody asked for. They leave the minutes alone and move one whole job, the children’s clothes, to Gareth.

You could say “Could you own the nursery bag from now on, including noticing when we’re low on nappies? I won’t check it.”

Dig deeper: small children, new babies and shift work

zqaxchapterx2xxonexpersonqzIf only one of you wants to try this

That is common, and you can still start. Log your own week, score your own tank and then share one small thing you noticed, without asking the other person to agree with your numbers. A dad noticed he was spending five hours a week driving his sixteen-year-old to training and back, said so without any accusation, and they agreed on a bus pass for two days a week. His son grumbled for a fortnight and then started enjoying the bus. Share one finding at a time and then let it rest for a few days.

If the other person refuses to talk about the split at all, ever, or makes you feel afraid for raising it, that isn’t a setup problem. Please read Not safe at home?

More for your situation

Money together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together) · Gaming and time together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/gaming-and-time-together) · Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends) · Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts) · Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) · Grandparents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grandparents) · Co-parenting (spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting) · Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home) · Empty nest (spreadloveandacceptance.com/empty-nest) · At work (spreadloveandacceptance.com/work) · For counsellors (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors)

To run the check, each of you first logs one week in Who did what (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-01), because the number only means something if you each wrote your own. Next, fill in the job list in One owner per job together, including any jobs nobody owns yet, and each score your own stress tank on the same day. Put the three numbers into the calculator (spreadloveandacceptance.com/is-the-setup-working), look first at the biggest shortfall, pick one small change together and check again in a month.

III

Part Two · Chapter III

Full tanks and different angles: stress and perspective

Why some reactions are bigger than what caused them, and why two people can see the same moment so differently.

In this chapter

  1. A full tank overflows
  2. Some stress is left over from earlier
  3. Check your stress tank in a minute
  4. Three everyday states
  5. There are seven angles on the same moment
  6. Both views can be true
  7. Say it instead of making each other guess
  8. A full tank means “later,” not “never.”
  9. Words this chapter uses
  10. On your own: reading your own tank
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. Two homes: co-parenting after a split
  13. If only one of you wants to try this
  14. More for your situation

In short

  • A full tank overflows, so stress left over from earlier makes small things feel big.
  • Check your tank in a minute, and say the band out loud so nobody has to guess.
  • Two people can see one moment from different angles, and both views can be true.
  • A full tank means later, so pause, name a time and come back.

Thursday, 5:15pm

They ask, perfectly pleasantly, whether you remembered to call the dentist. Your answer comes out about four sizes bigger than the question deserved, with a bit about the car thrown in, and you can hear it happening while it happens.

  1. A full tank overflows.

    If you’re already tired or stretched from somewhere else, a small question can get a big reaction, which is simply human. Anything decided in that moment is worth coming back to once you have both calmed down. A nurse gets in at eight in the morning after a night shift, and her housemate, eating cornflakes, asks whether she saw his message about the electricity meter. She bites his head off. Twelve hours on her feet did the biting; the meter just came at the end of them.

    You could say “Sorry. That was bigger than the question. I’m running on empty.”

    Dig deeper: how full your tank is

  2. Some stress is left over from earlier.

    Ask yourself how much of this feeling is about the thing in front of you and how much you brought in with you. Being upset about the dishes and being exhausted, with the dishes as the thing you noticed, are different problems. Some of what we bring in is much older, such as an understanding from growing up that whoever notices the mess has to clean it, and if a feeling seems a lot older than the moment, Where your lens came from (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up) helps you find where it started.

    A fourteen-year-old has a horrible day at school, the kind he won’t talk about, comes home and explodes because his brother has taken the phone charger. Again. The charger was the last drop in a tank that was already full at lunchtime.

    Words you could use “I think I brought this in with me. Give me ten minutes.”

    Dig deeper: leftover stress

    Professor Puddles

    Before a hard talk, check how full your own tank is. Five quick questions, about two minutes, and you’ll know whether now is the time.

    Workpaper WP-02: How much are you carrying? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-02

  3. Check your stress tank in a minute.

    How much are you carrying? measures how full your stress tank is, and a higher score means more stress in the tank. Score five things from 0 to 4, which are sleep, work elsewhere, any unsettled argument, how your body feels and time pressure today, then add them up and divide by 20. Under 0.30 is light, 0.30 up to 0.60 is medium and 0.60 or more is high. If it has been high for a long time it can start to feel normal, so a quick reading each week is worth it. A man caring for his wife after her hip operation scores 0.65 three days in a row. That tells him something he hadn’t let himself think, which is that he needs help more than he needs to try harder. He rings his son that evening. Score yourself tomorrow morning, before you look at your phone.

    Dig deeper: the stress-tank score

  4. Three everyday states.

    Knowing whether you are calm and connected, revved up or running on empty tells you whether now is a good time to talk. The Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks), a thirty-second self-check, helps you make a best guess. The labels come from polyvagal theory, whose main claims are still debated by scientists, and here they are used only as everyday words. In one long-distance couple, he takes the video call at midnight his time and is usually running on empty by then, so they move the hard talks to Saturday mornings. It helps to know one body clue for each state; a tight jaw is a common one for revved up.

    Dig deeper: the three states

  5. There are seven angles on the same moment.

    The seven angles are tiredness, time pressure, history, what home was like growing up, your sense of fairness, how you communicate and stress from outside. Many arguments are two people looking from different angles, each sure that the other sees what they see. The “See their side” step of Rewind the talk (spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder) is built on these seven angles and helps you picture how the same moment might look from the other side, with questions to ask in place of guesses. Planning Christmas, one parent sees it from family habit (they always go to her mum’s, and there’s a stocking with each child’s name on it) and the other sees it from fairness, since they went there last year too, and the year before.

    Ways to say it “Which angle are you seeing this from?”

    Dig deeper: the seven angles

  6. Both views can be true.

    You can each be right about what you see and still be looking at different parts of the same thing, so the useful question is which angle each of you is seeing it from. Two adult brothers argue about their late mother’s house. One sees thirty years of memories, the height marks on the kitchen door frame, the apple tree. The other sees a roof that needs £9,000 of work. Both of them are looking at the real house.

    Words to try “You’re right about what you see. Can I tell you what I see?”

    Dig deeper: two true views

  7. Say it instead of making each other guess.

    Before a hard conversation, each of you says how full your stress tank is and which angle you are seeing things from. It works best at the start. Two colleagues begin a tense meeting about a missed deadline with one sentence each about their tank and their angle. It feels a bit odd. The meeting is shorter and calmer than the last one, and nobody cries in the toilets afterwards.

    You could say “Before we start, I’m about half full today, and I’m seeing this from the time angle.”

    Dig deeper: using both together

    Tidbit

    Say your number out loud, as in “I’m about a seven today.” It takes two seconds, and nobody has to guess.

    Tool: My weather today spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

  8. A full tank means “later,” not “never.”

    A high score is a reason to pause and never a way out of the talk. Say when you will come back, and let the Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11) help in the meantime. After your calming steps, check your tank again. Under 0.50, go back at the time you said. From 0.50 to 0.59, take another round if you still feel hot, and if you are still at 0.60 or more after two rounds, pick a new time and say when. A dad and his fourteen-year-old get heated about phone time. He tells her he’s too wound up and will talk at seven. At seven he knocks on her door, which matters more than anything he says once he’s inside.

    Words you could use “I need a break. I’ll come back at seven. I promise.”

    Dig deeper: pausing without avoiding

Your part, and only your part. Your stress tank is the only one you can empty. You can’t calm someone else’s tank for them, and pouring yours into theirs leaves two empty tanks. Protect yours: rest, say “later,” and give energy where it’s met. When both tanks are full, the kindest thing you control is the timing. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

Monday morning

You both look at the same pile of post on the kitchen table, eleven envelopes and a pizza menu. One of you sees a to-do list, and the other sees proof that nobody else ever opens the post. You try saying your angles out loud, and it helps for about a minute before the old argument about the gas bill comes back. The pile is still there at lunchtime, and neither of you has decided whose it is.

Words this chapter uses

Your stress tank is how much stress you are already carrying before this moment even starts. Leftover stress is the part of a feeling you brought in from somewhere else, like poor sleep or a hard day, while this-moment stress is caused by what is in front of you right now. An angle is the point of view you are seeing a moment from, such as tiredness or fairness.

On your own: reading your own tank

On your own, the most useful habit is a one-minute reading of your tank before you react. Check it for a few mornings in a row and look for a pattern, ask yourself before a hard moment how much of it is left over from earlier, and decide on a calm day what settles you so that it is ready when you need it. Living alone after a breakup, Bryony noticed that she snapped at her sister on the phone every Monday. Her morning readings showed why: Sunday nights were her worst sleep of the week, every week. Now she asks for Tuesday instead (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Common mix-ups

A big reaction sometimes means it was a big deal. Quite often it means the tank was already full. A high score is never an excuse, either; it’s a note to come back later, never a pass to skip the talk. You can’t tell how full someone else’s tank is, however well you know them, which is why each person scores only themselves. And a pause isn’t the silent treatment, because a pause has a time to come back. That’s why you always say when.

zqaxchapterx3xxtwoxhomesqzTwo homes: co-parenting after a split

Children carry two homes, and changeover day fills their tank, so being quiet, clingy or cross for a few hours after a handover is common and usually says nothing bad about the other home. It helps to give them landing time, with a snack, something familiar and no questions about the other home for the first hour. The child is never the messenger, because adult news goes adult to adult. For money, follow any formal arrangement. Split the extras by a ratio you agree, and settle up once a month from one list. With an ex, share the band and keep the story, as in “I’m in a heavy week. Could we swap Wednesday?”, and your private life stays yours. If an ex won’t cooperate but isn’t dangerous, parallel parenting can work, with written messages only, short and business-like, handovers at school and your own list for your own home. When there are new partners, the parent stays the owner of anything involving the other home, and a step-parent starts as a friendly adult rather than the one who tells the children off.

Harriet gives Freya, who is eight, and Arlo, who is five, an hour of toast and blankets when they come back from their dad’s, and she has stopped asking what happened at Dad’s at the front door. Sunday evenings are calmer, though Arlo still cries at bedtime on changeover days, and she is waiting to see whether that eases.

Words you could use (a business-like message) “Hi Dylan. Freya’s school trip is on 6 November and costs £24. I’ve paid it and put it on the extras list. Thanks, Harriet.”

If you are afraid of your ex, a shared plan isn’t the right tool: see Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) Dig deeper: two homes, money and step-parents

If only one of you wants to try this

You can do all of this on your own side, by checking your own tank, naming your own angle and pausing and coming back on time. The other person doesn’t have to use the words for it to help, and when one person starts saying it out loud, the other often starts to as well. A daughter visits her dad every Sunday, and every week they clash over his health. She starts each visit by saying she is a bit tired today, so if she goes quiet it isn’t about him. He never scores anything himself, and still the visits get calmer, and one Sunday he says, unprompted, “I’m a bit tired today as well, love.”

A note on safety: A full tank explains a reaction. It never excuses shouting, threats or hurting anyone. If someone’s “stress” often turns into fear for you, that isn’t a tank problem. These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If sharing how you feel ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? lists free, private hotlines.

More for your situation

Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends) · Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) · Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts) · Co-parenting (spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting) · Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home) · When one of you is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill) · Long distance (spreadloveandacceptance.com/long-distance) · Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room) · Gaming and time together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/gaming-and-time-together) · For counsellors (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors)

Before your next hard conversation, score the five things in How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying), add them up and divide by 20, then say one sentence out loud about your tank and your angle. If either of you scores 0.60 or more, put off anything that doesn’t need deciding in the next hour, and agree on a time to come back.

IV

Part Two · Chapter IV

Two kinds of fair: equal vs fair at home

Agree on what “fair” means before you argue about it, and give a comment a moment to land before you answer it.

In this chapter

  1. There are two kinds of fair
  2. Fair by results
  3. Fair by promises
  4. Once a job has an owner, look to the owner
  5. Covering is kind. Say it out loud
  6. Let a comment land before you react
  7. Notice, name, decide
  8. Keep the two questions apart
  9. On your own: your own kind of fair
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. Money between you
  12. A couple and a housemate
  13. More for your situation
  14. A note on safety

In short

  • There are two kinds of fair, by results (did it all get done?) and by promises (did each of us do what we agreed?), so agree which one you are using.
  • Once a job has an owner, look to the owner, and when you cover for someone, say so out loud.
  • Let a comment land before you react by noticing it, naming it and then deciding what to say.
  • Keep the two questions apart, because whether the job was done is a fact and whether the comment hurt is a feeling.

The same argument, twice a month

One of you counts hours. The other counts who noticed that the job needed doing in the first place. You’re both counting honestly, in two different currencies, and then arguing about the exchange rate, usually on a Sunday evening, usually about the oven.

  1. zqaxchapterx4xxextwoxkindsqz

    There are two kinds of fair.

    One kind asks whether everything got done, and the other asks whether each person did what they said they would. Both are reasonable, and friction starts when each of you is using a different one without realising. Nisha and Kezia share a room in halls. Nisha thinks a week was fair if the room is tidy by Friday, whoever tidied it. Kezia thinks it was fair if each of them kept her own half clean. For most of the first term they each think the other is being unreasonable, and neither of them is.

    You could say “When you say fair, do you mean it all gets done, or that we each do our bit?”

    Dig deeper: the two kinds of fair

  2. Fair by results.

    This kind of fair judges by outcomes, by whether the right things got done by whoever had the time or energy. It is flexible and easy-going. Done carefully it counts the cost to whoever covered, and done carelessly it can hide who is always stepping in. A grandmother raising her grandchildren has a grown-up son who helps with whatever is needed when he’s home, cheerfully and well. The house runs. And she is always, always the one who notices what is needed. For one week, mark every job you picked up that wasn’t planned; the tally is often a surprise.

    Dig deeper: judging by results

  3. Fair by promises.

    This kind asks whether each person did the jobs they agreed to own. It is clear and steady, and it can feel rigid in a week when life gets in the way. Two business partners run a café. One owns the ordering, the other owns the staff rota. When the rota is late (it’s the Thursday before a bank holiday, it’s always late then) they ask the rota owner about it, rather than “the team”, and nobody takes it personally.

    Words you could use “It’s my job, and I can’t do it this week. Could you take it, and I’ll take the bins?”

    Dig deeper: judging by promises

  4. Once a job has an owner, look to the owner.

    The owner is the person who does the job from start to finish. A second name on the list is a backstop, who notices if it slipped and checks in gently without supervising, and it can be the same person. If the job is yours, the question is whether you did it, and somebody quietly covering for you doesn’t answer it. That protects the person who keeps filling the gaps. In one stepfamily the thirteen-year-old owns feeding the dog and his stepmum is the second name. When the bowl is empty at seven, she says “Dog’s dinner?” once, without doing it for him and without a lecture.

    Dig deeper: agreeing which kind you’ll use

  5. Covering is kind. Say it out loud.

    Helping out when the owner can’t is lovely, and it helps to mention it, so that the help is seen, as in “I put the bins out this week, since you were away.” Help that stays silent turns into unseen work, and unseen help slowly becomes expected (see Complacency, spreadloveandacceptance.com/complacency). Two grown-up sisters take turns driving their dad to his appointments. When one covers for the other, she texts the same day: “Took Dad on Thursday, you were on lates. All fine, bloods normal.” It takes ten seconds and it stops the help from going invisible.

    Dig deeper: covering without resentment

    Sugarfoot

    Covering for someone is kind. Say that you did, gently, and ask for what you’d like next time, so it doesn’t turn into quiet resentment.

    Tool: Small wins: Flip it spreadloveandacceptance.com/small-wins

  6. zqaxchapterx4xxexlandqz

    Let a comment land before you react.

    When a remark hits harder than it should, say “Give me a second.” The idea is borrowed loosely from brain science, where the brain turns down sounds and sensations automatically in a fraction of a second, while this pause is a few seconds you choose to take on purpose. Let the spike pass, then decide whether the remark needs an answer now or later, or at all. A nurse comes down at two in the afternoon after a night shift and her husband says, “Oh, you’re up.” She hears “at last”. She says she needs a second because she’s very tired, and it turns out he meant he was glad to see her and had saved her the last of the soup (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours). Agree your own “give me a second” phrase today, while things are calm.

    Dig deeper: giving a comment time to land

    Professor Puddles

    When a comment stings, give it a minute to land before you answer. This workpaper is a short check for your reply.

    Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

  7. Notice, name, decide.

    First notice that a comment landed hard, then name it kindly, as in “That hit harder than you probably meant,” and once you have settled, decide how to reply. Say it so it lands (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-09-say-it-so-it-lands) helps with the words. A fifteen-year-old tells her dad that he never listens. He feels his chest tighten. He says that stings, and that he wants to hear her properly, and he decides it needs a real talk, the next evening, after her swimming, in the car, which is where they talk best.

    Ways to say it “I want to answer that, just not this minute. Can we talk at eight?”

    Dig deeper: the three steps

  8. Keep the two questions apart.

    Whether the job was done is a question about a fact, and whether the comment hurt is a question about a feeling. Both matter, and each goes better in its own conversation. Separated parents share their children across two homes, and the bag comes back without the school shoes, along with a text about it that felt cold. They sort out the shoes first and talk about the text on Sunday (see Co-parenting, spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting). When a talk tangles, “Fact or feeling?” is a good question to ask out loud, and then you finish one before starting the other.

    Dig deeper: facts and feelings, separately

Your part, and only your part. You control whether, when and how you bring something up, and whether you cover a job out loud. How the other person responds is theirs. If you cover again and again with no thanks and no change, match the energy: cover less, and say so kindly. Fair by promises only works when both people keep theirs. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

The weekly catch-up

Sam and Alex share a home. Alex owns the bins but works late on Tuesdays, and Sam has quietly taken them out three weeks running. At the catch-up Sam mentions it, and Alex admits that Tuesday nights aren’t realistic with the late shifts. They agree to try a swap for the rest of the month, with Sam taking the bins and Alex taking the recycling and the weekly grocery order, and to settle it at the monthly look-back in Chapter V (page 136).

Wednesday, 7pm

“Thanks for doing the dishes,” one of you says, a little flatly. It was meant as a thank-you. It sounded like a criticism. Before you know it you’ve replied to the criticism, and the person who said thank you is now defending a thank-you.

On your own: your own kind of fair

Fair starts with knowing what it means to you and which jobs are truly yours. Write down what fair means to you in one sentence, and list the jobs you own alongside the ones you picked up without ever agreeing to. Olu lives alone and has his children every other weekend. His sentence, after some crossing out, is that fair means not doing their jobs for them just because he misses them (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). Pick one job you took on without agreeing, and either keep it on purpose or raise it on a calm day.

Common mix-ups

If it got done, there may still be a problem, because someone may be paying for it in time and energy. Holding the owner to the job isn’t being strict; it’s keeping the agreement you both made, which is kinder than quiet resentment. Letting a comment land doesn’t mean ignoring it. It’s about timing, and you still get to answer. And please don’t save up months of covering to bring out all at once. A long list lands like a bill. Mention covering as it happens.

zqaxchapterx4xxmoneyqzMoney between you

Money is where the two kinds of fair meet most often. Some couples put everything into one pot. Some keep their money separate and pay agreed bills, often half each, which is fair by promises, the same rule for both. Others each pay into a shared pot in line with what they earn and keep the rest, which is fair by results, since each is left with a similar share. Many couples mix them, with a joint account for bills and food and some money each that nobody has to explain. The right way is the one you both chose with your eyes open. To talk about it, start with your money stories, how money worked at home when you were growing up, then move on to the numbers and to a “talk first” amount for big purchases that applies to both of you. A limit you both chose and both keep is care, not control.

Niamh takes home £2,600 a month and Tariq £1,900, and their rent and bills will be £1,500. They split it 58/42, in line with their pay, so she pays £870 and he pays £630.

Words to try “Can we each say how money worked in our families growing up?” “Would half each, or in line with our pay, feel fairer to you?”

Dig deeper: money, step by step

zqaxchapterx4xxhousemateqzA couple and a housemate

A couple sharing a home with a housemate who isn’t a partner is a different shape from three equals. It helps to keep two lists, house jobs for all three of you, such as the bins, the bathroom, the bills and the landlord, and couple jobs for the two of you. Decide house questions with all three of you there, rather than in bed the night before, hear the housemate first on anything that affects them, keep couple arguments out of shared rooms and never ask them to referee. Ollie and Hamza share a flat with their friend Bex. They split the rent by room, since the couple has the bigger one, and the bills by person, and all three hold a short house meeting on the first Sunday of the month, with biscuits, which Bex insists is the only reason she comes.

You could say “That’s a house question. Let’s decide it when Bex is here.”

Dig deeper: two lists, and money with three

More for your situation

Each of these pages takes the ideas in this chapter into one kind of relationship. Start from your relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) lists them all.

  • Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends) · More than two partners (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two) · Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room) · Money together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together)
  • Foster and kinship families (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship) · When a child has ADHD (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids) · Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) · Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts)
  • Different hours · Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home) · When one is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill) · Two faiths (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths) · On my own

On a calm, easy day, each of you can say which kind of fair comes more naturally, results or promises. Then pick three regular jobs and write an owner for each in the job list in One owner per job (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-03-one-owner-per-job), with a second name for someone who notices if it slips. Finally, agree a short phrase for when something lands hard, such as “Give me a second”, along with the promise that the person who asked for a second will come back to it.

A note on safety

These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If talking about what’s fair ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private hotlines.

A promise is something both people chose and either can ask to change. Rules one person sets for the other, with checking, punishment or money held back, are control, and that is not your fault. See normal limits and control (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together#control).

Words you could use, with someone you trust “Things at home don’t feel fair, and I’m scared to bring it up. Can I talk it through with you?”

V

Part Two · Chapter V

The monthly look-back: a calm relationship check-in

Once a month, look back for the problems that keep coming back, and fix the setup instead of having the same argument again.

In this chapter

  1. Weekly check-ins miss patterns
  2. You need four weeks of notes and one list
  3. Mark an ✗ for each week a job slipped
  4. A problem that keeps coming back usually has no real owner
  5. Sort each repeat into one of three kinds
  6. Count the gaps each month
  7. Look back even when nothing is slipping
  8. It’s not a review of either person
  9. Keep it short and kind
  10. A look-back, three months in
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. Starting out: before you move in
  13. Raising a grandchild (kinship care)
  14. More for your situation
  15. On your own: a monthly look at yourself

The third Tuesday in a row

The bins again. You could have the same ten-minute back-and-forth about Tuesday that you had last Tuesday, word for word, or you could notice that this has now happened three Tuesdays running and wonder what it is about Tuesdays.

  1. Weekly check-ins miss patterns.

    One missed job looks like bad luck. The same job missed week after week is a pattern, and patterns are easiest to see when you look at the whole month. The look-back is a careful, friendly glance over that month, closer to a self-check than an inspection.

    Four flatmates had an overflowing bathroom bin every week, and every week it seemed like bad luck, until they looked at the month together and saw it had happened every single week since September. In my old job the step that got skipped more than any other was going back afterwards to check that the fix had actually held, and skipping it is exactly how the same problem turns up again three years later. This chapter is that step, made small. Choose a monthly date now, the last Sunday, say, and put it in everyone’s calendar.

    Dig deeper: why once a month

  2. You need four weeks of notes and one list.

    Bring the month’s four weekly notes from Who did what (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-01), where a few lines a week is enough, and your job list from One owner per job (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-03-one-owner-per-job). Twenty minutes is usually enough. If either of your stress tanks is high that day, at 0.60 or more on How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying), move it a day or two. A couple on different shifts keep their weekly notes in one shared note on their phones and do the look-back on the one evening a month they’re both off, with a takeaway, which has become the part they look forward to.

    Dig deeper: getting ready

  3. Mark an ✗ for each week a job slipped.

    A job slipped if it was noticed and not done, only done after being raised more than once, or quietly covered by someone who isn’t its owner. Look closely at every job with two or more ✗, because three or four in a month is a real pattern. Two foster carers find the reading log was missed three weeks out of four. They mark the ✗ in pencil, together, before either of them explains anything, which is harder than it sounds and much the best order.

    Dig deeper: gathering the month’s notes

  4. A problem that keeps coming back usually has no real owner.

    Such a problem gets patched every week and never fixed. The owner is the person who does the job from start to finish, so the fix is to give the job one owner whose name sticks, or to talk honestly about whether anyone has the time and energy for it. In a home with three partners, “whoever’s free” does the online grocery order, and it was late three times this month. With nobody owning it, everybody assumed someone else had it. One Friday there was no milk at all, and four jars of mustard.

    Dig deeper: spotting the gaps that keep reopening

  5. Sort each repeat into one of three kinds.

    If a job has no clear owner, update the job list. If its owner can’t keep up, have a kind, honest talk. If there was a short-term cause, like a bout of flu, note it and move on. Separated parents looking at the missed homework folder ask whether nobody was sure which home signs it, whether one of them is swamped, or whether it was simply the week she had flu (see Co-parenting, spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting).

    Dig deeper: sorting each gap

  6. Count the gaps each month.

    Write down how many gaps of each kind you found. If the number of jobs with no clear owner falls over several months, the setup is working, and a single month can be a normal swing. If it keeps rising, something bigger has changed and it is worth a talk. Two business partners write their monthly count on a whiteboard in the back office, next to the fire-drill notice. In March four jobs had no clear owner. By June, one did, and they argue cheerfully about whose fault that one is.

    Dig deeper: keeping count

    Professor Puddles

    The look-back has its own workpaper: a month of notes, one list, and an ✗ for each week a job slipped. It makes a pattern easy to see.

    Workpaper WP-04: What keeps coming back? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-04

  7. Look back even when nothing is slipping.

    A month with no gaps is good news, and it is also the month most likely to go unchecked. When something has worked for a while, people stop looking, and nothing breaks on the day that happens. Keep the look-back going in quiet months and add one question, “What’s something we’ve stopped noticing or mentioning?”, which is how a look-back guards against complacency (spreadloveandacceptance.com/complacency). The children have left home and nothing at all is slipping. At the look-back one of them says, quietly, that they don’t really talk at dinner any more. No list would have shown that.

    Dig deeper: the quiet months

  8. It’s not a review of either person.

    You don’t add up old hours or punish old mistakes. You can thank someone for what they carried before, and you leave the past unbilled. The only question is where the setup isn’t working yet and what you will try next month. After a month in hospital, one partner comes home to a long list of what slipped. They thank each other for what each carried, and set up the month ahead, and that’s all.

    Dig deeper: what the look-back is for, and what it isn’t

    Tidbit

    A look-back can start with something that went well. Name it first. The weekly card has a nice way to begin.

    Tool: Kitchen-table check-in spreadloveandacceptance.com/check-ins

  9. Keep it short and kind.

    Start with something that went well and talk about the job instead of the person. If a gap needs a proper talk, set it for another day using Check-ins (spreadloveandacceptance.com/check-ins). If a talk starts going badly, either of you can call a pause, and whoever paused names a time to come back. A mum and two teenagers hold their look-back over pizza on the last Friday. Each says one good thing first (the younger one’s is always “the pizza”), one gap gets a new owner, and it’s over in fifteen minutes.

    Dig deeper: how to talk about a pattern

Your part, and only your part. In the look-back you can only fix the gaps you own, and offer help with the rest. You can’t make someone keep a rhythm. Keep the rhythms you can keep, notice which ones are kept in return, and let your effort follow: more where it’s shared, less where it isn’t, so the rhythm doesn’t run on one person’s energy. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

The last Sunday of the month

Two mugs of tea, four weeks of notes, twenty minutes. You go down the list together. Most weeks went fine. Two jobs keep coming up, the recycling and the call to the landlord about the window, so you give each of them a name and finish your tea while it’s still warm, for once.

A look-back, three months in

Sam and Alex’s bins slipped three weeks in a row because Alex works late on Tuesdays. After the trial swap they make it official, so Sam owns the bins and Alex takes the recycling and the weekly grocery order, which keeps the hours even. The second month is clean. In the third, the grocery order slips twice, both times in a week when Alex’s mother was in hospital, and they mark it as a one-off and leave the list alone. What changes in month three is that Alex mentions, almost in passing, that he has stopped enjoying their Saturday mornings, which no list had shown, and they agree to talk about it properly on Thursday.

You could say “I don’t think anyone dropped this. I think nobody ever picked it up.”

Common mix-ups

This isn’t where you settle who owes what. Past hours are never billed to anyone, though you can still say thank you for them; you only fix the setup going forward. A slipped job doesn’t mean its owner failed, either, because the gap might be in the list, or in the owner’s capacity, or in one strange week. And you can’t skip the weekly notes and just do this. The look-back only works if the weekly notes feed it.

A note on safety: These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If looking back together ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private hotlines.

A look-back is something you both choose. If one person demands logs of the other’s every hour, checks their phone without agreement, or uses the ✗ marks to punish, that is control, not a look-back, and it is not your fault. See Not safe at home? and normal limits and control (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together).

zqaxchapterx5xxmovingxinqzStarting out: before you move in

If you are new together and about to share a home, the tools work best now, before habits set, at about one step a week. In the first week, each of you writes down the rulebook from the home you grew up in (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up) and then you swap, with curiosity. In the second, talk about money, starting with your money stories and moving on to the split (Chapter IV, page 133). In the third, write your first job list, with one owner per job and the thinking jobs included (One owner per job, spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/fill/wp-03), and in the fourth, make a pause plan (spreadloveandacceptance.com/pursue-withdraw) on a calm day. In the fifth, each name three things that matter most to you about a home (Part Three, Chapter 10, page 280). After the move, log one ordinary week once two weeks have passed, and do your first short look-back after four. None of it is a test, and the point is that neither of you has to guess.

Niamh and Tariq, eight months together, find that their families meant different things by “tidy”, and they agree on the kitchen every night and the rest on Sunday.

Dig deeper: the plan, week by week

zqaxchapterx5xxkinshipqzRaising a grandchild (kinship care)

Many grandparents and other relatives raise a child whose parents can’t, and much of it involves things that keep coming back, such as cancelled calls and the hard evenings after contact. A monthly look-back helps. Some repeats you can own, and some, like a parent who misses calls, you can’t, and for those you can own the plan for the evening after. The child may love both the parent who can’t look after them and you, so tell them they don’t have to choose, and don’t run the parent down in front of them. Explain an absent parent in short, true words that fit their age, always with the message that it isn’t their fault. When the parent is your own adult child and things are hard between you, keep messages about the child short and civil for the child’s sake, and leave the door open. Look after yourself too. Ask for respite, and find other kinship carers. In England and Wales, the charity Kinship (kinship.org.uk) can help.

Maureen, who is sixty-three, is raising her grandson Tyler, who is nine. Her look-back shows that his mum’s Sunday call fell through three times this month, so she plans those evenings with hot chocolate and his football annual, and asks her brother to take Tyler swimming on Sunday afternoons.

Words you could use, with the child “Mum loves you. She isn’t well enough to look after you right now, and that’s not your fault.”

Dig deeper: loyalty, explaining by age, and rifts with your adult child

More for your situation

A look-back works in every kind of relationship, with small changes. Start from your relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) lists pages for each one.

  • More than two partners (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two) · Money together · Gaming and time together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/gaming-and-time-together) · Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room)
  • Foster and kinship families (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship) · When a child has ADHD (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids) · Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) · Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts) · Kids grown and gone (spreadloveandacceptance.com/empty-nest)
  • Different hours (spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours) · Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home) · When one is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill) · Two faiths (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths) · On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own) · For counsellors (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors)

On your own: a monthly look at yourself

Once a month, look back at your own month kindly, more like a weather report than a scorecard. Ask what filled your battery and what drained it, which of your limits held and which slipped, and choose one small thing to keep and one to change. Gillian lives on her own after a divorce, and her look-back shows the same ✗ three weeks running: she skipped her Thursday swim to answer work emails. So she moves the emails to Friday morning and keeps the swim (see On my own).

To begin, put a relaxed twenty-minute date in the calendar once a month and keep your weekly notes somewhere you can both find them. At the look-back, start by naming one thing that went well, and end by writing down how many gaps of each kind you found, so that over the next few months you can see whether the number is falling. What keeps coming back? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-04-what-keeps-coming-back) is the workpaper for that conversation.

That’s the end of Part Two. The book goes on in Part Three: Understanding people (page 152), chapters on how people work, for anyone. To put Parts One and Two into practice first, try the six-week program (spreadloveandacceptance.com/prog-01): six gentle weeks, with one chapter and one small tool each week.

What to remember

  • Weekly check-ins miss patterns.
  • Mark an ✗ for each week a job slipped.
  • Sort each repeat into one of three kinds.
  • Look back even when nothing is slipping.
  • Keep it short and kind.
