Part Three · Chapter 6

Habits and change: why change is hard and how small steps work

Why it’s so hard to change, even when we really want to, and what actually helps: small steps, a kinder setup, patience with slips, and remembering that other people’s change belongs to them.

In this chapter

  1. Change is hard for good reasons
  2. Habits run on cues
  3. Start smaller than feels useful
  4. Change the setup, not just your willpower
  5. Being in two minds is normal
  6. Slips are part of change
  7. Change sticks when it fits who you want to be
  8. You can support change, but not force it
  9. In everyday life
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. When to get more help
  13. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In short

  • Change is hard for good reasons. Habits save effort, so the old way is always the easy way.
  • A small step and a kind setup outlast willpower. Make the first step tiny and change what is around you.
  • Slips are part of change. A missed day tells you something about the plan and nothing about your character.
  • Other people’s change is theirs. You can support it, though you can’t force it.

Monday, 7:05am

The plan was a walk before work. The trainers are by the door. Somehow the phone is in your hand instead, and at 7:40 you’re still scrolling, past a video of a man restoring a rusty axe, next to a cup of coffee that went cold twenty minutes ago. By evening a quiet voice is telling you that you never stick to anything. What you actually ran into this morning was a habit with years of practice behind it, and it won.

This chapter is the reason several tools in these books are so small. One small step a week (Part One, Next, page 50) starts smaller than feels useful and decides ahead of time. The setup score and One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, page 88) change the setup rather than asking anyone for more willpower. And What keeps coming back? (Part Two, Chapter V, page 136) treats a repeat as information about the plan, because slips are a normal part of changing anything.

  1. Change is hard for good reasons.

    Much of what we do each day runs on autopilot. That saves energy, and it’s the whole reason habits exist. The downside is that the old way is always quicker and easier than the new one, so change asks your brain to do something effortful again and again, for weeks, until the new way becomes the easy one.

    Jodie wants to stop snapping at her children in the morning rush, and she means it every night. Every morning the same rush brings the same snap, somewhere between the lost reading book and the cold toast, because the morning has worn a groove deeper than her good intentions.

    Things to tell yourself “This is hard because it’s a habit.” “Old grooves take time to fill in.”

    Pick one thing you’d like to change and write down when it usually happens, where, and what’s going on just before. That’s the start of the next idea.

    Dig deeper: why change is hard

  2. Habits run on cues.

    Most habits have a trigger: a time, a place, a feeling, a person, or the thing you’ve just done. The cue starts the routine, and some kind of reward (relief, comfort, a little buzz) keeps it going. Once you know the cue, you can plan for it.

    A man notices that he reaches for the biscuit tin the moment he opens his laptop after dinner, hungry or not. The laptop is the cue. So he starts making a pot of tea before he opens it, and the biscuits, mostly, stay in the tin. For three days, each time your habit happens, jot down the time, the place, the feeling and what you were doing just before.

    Things to tell yourself “What happened right before I did that?” “What was I getting from it?”

    Dig deeper: cues and routines

  3. Start smaller than feels useful.

    Big goals are inspiring but easy to drop. Tiny steps feel almost silly, and they work because they are easy enough to do on a bad day. It helps to tie the new step to something you already do, as in “After I put the kettle on, I’ll…”, and to grow it only once it has stuck.

    Two housemates want a tidier kitchen. They’ve been promising each other a big Sunday clean since March, and it has happened once. So they agree instead that after dinner each of them wipes one surface. It takes two minutes. By the second week the hob has stopped being a source of tension, and by the fourth somebody has descaled the kettle without being asked.

    You could say “Let’s start with something tiny, and see if it sticks.” “After I ..., I will ...”

    Dig deeper: why small steps work

  4. Change the setup, not just your willpower.

    Willpower runs low when you’re tired or hungry. Your surroundings stay the same all day. So make the new habit easier, by putting it in sight or getting things ready the night before, and make the old one a little harder, by moving it out of reach or adding a step. I’d back a small change to the setup over a big push of effort almost every time.

    A teenager wants to sleep better and has tried for weeks to stop scrolling in bed. Then he starts charging his phone in the kitchen overnight, next to the bread bin, and within a week he’s asleep before midnight most nights. He grumbles about it. He also keeps doing it.

    Words you could use (to yourself or a partner) “What could we change about the setup so this gets easier?”

    Dig deeper: shaping your setup

    Professor Puddles

    Changing the setup is often easier than changing a person. At home, that can be as simple as one owner for each job.

    Workpaper WP-03: One owner per job spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-03

  5. Being in two minds is normal.

    Part of you wants to change and part of you doesn’t, and the reluctant part usually has its reasons. The old habit may give comfort, or protect you from something. Pushing harder against that part rarely works, while listening to it often does.

    Asif wants to drink less, but he also loves Friday evenings in the pub with his team. When he asks himself what Friday gives him, the answer is friends, laughter and a way to unwind, so he keeps the Friday and switches to alcohol-free after the first pint. Nobody at the table notices, or if they do, nobody says.

    Thoughts you could try “What does the old habit give me?” “What would make the change worth it to me?”

    Try two lists, one of what you like about how things are and one of what you’d like about changing. Both lists are allowed, and the first one is usually more honest.

    Dig deeper: readiness and mixed feelings

  6. Slips are part of change.

    Nearly everyone who changes something slips back sometimes, and one slip doesn’t undo your progress. What often does the damage is the thought that follows, the “I’ve blown it, so why bother?” Treating yourself kindly after a slip makes it more likely that you will start again.

    After three calm weeks, a dad shouts at his son over homework. That night he sits on the end of the bed and says, “I shouted, and I’m sorry. I’m working on it.” The next evening they do the homework at the kitchen table with the radio on, and nobody raises their voice.

    Things to tell yourself “A slip is one moment out of many.” “What made today harder, and what can I plan for next time?”

    Decide now, while things are going well, what you’ll do after a slip: one kind sentence to yourself, and one small step to start again.

    Dig deeper: slips and starting again

    Tidbit

    A slip is a stumble, not a fall. Try the tiny step again tomorrow. A game for small kind acts can make the practising easier.

    Tool: Gentle games: the Re-check Drive (calm football) spreadloveandacceptance.com/recheck-drive

  7. Change sticks when it fits who you want to be.

    Change made only to please others, or out of shame, is hard to keep. Change that connects to what you care about, to the kind of person you want to be, has deeper roots, and each small action becomes a vote for that person.

    A woman who keeps meaning to be better at keeping in touch starts thinking of herself as someone who shows up for her friends. Sending one voice note on a Sunday evening becomes part of who she is, and some weeks it turns into an hour on the phone.

    Things to tell yourself “Who am I becoming with this step?” “This matters to me because...”

    Dig deeper: values and who you’re becoming

  8. You can support change, but not force it.

    It is natural to want the people we love to change, perhaps to drink less or look after themselves better. Their change belongs to them, though, and pressure tends to make people dig in. It helps more to say clearly what you need, ask what would help, and notice their small steps out loud.

    A colleague keeps missing deadlines. His teammate has the lecture about being organised all ready to go, and skips it. She asks what would make the handover easier, and the two of them set up a shared checklist that he now updates every Friday before lunch.

    Ways to say it “I can’t change this for you, but I’d love to help if you want me to.” “I noticed you did that this week. That really helped.”

    Dig deeper: change with other people

Two weeks later, 7:05am

The trainers are still by the door, but the phone charges in the kitchen overnight now, and the plan has shrunk to shoes on and out to the end of the road. Some mornings that is all you manage. Most mornings it turns into a walk past the allotments and back. On the Thursday you miss, the voice starts up again, and you tell it that tomorrow you will get as far as the end of the road.

In everyday life

Take one couple who want to spend less time on their phones in the evening. Earlier attempts failed because each of them watched the other, so this time they agree on a basket by the door where both phones go at nine, with one exception for whoever is on call for an elderly parent. The first week is awkward, and on the Wednesday one of them sneaks a look at the football scores. By the third week the basket has become part of the furniture, and the evenings have a shape again, with a film, a crossword or an early night.

Big life changes, a move or a new baby, break old routines, which is disruptive and also a good moment to start new habits. If you have ADHD, make the cue impossible to miss, do the step the moment it appears and make the reward come straight away. Expect the novelty to wear off, and swap the method when it does instead of blaming yourself. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-6-change-in-depth).

On your own: a kind plan for change

If you are working on something alone, the ideas fit into one small plan. Choose one change, the one that would make the most difference or the one that feels most doable. Give it one cue, written as “After I ___, I will ___.” Make one tweak to your setup so it is easier to start, decide on the smallest version you could still do on a tired day, and write down one kind sentence to use after a slip. The self path (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) and Know yourself, next (page 50) walk through this step by step.

Common mix-ups

“If I really wanted it, I’d just do it” is the cruellest of these, and it’s wrong. Wanting is only the start; habits, setup, tiredness and stress all have a vote. Then there’s the famous 21 days. There’s no magic number. In one study, led by Phillippa Lally (2010), it took about two months on average, with a very wide range. Being hard on yourself doesn’t keep you on track either. Harshness tends to make people give up, and kindness makes it easier to try again. And routines don’t have to mean being rigid. For a lot of people, autistic people especially, routines are what make life manageable, and change can respect that.

If you want to help someone else with this

Ask before you advise, perhaps with “Would ideas help, or would you rather just talk it through?”, and help them find their own reasons by asking what would be different for them if this changed. Practical help with the setup (a lift to the gym, say) often does more than encouragement alone. Notice small steps out loud and be kind about slips. Look after yourself as well, because you can care deeply and still set limits on what you will put up with.

Words to try “I’m on your side with this. What would help?” “You’ve done this three days running. That’s not nothing.”

When to get more help

  • If a habit is harming your health or life, such as drinking, drugs, gambling, eating or self-harm, please talk to a doctor or a specialist service. Needing help with this is common and nothing to be ashamed of.
  • If you can’t stop even though you’ve tried many times, professional support can make a real difference. It isn’t a sign of weakness.
  • If change feels impossible because you’re exhausted or low most days, that may be burnout or depression. A doctor or counsellor can help.
  • If someone is demanding you change in ways that frighten you, or punishing you when you don’t, that isn’t support. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private help.
  • If you’re overwhelmed right now, start with Upset right now (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now).

Workpapers, tools and reading on the website

Pick one tiny change and try it for a week. The 90-second daily check-in (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-13-daily-check-in), the quick checks (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) and the self path can help you keep track.

Part Three · Chapter 7

Self-worth, shame and self-compassion

Why your worth isn’t a score you keep earning, how shame differs from guilt, and why being kind to yourself makes it easier to grow.

In this chapter

  1. Your worth isn’t a score
  2. Guilt says “I did a bad thing.” Shame says “I am bad.”
  3. Shame makes you want to hide
  4. The inner critic is trying to protect you
  5. Self-compassion isn’t letting yourself off
  6. Comparing yourself pulls your worth outside you
  7. You can own a mistake without drowning in it
  8. Worth is learned between people, and we can give it
  9. In everyday life
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. When to get more help
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

Thursday, 11:20pm

You sent the wrong spreadsheet to the whole team. Last quarter’s, not this one’s. Priyanka spotted it in four minutes, sent the right one round and added “no worries!!” with two exclamation marks, which somehow made it worse.

It’s nearly midnight. The file stopped being the point some time around ten. The voice has moved on to bigger things now, like how you’ve always been a bit useless, really, and now they all know.

This chapter is about how self-worth and shame work, and then about what you can actually do with them. None of it is a diagnosis. Take what helps.

  1. Your worth isn’t a score.

    A lot of us carry a quiet scoreboard. I’m worth something when I’m useful. Or liked, or slim, or busy, or never any bother. Psychologists call these “conditions of worth”, and the trouble with a score is that it can drop. If your worth goes up and down with each day’s results, then every bad day is a verdict.

    Pam taught Year 4 for forty years. In the September after she retired she found herself in the big Tesco at ten on a Tuesday morning, holding a basket with nothing in it, feeling lost in a way she couldn’t have explained to anyone. Nothing was wrong. But for four decades being needed was how she knew she mattered, and the bell had stopped ringing.

    Try finishing “I feel okay about myself when I…” three times, then look at what you wrote. Those are your scores. Just noticing them is enough for now.

    Dig deeper: worth that doesn’t have to be earned

  2. Guilt says “I did a bad thing.” Shame says “I am bad.”

    Guilt is about something you did, so it points somewhere useful. Say sorry. Put it right. Shame is about who you are, which feels impossible to fix, and so it makes people hide, or freeze, or blame someone else, or lash out. Research on the two feelings, such as June Tangney and Ronda Dearing’s (2002), suggests guilt is the one more likely to lead to repair.

    Rhys is twelve and he has just knocked his mum’s favourite mug off the side, the one with the hare on it from Whitby. There are two ways this can go. Guilt says go and tell her, and maybe offer some birthday money. Shame says you ruin everything, and this time shame wins. He wraps the pieces in yesterday’s paper and pushes them right down to the bottom of the bin, under the potato peelings, where his mum finds them on Sunday.

    It was the hiding that upset her. She told him so. It took him a while to see what she meant.

    Dig deeper: guilt, shame and repair

  3. Shame makes you want to hide.

    You feel shame in the body before you think it. Hot face, eyes down, stomach dropping, a strong wish for the floor to open. It also comes out sideways, as sudden anger or a closed, cold face, which is how a small comment turns into a big row.

    “Didn’t we already cover this?” It was a mild question, asked in a Tuesday meeting by a man who genuinely couldn’t remember. Becky snapped at him. Properly snapped, in front of nine people. That evening, scraping a plate into the bin, she worked out that it had nothing to do with him. She’d felt stupid in front of everyone, and stupid had come out as sharp.

    Learn your own signs, if you can. Next time you suddenly want to vanish, or bite, you can name it quietly to yourself, and now and then out loud. “Sorry, I think I felt embarrassed and it came out sharp. Can I try that again?”

    Dig deeper: how shame works in the body

  4. The inner critic is trying to protect you.

    That harsh inner voice usually started as protection. If you criticise yourself first, perhaps nobody else gets the chance. If you’re hard enough on yourself, perhaps you’ll never fail again. It meant well, in its way. But a voice that only threatens keeps your body on alert, and it’s exhausting to share a head with.

    Every time Craig forgets something for the baby he calls himself an idiot. Out loud, sometimes. The wipes. The rabbit she won’t sleep without. It’s the word his own dad used about him, all through his childhood. Patting his pockets in the nursery car park for a rabbit that’s on the kitchen table, he hears it in his dad’s voice, exactly, and it strikes him as odd that he’s still using it.

    Write down one thing your critic says a lot. Would you say it to a friend you loved? Some people find it helps to answer the critic directly. “Thanks. I know you’re trying to protect me. I can take it from here.”

    Dig deeper: the critic and the soothing system

  5. Self-compassion isn’t letting yourself off.

    Self-compassion means treating yourself the way you’d treat a good friend who’s having a rotten time. One well-known model has three parts. Kindness instead of attack. Remembering that everyone struggles. Noticing the pain without drowning in it. Studies, such as one by Juliana Breines and Serena Chen (2012), suggest that people who are kind to themselves after a failure are often more likely to try to improve.

    Lindy failed her driving test for the third time. The reverse round a corner, again, the same kerb. She sat in the test centre car park for a while. Then she told herself what she’d have told her sister, more or less. This is hard. Loads of people need more goes. You’re fine everywhere except that one corner. On Sunday morning she was on the empty industrial estate behind B&Q with her dad in the passenger seat, reversing round the same lamp post eleven times.

    If it feels all right, try putting a hand on your arm once today and saying, slowly, “This is a hard moment. Other people feel this too. What do I need?” It feels daft. That’s fine.

    Dig deeper: what self-compassion is, and isn’t

    Sugarfoot

    Speak to yourself the way you’d speak to a friend having a hard day, slowly and kindly. Writing it down first helps.

    Tool: Write it through spreadloveandacceptance.com/write-it-through

  6. Comparing yourself pulls your worth outside you.

    Everyone measures themselves against other people. It’s how we work out where we stand. But a feed full of other people’s best moments makes the measuring wildly unfair, and self-esteem that depends on being better than others swings about all over the place.

    Two old friends met for a curry. One had just bought a house. The other rents a room in a shared flat in Leyton where the shower only works if you hold it. The renter spent the whole evening quietly ranking herself, and she missed what was right in front of her. Her friend was lonely in the new house. She’d wanted to say so, all evening, and never found the gap. You’re comparing your inside with somebody’s outside. When you catch yourself at it, try a question instead. “How are you, really?”

    Dig deeper: comparison and steady self-worth

  7. You can own a mistake without drowning in it.

    Owning a mistake gets a lot easier once it doesn’t mean you’re worthless. Say what you did. Say what it did to the other person. Say what you’ll do now. Then stop. Beating yourself up afterwards proves nothing about how sorry you are, it just pulls everyone’s attention back onto you.

    Jess forgot to pay her share of the broadband and it got cut off for the whole of the bank holiday weekend. On the Tuesday she put her head round the living-room door. “I forgot to pay, and it left you all without internet for three days. I’ve paid it and set a reminder for the 28th.” Someone said “Cheers,” and that was more or less the end of it.

    If it went wrong in a conversation, Rewind the talk (spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder) helps you find the words. Then decide whether to send them or let it rest.

    Dig deeper: owning it, repairing it, letting it rest

    Professor Puddles

    Owning a mistake can be short and plain: what happened, that it was yours, what you’ll do. If it went wrong in a talk, Rewind the talk helps you find the words.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  8. Worth is learned between people, and we can give it.

    Children learn their worth from how they’re treated, and adults never entirely stop. The words matter. “You did a careless thing” leaves room to change. “You’re so careless” shuts the door. Notice effort, and who someone is, as well as results, and people feel they matter on bad days too.

    Gill took over a team that hid its problems until week ten. She started every project review with the same question, “What did we learn?”, and refused, politely and repeatedly, to discuss who had got what wrong. Within six months people were bringing problems to her in week two, which saved everyone a great many Friday evenings, and the soppy question stayed.

    Today you could say one thing to someone that has nothing to do with how well they’ve done. Even just “I’m glad I know you.”

    Dig deeper: how worth is given and learned

Your part, and only your part. You can’t control how other people judge you, or what you were taught about your worth growing up. You can control how you speak to yourself now, whether you repair what you can, and where you spend your time. Give your energy to people who treat you as someone who matters. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

Friday, 9:15am

You send one line. Sorry about the mix-up with yesterday’s file, right one attached. When the voice starts up again you try answering it the way you would a friend. You got it wrong and you fixed it. That’s what a decent colleague does. The voice is not convinced. Priyanka sends a thumbs-up, and by lunch you’ve mostly stopped thinking about it.

In everyday life

Shame turns up in very ordinary places. Between partners, “You forgot to call” can land as “You’re a terrible partner”, so what comes back is a defence instead of a sorry. A child who hears “You’re so naughty” learns something about who they are, while “That was a naughty thing to do” leaves a way back. A friend who says yes to everything may be quietly burning out, because no feels like risking being dropped. At work, someone may sit on a small error for weeks because owning it feels like proof they never belonged there.

On your own: a kinder voice to keep

You don’t need anyone else for this. Notice how you talk to yourself and practise one gentler sentence. Catch the critic’s favourite words (“always”, “useless”, “pathetic”, “should”) and swap one for a plain fact. “I’m hopeless” becomes “I was late twice this week.” On bad days, keep a short list of what you did, and let getting up count. You’re allowed to be disappointed in what you did and still be on your own side.

Common mix-ups

People worry that self-compassion is just self-pity. They feel quite different from the inside. Self-pity says “only me, poor me”. Self-compassion says “this is hard, and other people go through it too”, which joins you to other people instead of shutting you away from them. Others fear that being kind to themselves will make them lazy. The research leans the other way, because it’s fear of your own attack that makes people stop trying and hide their mistakes. And self-worth doesn’t mean thinking you’re great. It means you matter on the days you aren’t.

If you want to help someone else with this

Talk about what happened, never about what sort of person they are. Arguing with someone’s shame (“You’re not useless!”) can feel like being told they’re wrong to feel it, so you might try “It sounds like you feel really low about it. I don’t see you that way.” Helping them find one small thing they can do gives the feeling somewhere to go. And kindness on ordinary days, when nothing has gone wrong, teaches worth far better than anything said in a crisis.

You could say “That sounds like it’s weighing on you. Want to work out one thing that would help?” “You don’t have to earn being cared about.”

When to get more help

Everyone feels shame and self-doubt sometimes. It’s worth talking to a doctor, counsellor or therapist if harsh thoughts about yourself are there most days, if they stop you working, eating, sleeping or seeing people, or if you feel you deserve to be hurt. Therapies such as compassion-focused therapy and cognitive behavioural therapy are built to help with exactly this.

If you are having thoughts of hurting yourself or not wanting to be here, please tell someone today. In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number.

If someone close to you keeps telling you you’re worthless, stupid or lucky to have them, that isn’t a self-esteem problem. It can be a way of controlling someone. Signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) and Not safe at home? have free, private help.

Loss, grief and big life changes

What grief is, why it comes in waves, how it shows up in the body, and how to carry a loss, or a big change, without having to “get over it.”

  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In short

  • Grief is love with nowhere to go. It hurts because the person, place or life mattered.
  • It comes in waves. A good week followed by a bad day is part of grieving, and it doesn’t send you back to the start.
  • You don’t have to let go. Many people keep a bond with the person they lost, and that is healthy.
  • Most people find a way through. Support helps, and some losses need more help than friends can give.

Saturday, 9:05am

Six months on, you’re doing fine, or so you tell people. Then in aisle seven you see the cereal your dad always bought, the one with the faded blue box that he said tasted of cardboard and ate every single morning anyway, and you have to leave your trolley where it is and go and sit in the car. Nobody around you knows why.

This chapter is for anyone who has lost someone or something, whether a person, a pet, a marriage, a friendship, their health, a home, a job, a country or a future they had pictured. It looks at how grief works and then at what can help. There’s no right way to grieve. Nothing here is a timetable, and if any of it doesn’t fit you, leave it.

  1. Grief is love with nowhere to go.

    Grief is what we feel when something we were attached to is gone, and it isn’t only for deaths. A divorce, a miscarriage, a diagnosis, a move, a friend who drifted away or children leaving home can all bring real grief. Its size usually matches the size of the bond, whatever other people think the loss ought to mean.

    When Bramble dies, his owner is shaken by how hard he takes it, and his friends at the pub tell him, kindly enough, that it was only a dog. That dog walked beside him along the same stretch of river every morning for twelve years, through two jobs and a divorce. The lead is still on its hook by the back door, and he can’t move it yet.

    It can help to say a loss out loud to yourself, especially one you’ve never called grief. “I’m grieving the friendship.” “I’m grieving the life we planned.” They’re small sentences, and they often bring some relief, because they give the feeling a name and a reason.

    Dig deeper: what grief is, and what counts

  2. Grief comes in waves, not neat stages.

    You may have heard of five stages of grief, running from denial through anger, bargaining and depression to acceptance. They came from listening to people who were dying, and they were never meant as steps that everyone follows in order. Most people swing back and forth, some hours deep in the loss and some hours getting on with life, and researchers who study grief see that swing as healthy. A widow laughs properly over a jacket potato with her sister on a Wednesday, feels guilty about it on the bus home, and cries all evening. The lunch was grief too.

    A small break from grief, a walk or a programme you like or a meal with a friend, takes nothing away from the person you lost. And when a wave comes, it does usually pass, even if it knocks you over first.

    Dig deeper: waves, and the swing between loss and life

  3. Grief lives in the body, too.

    Grief can bring tiredness, poor sleep, no appetite or extra appetite, aches, a tight chest, forgetfulness and a foggy head. Your brain is slowly learning that someone or something it expected to be there has gone, and that learning takes time and uses energy. A deputy head whose mother has died loses her car keys three times in one week and walks into a governors’ meeting on the wrong day, and she starts to worry that something is wrong with her memory. It’s grief fog. It eases as the months pass, though nobody can tell her exactly when.

    While it lasts, protect a few basics: one regular meal, a set bedtime, a short walk outside. It’s fine to tell people at work or at home, “I’m grieving, so I’m slower than usual. Could you send me a reminder?”

    Dig deeper: the grieving body and brain

  4. Some losses nobody sees.

    Some losses are hard to explain to anyone else. Someone may still be alive but changed by dementia or illness, or gone without having died, like an estranged parent or a missing relative. Other losses go unrecognised, such as the death of an ex-partner, a pregnancy loss or a friend you only ever knew online. A woman whose father has dementia still visits him at the care home every Sunday at two. He’s pleased to see her. He thinks she’s his sister. The dad who knew her is fading, and she is grieving someone who hasn’t died, which is a very lonely kind of grief because there’s no ceremony for it and hardly anyone notices.

    If a loss of yours had no ceremony, you can make a small one of your own by lighting a candle, writing a letter, planting something or visiting a place that mattered. You might also tell one person, “I’m grieving something people might not see as a loss. It is one for me.”

    Dig deeper: ambiguous and unrecognised grief

  5. People grieve in different ways.

    Some people grieve by talking and crying, and others by doing, whether that means fixing things, organising, working or building something. Neither way is more loving. Families often clash because one person thinks another isn’t grieving, when they’re grieving differently, and culture, faith, age and how your mind works all shape the way it comes out. After their son’s death, one parent wants to talk about him every evening. The other spends every weekend in the garage, restoring the old Raleigh he never got round to fixing. Each feels the other is getting it wrong. Each is grieving the same boy.

    A question can bridge the gap. “What has helped you most, even a little?” asked of someone who shares your loss, and listened to without correcting, often shows that the two of you want the same thing by different roads.

    Dig deeper: grieving styles and families

  6. You don’t have to let go.

    An older idea said that healthy grief meant moving on and cutting ties. Many grief researchers now see it differently. People often keep a bond with the person they lost, in memories, rituals, conversations in their head and values they carry forward, so the relationship changes shape without having to end. A teenager wears her grandfather’s watch to every exam, a heavy old thing that she has to push up her arm to write. She doesn’t believe in luck, and she’d find it hard to explain why the watch matters, except that it feels as if he’s in the room.

    You might choose one way of keeping a bond, such as cooking their recipe, telling a story about them at a family meal or keeping one of their habits. Some people find it helps to ask, in a hard moment, what the person they lost would have said.

    Dig deeper: continuing bonds

  7. Big changes are losses too, even the good ones.

    A new baby, a promotion, retirement, moving country, a child starting school, coming out or getting well after a long illness can all bring grief for the old life. Change often has three parts, an ending, a confusing time in between and a new beginning, and the middle part is both the hardest and the easiest to rush. A couple move to Bristol for a job they both wanted. Six months in, one of them feels low, then guilty for feeling low, because this was the plan and they’d toasted it with fizz. What they also lost was a circle of friends, a café where nobody had to ask what they wanted, and a whole way of life.

    You can be glad about a change and still miss what came before. For one change you are going through, it may help to write down what ended, what still feels unclear and one small thing that is new and good.

    Dig deeper: endings, the in-between, beginnings

    Professor Puddles

    When a change is hard to talk about, writing can come first. This is a quiet place to put the words down, at your own pace, and to send them only if you want to.

    Tool: Write it through spreadloveandacceptance.com/write-it-through

  8. Most people find a way through, and support helps.

    Research suggests that, over time, many people find they can live with a loss and still feel joy, even though they never forget. Being with people who let you talk, or let you stay quiet, helps. For some people, though, grief stays at full strength for a long time and makes daily life very hard.

    Doctors call this prolonged grief. It means a strong longing for the person, or being taken over by the loss, most days, still going many months after the death (6 to 12 months or more, depending on the guideline) and getting in the way of life. It has nothing to do with weakness, and there is specific help for it. A year after his wife died, a man still can’t go into their bedroom or face his friends, and his doctor refers him to a grief counsellor. Things begin to move, slowly, starting with one evening a week at his brother’s, where they watch the snooker and don’t talk much.

    On a good day, write down two people you could text on a hard one, and one place you could call if those people aren’t enough. If it has been a long time and nothing is easing, it is reasonable to say, “I think I need more help.”

    Dig deeper: resilience, support and stuck grief

Your part, and only your part. You can’t control the loss, how long grief lasts, or how other people react to it. You can control small things: eating something, resting, telling one person how you are, and saying no to what you can’t manage right now. That is enough for a hard season. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

Saturday, 9:40am

You sit in the car for ten minutes and let the wave come. Then you go back in. Your trolley is where you left it, next to the porridge, and you put the cereal in. At home you text your sister that you saw Dad’s cereal and cried in the car park. She replies straight away that the same thing happened to her with his aftershave in a chemist’s, and asks whether you can call tonight.

zqaxunderstandingx8xlossxxlaterxlifeqzLosing a partner in later life

After a long marriage the loss is in everything, from the empty chair to the jobs that were always theirs, the paperwork done alone and the first birthday and anniversary without them. Do one small thing at a time, and let one drawer count as a day’s work. It is fine to ask someone to sit with you while you fill in the forms.

Your grown-up children have lost a parent while you have lost a partner, and you may grieve on different timetables. If they start checking on you every day, that comes from love and worry. It isn’t control. You can still say what helps: “I love that you ring. Could we make it two evenings a week, and I’ll ring you if I need you?”

Dig deeper: the first year, and grown-up children

In everyday life

After a miscarriage, one partner may want to talk while the other goes quiet, and each can end up worrying that the other doesn’t care. A child may laugh and play the day after a funeral and then cry at bedtime, and both belong to grief. A friend who stops calling after your diagnosis is often stuck for words more than cold, and colleagues who avoid the subject when someone returns after a death can leave that person feeling as if the loss has been erased. A whole community can grieve together too, when a town loses its library or its factory.

On your own: carrying it gently

Grief can be lonely even with people around you. When you are carrying it alone, it helps to give the day a small shape, with one meal, one walk and one person you message. Expect harder days around birthdays and anniversaries, and plan something gentle for them. Writing to the person you lost, or about what you lost, can help too, and nobody else ever needs to read it. Some days the only goal is to get to tonight, and that is allowed.

If someone close to you has died. Grief and later life (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grief) goes further, with family after a loss, coming back to people, and a new chapter on your own. On a heavy night, the page called For a hard evening (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grief#hard-evening) may help.

If you want to help someone else with this

Show up, and then keep showing up. Support tends to flood in for two weeks and then stop, so a text at three months, or on a birthday, can mean a great deal. Offer something specific; “Can I drop off dinner on Thursday?” is far easier to say yes to than “Let me know if you need anything.” Say the name. Many grieving people find it a comfort to hear the name of the person they lost, and a memory of them, and if you’re unsure, ask. Leave out the explanations, because “Everything happens for a reason” and “At least…” tend to hurt, while “I’m so sorry. I’m here” rarely does. And if you’re upset too, lean on people further from the loss rather than on those closest to it. Comfort goes in towards the centre; venting goes out.

You could say “I don’t know what to say, but I’m here.” “I was thinking about your mum today. I remember her laugh.” “I’m going to the shop. What can I bring you?”

When to get more help

Grief is not an illness. But it’s worth talking to a doctor or a grief counsellor if, after many months, the pain isn’t easing at all, you can’t manage daily life, you feel life has no meaning without the person, or you are drinking or using other things to get through. Many hospices, faith communities and charities offer free bereavement support, including for children.

If you are having thoughts of not wanting to be here, please tell someone today. In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number.

If a loss involved violence, or you are grieving a relationship you left because you weren’t safe, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has free, private help, including after you separate (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#after-separation).

Part Three · Chapter 9

Minds that work differently

How autistic, ADHD, sensory and learning differences work, why none of them is a character flaw, and how people with different minds can meet in the middle.

In this chapter

  1. Brains vary, like bodies do
  2. Autism is a different way of sensing and connecting
  3. ADHD is about steering attention, not lacking it
  4. Everyone has a sensory profile
  5. Learning differences aren’t about intelligence
  6. Masking costs energy
  7. Autistic burnout is more than being tired
  8. Meltdowns and shutdowns aren’t choices
  9. Stimming helps, so let it be
  10. Deep focus makes switching hard
  11. Deep interests are a source of joy and rest
  12. Meet in the middle, out loud
  13. Labels are tools, and they belong to the person
  14. Finding out later in life
  15. Getting things started and finished is a skill of its own
  16. When demands feel like a threat
  17. Not recognising faces isn’t rudeness
  18. Not speaking isn’t the same as having nothing to say
  19. Telling friends and dates is your choice
  20. Finding your people
  21. In everyday life
  22. Common mix-ups
  23. If you want to help someone else with this
  24. When to get more help
  25. Tools and reading on this site
  26. More for your situation

In short

  • Brains vary, like bodies do. A different mind is not a broken one, though differences can still be disabling in a world built for one kind of mind.
  • Nobody chooses overload. Meltdowns, shutdowns and burnout are what happens when a nervous system has had too much.
  • Less masking, room to stim, time for deep interests and real rest help a great deal.
  • Meet in the middle, out loud. Ask what helps, say what helps you, and use the words each person chooses.

Monday, 8:15am

“Shoes. Please. Just put them on.” Third time.

Your son is lying on the hall floor with his hands over his ears. The new socks are wrong. From where you’re standing, they are socks. From where he is, the seam across his toes is sandpaper, and the alarm clock upstairs that nobody has switched off is going straight through the middle of his head. You are already late. So is he, in a way you can’t see.

This chapter is for neurodivergent people, diagnosed or not, and for the people who live and work with them. It can’t diagnose anyone, and only you get to choose the words you use for yourself. I should say that some of it is personal. I’m autistic, with ADHD in the mix too, and the About page on the website tells that story. I’ve tried to write this the way I’d want it written about me.

Two tools elsewhere rest on it. The “How to talk to me” card (Part One, Now, page 35) works because different minds need different input, and saying things plainly helps almost everyone. One owner per job and the written job list (Part Two, Chapter II, page 88) move memory out of anyone’s head and onto paper, which helps ADHD and autistic minds most and everybody a bit.

  1. Brains vary, like bodies do.

    Brains differ in how they take in the world, focus, move, read, remember and connect with people. “Neurodiversity” is the idea that this variety is natural. “Neurodivergent” describes people whose minds work differently from what gets treated as typical. A different mind isn’t a broken one. Differences can still be disabling, though, especially in a world built for one kind of mind. Both are true at once.

    Gary found out he was dyslexic at forty. He sat in the car outside the assessment centre for twenty minutes afterwards with the report on the passenger seat, not reading it, obviously. What he mostly felt was relief. For thirty years he had half believed the teachers who wrote “lazy” in red pen.

    Dig deeper: neurodiversity and disability

  2. Autism is a different way of sensing and connecting.

    Autistic people often communicate more directly and literally. Many have deep, focused interests, feel senses more (or less) intensely than others do, and find predictability calming. Autism doesn’t run along one line from “mild” to “severe”. Each autistic person has their own mix of strengths and needs, which can change from day to day, and the misunderstandings between autistic and non-autistic people usually run both ways.

    “Your slides have three typos,” Kate told her colleague, kindly. “One on slide four and two on the summary.” It was exactly what she would have wanted to be told. He went quiet for the rest of the afternoon and she had no idea why until a mutual friend explained it to her in the pub, Two sets of rules for what kindness sounds like. Neither is wrong. They just don’t come with subtitles.

    You could say “I like it when people say exactly what they mean. You can be direct with me.” “Do you want my honest view, or just support right now?”

    Dig deeper: autism and the double empathy problem

  3. ADHD is about steering attention, not lacking it.

    People with ADHD usually have plenty of attention. The hard bit is pointing it. Boring tasks feel like pushing a car uphill, interesting ones swallow whole evenings, and time is slippery (there’s “now” and there’s “not now” and not much in between). Feelings arrive fast and big. It’s a real difference in how the brain manages itself. Effort and caring don’t come into it.

    Bex forgot her best friend’s birthday. Completely. Not a text. Then she spent six hours making a card with pressed flowers from the garden, glued on one at a time with tweezers, and posted it four days late with a note that said “I KNOW”. The forgetting and the six hours came out of the same brain. If something keeps falling out of yours, move it into the world. A labelled alarm. A note on the door. A basket by the front door for the keys.

    Dig deeper: ADHD, time and motivation

  4. Everyone has a sensory profile.

    We all take in sound, light, touch, smell, taste, movement and signals from inside the body. Some people feel these strongly and get overloaded by noise, or a label in a jumper. Others need more input, like movement or strong flavours or firm pressure. Overload is a body at its limit. It is a very different thing from being fussy.

    For what it’s worth, mine is turned up high. A loud restaurant costs me a great deal, and so do supermarkets, and I notice the hum from a vent or a picture hanging half an inch off level whether I want to or not. Two housemates of the made-up kind fell out over the kitchen radio, because one found silence creepy and the other found Radio 2 at breakfast physically painful. They settled on the radio until nine and headphones after, which has lasted two years.

    Notice one sound, light or texture that drains you and one that calms you, and change one small thing today.

    Dig deeper: senses, overload and needs

    Professor Puddles

    Knowing your own sensory profile is useful information, not a complaint. A one-page card lets you share what helps, in your own words.

    Tool: How you connect: how I like to be spoken to spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card

  5. Learning differences aren’t about intelligence.

    Dyslexia (reading and spelling), dyscalculia (numbers), dyspraxia (coordination and planning movement) and language disorders are specific differences, and none of them measures how clever someone is. Plenty of people have a “spiky” profile, very strong in some areas and struggling in others. The right tools can level things a good deal. Audiobooks. Extra time.

    Every Wednesday afternoon on the football pitch, fourteen-year-old Ewan is called clumsy, usually by a PE teacher who should know better. The same term he wrote and directed the school play, which had a revolving set made out of a bike wheel. Ask the people you live or work with how they find it easiest to take things in, and then actually use it.

    Words to try “I learn better when I can listen than when I read. Could you send a voice note instead?”

    Dig deeper: spiky profiles and learning tools

  6. Masking costs energy.

    Many neurodivergent people learn to hide their differences. They copy other people, force eye contact, hold back movements, rehearse small talk in the car. This is called masking. It can get someone through a day. It also uses a great deal of energy, and over years it can wear a person down into exhaustion and burnout. I spent years masking, and for a long time the cost was invisible even to me, which is rather the point of a mask.

    Mia seems completely fine at college. Chatty in the canteen, helpful in class, laughs in the right places. She gets home at quarter past four, goes straight up to her room, and can’t say a word to anyone for an hour. Her dad used to knock and ask what was wrong. Now he leaves a cup of tea outside the door and goes away.

    Notice one place where you could drop the mask a little, and one person you can be fully yourself with. Spend a bit more time there.

    Dig deeper: masking, energy and burnout

  7. Autistic burnout is more than being tired.

    Autistic burnout is a deep, long-lasting exhaustion. Working with autistic adults, Raymaker and colleagues (2020) described it as long-term exhaustion, loss of skills (like speech, planning or self-care) and lower tolerance of noise, light and other input. It comes from long stress without enough support, and it often lasts months. Rest helps, and so do fewer demands and less masking. Pushing harder usually makes it worse. If you think you might be there, list three demands you could drop or hand to someone else for a month. If it goes on, or you feel hopeless, talk to a doctor.

    Words you could use “I’m in burnout. What I need for a while is fewer demands.” “I can’t do phone calls at the moment. Can we message instead?”

    Dig deeper: burnout, rest and recovery

  8. Meltdowns and shutdowns aren’t choices.

    A meltdown is an involuntary loss of control when overwhelm gets too much, and it can look like crying, shouting, running off or lashing out. A shutdown is the quiet version: going still, losing speech, not being able to respond. Neither is a tantrum. In interviews by Phung and colleagues (2021), autistic young people described meltdowns and shutdowns as separate experiences, both linked to overload.

    In my own case words go first. What helps is less of everything. Less noise, fewer words, no questions, more space. Talking can wait, sometimes until the next day. On a calm day, agree a simple signal for “I’m overloaded” and a quiet place to go.

    Ways to say it (to someone else) “You’re safe. I’m right here. No need to talk.” (for yourself) “I’m overloaded. I need quiet for twenty minutes.”

    Dig deeper: meltdowns and shutdowns

  9. Stimming helps, so let it be.

    Stimming means repeated movements or sounds. Rocking, flapping, tapping, humming, pacing, fiddling with something. Most people stim a little. (Watch any meeting and count the jiggling feet.) For many autistic people it matters a lot. In interviews by Kapp and colleagues (2019), autistic adults described stimming as a way to cope with overwhelming emotions and sensations, and objected to efforts to stop harmless stimming. If it isn’t hurting anyone, it doesn’t need stopping. Notice what your own hands do when you’re stressed or focused or happy. That’s yours.

    Dig deeper: stimming

  10. Deep focus makes switching hard.

    Some minds go deep into one thing at a time, often autistic and ADHD ones. That focus can be a real gift. It builds expertise and it brings a lot of joy. It also makes switching hard. Being interrupted can feel like being yanked out of water.

    “Dinner!” Nothing. “Tilly, dinner!” Nothing. Third time, louder, and the fish fingers are going cold, and Dominic is getting properly cross. His daughter is upstairs building a castle and has reached a delicate stage with the drawbridge. The next night he tries a ten-minute warning, then a five. She comes down on time, still talking about the drawbridge, and tells him at length what the problem with it is. He doesn’t entirely follow. He eats his fish fingers warm, which is the main thing.

    You could say “Dinner is in ten minutes. I’ll come and get you at five to.” “Can you give me a warning before we switch?”

    Dig deeper: monotropism, flow and transitions

  11. Deep interests are a source of joy and rest.

    Many autistic people have deep, intense interests, often called special interests. The theory of monotropism (Murray, Lesser and Lawson, 2005) describes autistic attention as pulled strongly into a few things at a time. In a survey of autistic adults by Grove and colleagues (2018), people who were more motivated by and engaged with their special interests reported higher wellbeing, though very intense engagement went with lower wellbeing.

    I am, by my own admission, a geek about a long list of things. Ask someone about their favourite subject and let them talk for five minutes without steering. It costs you five minutes. It’s one of the warmest things you can do for anyone.

    Words you could use “Can I tell you about this for five minutes? It’s how I unwind.” “Tell me more. What’s the best bit?”

    Dig deeper: special interests and wellbeing

    Tidbit

    The website can change to fit your mind too, with bigger text, calmer pages and fewer surprises. The settings are worth a look.

    Tool: Read your way spreadloveandacceptance.com/how-you-take-things-in

  12. Meet in the middle, out loud.

    When two kinds of mind live or work together, neither should have to do all the adjusting. Clear, plain words help everyone. Say what you mean, give times, write things down, ask what helps. And changes made for one person (a quiet space, an agenda, flexible hours) usually help plenty of other people too.

    A team started sending meeting agendas a day early, for one autistic colleague. Within a month most of them said meetings had got shorter. Two people who had never said a word in a meeting started saying things.

    Today, swap one “how I work best” fact with someone. Tell them one thing that helps you and ask for one that helps them. The website can bend a bit to your mind too, with Read your way (spreadloveandacceptance.com/how-you-take-things-in) (bigger text, calmer pages, fewer surprises).

    Dig deeper: adjustments that help everyone

  13. Labels are tools, and they belong to the person.

    A diagnosis can bring understanding, and sometimes support and a community too. Some people find their way to a label through self-discovery first. Many autistic adults prefer “autistic person”. Others prefer “person with autism”. The kindest rule is to ask, use the words the person chooses, and never try to diagnose somebody else, least of all in an argument.

    The row was about the washing-up. It was going badly. “You’re so autistic,” Danny said, and the conversation ended right there, as it deserved to. In the morning, over toast that neither of them was eating, he said sorry, properly, and then asked what his partner actually needed from him when the kitchen was a mess. It was the conversation they should have had the night before.

    If you’ve wondered about yourself, write down what you’ve noticed and pick one small next step, like talking to someone or asking a doctor.

    Dig deeper: diagnosis, identity and words

  14. Finding out later in life.

    More and more adults are finding out they’re autistic, or have ADHD, in their thirties or fifties or seventies. Many were missed as children, especially women. In interviews by Leedham and colleagues (2020), women diagnosed at forty or older described how exhausting it had been to go so long without an explanation, and how much the diagnosis changed the way they understood their own lives. Relief and grief and something like joy can all turn up together, on the same afternoon. If that’s you, look for one autistic-led group or online space, and give yourself time.

    You could say “I’ve just found out I’m autistic. I’m still working out what it means.” “That explains so much about my life.”

    Dig deeper: diagnosis later in life

  15. Getting things started and finished is a skill of its own.

    Planning, starting, switching, remembering what you were doing and keeping track of time are called executive function. Many autistic and ADHD people find some of these harder, and harder on some days than others. A review of 235 studies by Demetriou and colleagues (2018) found differences in executive function in autism on average, with a lot of variation between people. The brain’s self-management system is working differently. Laziness doesn’t come into it.

    Siân wrote a forty-page report for her board in a week, and it was brilliant. The same three weeks, she could not post one parcel. It sat on the hall table while she walked past it forty times. Then she put it on the doormat with a yellow sticky note on top (“POST ME”) and set an alarm for Tuesday at 8.10, and on Tuesday at 8.11 it went. See routines that help (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids) and Wired differently (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wired-differently).

    Words you could use “Could you send me that as a list? Spoken steps fall out of my head.” “I’m not ignoring it. Starting is the hard bit for me.”

    Dig deeper: executive function in daily life

  16. When demands feel like a threat.

    Some people, often autistic, feel strong anxiety when asked or expected to do things, even things they want to do. Avoiding the demand can look like refusing, joking, changing the subject or a meltdown. The profile was first described as “pathological demand avoidance,” or PDA, by Newson and colleagues (2003).

    It isn’t in the main diagnostic manuals, and researchers disagree about it. A review by Kildahl and colleagues (2021) found the evidence limited and mostly based on parent reports. Many people who identify with it prefer the phrase “persistent drive for autonomy.” Honestly, I’d hold this one loosely until the research settles. What helps tends to be the same whatever it’s called. Less pressure. Requests that feel like invitations. “Put your coat on now” gets a flat no from Reuben every morning. “It’s cold out. Coat or jumper, your choice?” gets the coat, usually.

    Dig deeper: demand avoidance, carefully

  17. Not recognising faces isn’t rudeness.

    Prosopagnosia, or face blindness, means finding it hard to recognise faces, sometimes even close friends seen out of context. It can be something you’re born with, and it often runs in families (NHS). Many autistic people also find remembering faces harder, as a review by Weigelt and colleagues (2012) found. People who don’t recognise you may be relying on your voice, your hair, your coat or where they usually see you.

    Clive walked straight past his neighbour in the big Sainsbury’s without a flicker, and she went home feeling snubbed and told her sister about it on the phone. When he explained, a week later and very embarrassed, that he hadn’t known her without her spaniel, she laughed. Now she says “Hi Clive, it’s Jo from number twelve” every time, even when the spaniel is right there.

    Words to try “I’m bad with faces, so please say who you are when you say hi.” (to someone else) “Hi, it’s Jo from next door.”

    Dig deeper: face blindness

  18. Not speaking isn’t the same as having nothing to say.

    Some autistic people speak rarely, sometimes or not at all, and some lose speech when stressed. Many communicate through AAC (augmentative and alternative communication), which can mean typing, letter boards, picture cards, apps or sign. Using AAC doesn’t stop speech developing: a review by Millar, Light and Schlosser (2006) found it did not hold speech back, and may help it. The safest place to start is to presume competence, which means assuming the person understands and has something to say, and giving them the time and the tools to say it.

    Sunday lunch at her nan’s. Fifteen-year-old Ruby types on her tablet. Her uncle used to talk about her across the table as if she wasn’t there (“Does she want gravy?”). Now he asks her, and waits, a bit longer than he’d like, while she types. Her answer was “Yes. Obviously.” Wait longer than feels natural. It will feel very long. It isn’t.

    You could say “Take your time. I’ll wait.” “Would you rather type or point?” (for yourself) “I can’t talk right now. I can type.”

    Dig deeper: non-speaking people and AAC

  19. Telling friends and dates is your choice.

    Whether to tell someone you’re autistic or ADHD, and when, is up to you. Telling can bring understanding. In a study by Sasson and Morrison (2019), people formed better first impressions of autistic adults when they knew they were autistic, especially if they knew more about autism.

    People don’t always respond well, though, and interviews by Au-Yeung and colleagues (2025) describe autistic adults weighing hope for support against fear of not being believed. Many share a little at a time, starting with what helps and leaving the label for later. Second date, outside a bar with a queue. “I’m autistic,” Nina said, “so I’m quite direct, and I’d rather walk than sit in there.” Her date looked at the bar, and the queue, and back at her. “Oh, thank God,” he said. They walked along the canal as far as the lock and back.

    Words you could use “I’m autistic. For me that means…” “I won’t always pick up hints, so please just tell me.” (if someone shares with you) “Thanks for telling me. What helps?”

    Dig deeper: disclosure in friendships and dating

  20. Finding your people.

    Lots of autistic people describe meeting other autistic people as a turning point, because at last they don’t have to translate or explain or mask. The research backs this up. Cooper, Smith and Russell (2017) found that autistic people who felt more connected to other autistic people had higher self-esteem, and through that, less anxiety and depression. Being autistic can be an identity and a community as well as a diagnosis.

    After his diagnosis at fifty-three, Bernard joined an online group of autistic adults who love old maps, specifically the Ordnance Survey kind with hand-drawn hachures. The first evening he talked to them for three hours about contour lines. When he logged off he had more energy than when he’d started, which hadn’t happened after a conversation in years,

    Dig deeper: autistic community and identity

Your part, and only your part. You can’t change how your brain, or anyone else’s, is wired. You can learn how yours works and say what helps, and ask others what helps them. Meeting in the middle means both people move a little. If you’re always the one adjusting, it’s fair to say so. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

Monday, 8:30am

You stop asking. You sit down on the hall floor next to him, which is cold, and say, “Socks feel wrong?” He nods without opening his eyes. You go upstairs, switch the alarm clock off, dig the old seamless pair out of the wash basket Two minutes later his shoes are on. You’re ten minutes late and nobody has shouted, which on a Monday is about as good as it gets. That night you order three more pairs and let him pick the colours.

In everyday life

On your own

Knowing how your mind works helps you build a life that fits it, and spot burnout before it’s on top of you (see Get to know your wiring, spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path). Partners can swap “how I work best” notes about plans, messages, touch and time alone. With children, behaviour very often has a sensory or overload reason, so “What’s too much right now?” is worth asking before “Why are you doing this?” A friend who cancels at the last minute may just be out of energy, and offering something easier, like a walk, keeps the door open. At work, written agendas, clear deadlines and quiet spaces help far more people than the ones they were made for.

If you have ADHD and share a home, make the chore tools lighter. Log three days instead of seven, with a tally on the fridge. Own a few jobs completely, each with a labelled alarm, instead of helping a bit with everything. Forgetting is a setup problem to fix together. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-9-minds-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

“Everyone’s a bit autistic” is probably the commonest, and it makes real needs sound small. Everyone shares some traits. Autism is a whole pattern, present across life. ADHD doesn’t just mean not sitting still. Many people with it, girls and women especially, are mostly inattentive or restless on the inside. “They seem fine to me” overlooks how much masking can hide, and seeming fine can cost someone their whole evening. Adjustments aren’t special treatment. They remove a barrier, the way glasses do. And the idea that autistic people lack empathy is simply out of date. Many feel other people’s feelings very strongly, and the differences in how empathy is shown run both ways.

If you want to help someone else with this

Believe them about what’s hard and what helps, even when it’s different for you. Be clear. Say what you mean, give times, write down anything important. Ask what helps, because every neurodivergent person is different and their answer will beat any list, this one included. Protect their energy. Quiet time, warnings before changes and a way out of loud places matter more than they look. And enjoy their interests with them, if you can. It’s rarely wasted.

Ways to say it “Is there anything about this place, or this plan, that would make it hard for you?” “You don’t have to explain. Just tell me what you need.”

When to get more help

If you wonder whether a difference is part of ongoing difficulties at school, work or home, for you or someone you care for, a doctor, school support staff or a psychologist can talk you through an assessment. Waiting lists can be long, so start early and write down what you notice.

Burnout, depression and anxiety are more common among neurodivergent people, often because of the stress of living in a world that doesn’t fit. If you’re exhausted most days, losing skills you used to have, or feeling hopeless, please talk to a doctor. If you are having thoughts of hurting yourself, please tell someone today.

In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines.

A difference never excuses harm, and it never makes someone deserve harm. If someone uses your differences to control or belittle you, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has free, private help.
