10

Part Three · Chapter 10

Values, meaning and a good life: what philosophy offers everyday life

What matters to you, how to find it, what to do when two good things pull against each other, and what a few very old ideas can offer an ordinary, busy week.

In this chapter

  1. Values are directions you keep walking in
  2. Your strong feelings point to what you value
  3. Two good things can pull in different directions
  4. Put your effort where it can land
  5. A good life is more than a good mood
  6. Meaning comes from ordinary places
  7. Different values aren’t wrong values
  8. Values live in small, everyday acts
  9. In everyday life
  10. If you want to help someone else with this
  11. When to get more help
  12. Tools and reading on this site
  13. More for your situation

In short

  • Values are directions you keep turning towards. You never finish being kind, and that is why values still work on days when goals fall apart.
  • Strong feelings point to what you value. Anger often guards fairness, and hurt often guards closeness.
  • Meaning comes from ordinary places. People, care and everyday work give most of us most of our meaning.
  • Values live in small acts. One small thing this week, done because it matters, counts.

Sunday, 9pm

The week ahead is full: the MOT on Tuesday, a dentist, two late meetings, your turn for the school run. None of it feels like yours. You aren’t sad, exactly. You just can’t remember the last time you did something because it mattered to you, rather than because it was next on the list.

This chapter is about values, the things you care about and the direction you want your life to face, and about what makes a life feel worth living. It borrows from psychology and from philosophy, which has been asking how we should live for more than two thousand years. You don’t need to have read any of it. I’ve tried to keep the old names to a minimum and the words plain.

  1. Values are directions you keep walking in.

    A goal is something you can tick off, like painting the hall or passing a test. A value is a direction you keep walking in, such as looking after your health, making your home feel cared for or being a fair friend. Nobody ever finishes being kind, and that’s exactly why a value still works on a day when a goal falls apart.

    Bethan planned to go to the gym three times this week and went once, and on Thursday evening, eating crisps on the sofa in her gym kit, she felt like a failure. When she asked herself what the gym was for, the answer was looking after her body so that she had energy for her children. On Friday she walked for twenty minutes at lunchtime, round the park behind the office, and it counted. If you have a goal that has stalled, try asking “what is this for?” three times in a row, and write down where you end up.

    Dig deeper: goals and values

  2. Your strong feelings point to what you value.

    You don’t have to invent your values from nothing. They show up in your strongest reactions. Anger often means something you care about has been stepped on. Envy can point to something you want for yourself. Sadness tends to show what you love. Sacha is furious when a colleague takes credit for the team’s work. Under the anger is a value, which is fairness and seeing people’s effort, and once he names it he can raise fairness at the next team meeting instead of seething at one person for a week. He might say, “I think I’m upset because fairness really matters to me, more than winning this one.”

    Think of the last time you felt strongly, in a good way or a bad one, and finish the sentence “That mattered to me because I care about…”

    Dig deeper: finding your values

  3. Two good things can pull in different directions.

    Most hard choices aren’t between a good thing and a bad one. They’re between two good things, honesty and kindness, say, or family and rest. Feeling torn usually just means you care about more than one thing, and even when you choose well it’s normal to feel a little sad about the side you didn’t pick. A mum cares about being honest and about protecting her eight-year-old. When the family dog is very ill, she finds a way to honour both and tells the truth gently, in words a child can hold. “Biscuit is very poorly. The vet is helping, and we’ll look after him together.”

    If you feel stuck on a choice, write down the good thing on each side. It often helps to ask whether you can honour some of both, even if you can’t have all of either.

    Dig deeper: when values clash

  4. Put your effort where it can land.

    About two thousand years ago a teacher called Epictetus, who had been born into slavery, taught that some things are up to us and some aren’t. It’s one of the oldest ideas in this book and still one of the most useful. (I spent my career as a government auditor, and the sorting matters there too: mix up two different problems and you keep solving the wrong one.) Your own choices and how you treat people are up to you. Other people’s choices, and the weather, and the past, are not. Worry tends to collect in the second pile, and values do their work in the first. Ingrid wants her partner to enjoy Christmas with her family, and she can’t make him enjoy it. She can plan a shorter visit, put a long muddy walk on Boxing Day into it, which he’ll like, and be warm herself. That’s her part, and it turns out to be quite a lot.

    One way to try this is to write a worry in two columns, the parts that are up to you and the parts that aren’t, then pick one small thing from the first column and do it.

    Dig deeper: what is up to us

  5. A good life is more than a good mood.

    Feeling good matters. Many thinkers, from the Greek philosopher Aristotle to psychologists today, also describe a second kind of wellbeing, which comes from growing, using your strengths, being a good friend and doing things that matter even when they are hard. Aristotle called it flourishing, and he thought we build it the way we build any skill, by practice, a little at a time. Jade spent a month of evenings helping a friend move out of a damp, unhappy flat, scrubbing black mould off a bathroom ceiling and carrying boxes down three flights. It was tiring and not much fun. When she looks back on her year, she counts it among the best months of it.

    Tonight you might write down one thing that felt good today and one that felt worthwhile, and notice whether they turn out to be the same thing.

    Dig deeper: happiness and flourishing

    Professor Puddles

    If you enjoy big questions, put philosophy next to psychology and see what they share. It’s one of my favourite rainy-day pastimes.

    Tool: Learn by doing: connect two fields of study spreadloveandacceptance.com/polymath

  6. Meaning comes from ordinary places.

    Researchers who study meaning often describe three parts to it. Your life makes some sense to you, you are heading somewhere, and your life matters to someone. Most meaning comes from people, from work done with care and from small roles that others count on, far more than from big moments. Walter has lived alone since his wife died, and for a long time his days went quiet. Now he reads to children at the library one morning a week, which gives him a reason to iron a shirt on Tuesday nights and a small group of people who notice when he isn’t there.

    Try listing the roles you play, big or small (neighbour, sister, the one who waters the office plants), and next to each one write who it matters to.

    Dig deeper: where meaning comes from

  7. Different values aren’t wrong values.

    Two people can share a home, a family or a team and still put the same good things in a different order, with one putting safety first and another adventure. The philosopher Isaiah Berlin argued that there are many real goods in life and that they can’t all be ranked on one scale, which leaves room to disagree without either person being bad. Jasper values a calm, tidy home, and his housemate Darnell values an open door and friends dropping by. For months each privately thought of the other as messy or uptight. Once they named what each of them cared about, they could make a plan, and Friday nights became open house while Sundays stayed quiet.

    In your next disagreement, it may help to ask, “What matters to you about this?”, and to listen for the value underneath the position.

    Dig deeper: living with different values

  8. Values live in small, everyday acts.

    A good life is built mostly from small things done again and again, such as how you greet people, whether you keep small promises and how you talk about someone who isn’t in the room. The Chinese teacher Confucius taught that small, everyday courtesies shape who we become, and later thinkers who wrote about care said that being good starts with paying attention to the person in front of you. At the supermarket an older man is struggling with the card machine, and the queue behind him is growing; someone near the back tuts. You wait without sighing and tell him there’s no rush. It costs you about forty seconds.

    Pick one value, choose one tiny act that shows it, and do it each day this week. You’ll drift. Everyone does. Turning back is the practice.

    Dig deeper: everyday ethics

    Sugarfoot

    A value can be as small as a cup of tea made just the way someone likes it. A “What feels like care” card helps you learn what that is for each of you.

    Tool: How you connect: what feels like care spreadloveandacceptance.com/love-languages

Your part, and only your part. You can choose your direction. When you notice you’ve drifted, you can turn back without shame. You can’t choose other people’s values for them, and you don’t have to adopt theirs to love them. You can share what matters to you, listen to what matters to them, and look for the places where your directions overlap.

Sunday, 9:20pm

You write three words on the back of an envelope, people, health and making things, and under each one a small thing for this week. Ring Gran. Walk on Wednesday. Finish the shelf in the spare room, the one that has been “nearly done” since Easter. The week is still full. You prop the envelope against the kettle, where you’ll see it in the morning before you see anything else.

In everyday life

Partners may rank the same values differently, such as security and adventure, and it helps to say what each of you is protecting before you argue about the plan. Two generations of a family can both value family and mean quite different things by it, from living close by to being free to go, so it is worth asking what the word means to each of you. When a job keeps asking you to act against a value, the strain often shows up as tiredness or cynicism, and naming the clash is a first step. A club, a faith group or volunteering can give you a place to act on a value alongside other people.

If you want to help someone else with this

Asking “What matters most to you about this?” helps more than telling someone what they ought to care about. People often see their values for the first time in someone else’s words, so it can help to notice them out loud, as in “You stayed late to help your friend. Loyalty really matters to you, doesn’t it?” With children, naming the value when you see it teaches more than a lecture. Try not to use values as a weapon, because “I thought you valued family” lands as a guilt trip. You can disagree with someone’s choice and still see the good thing they were reaching for.

You could say “What would a good outcome look like to you?” “What do you want to be able to say about how you handled this, a year from now?”

When to get more help

Feeling a bit lost or flat for a while is part of being human. But some signs mean it’s worth talking to someone trained:

  • Life has felt empty or pointless for more than two weeks, and things you used to enjoy don’t reach you. That can be depression, which is common and treatable. A doctor or counsellor is a good first step.
  • You have thoughts of not wanting to be alive. Please talk to someone today. In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines. If you are in danger now, call your local emergency number.
  • Someone in your life is pushing you to give up what matters to you, cutting you off from friends, or making you afraid to disagree. That’s about control. It has nothing to do with values. The page When it’s more than a rough patch (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) can help you think it through.

Some therapies, such as acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), work directly with values. A counsellor can help you find yours when everything feels foggy.

A limit to keep in mind: This chapter shares ideas to think with, not answers to follow. Your values are yours to find, and it’s fine if they change as your life does.

Part Three · Chapter 11

Healing after hurt: repair, forgiveness, and when to get help

How hurt heals, why it lingers, how small breaks get mended, what a real apology sounds like, what forgiveness is and isn’t, and when it’s time to get more help.

In this chapter

  1. Hurt is real, and healing takes time
  2. Every close relationship has breaks. Repair is what counts
  3. Telling someone they hurt you
  4. A real apology names it, owns it, and mends it
  5. Forgiveness isn’t forgetting, excusing or going back
  6. You can heal even if they never say sorry
  7. Trust comes back in small, kept promises
  8. Going back is a choice. Safety comes first
  9. Look after the hurt part of you
  10. In everyday life
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. When to get more help
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In short

  • Hurt is real, and healing takes time. Replaying a hurt says more about how much it mattered than about any weakness in you.
  • Repair is what counts. Every close relationship has breaks, and a real apology names what happened, owns it and offers to mend it.
  • Forgiving and going back are separate choices. You can forgive without forgetting, excusing or letting someone back in.
  • Safety comes first. You can heal even if they never say sorry, and you never owe anyone a risk to your safety.

Thursday, 2am

It was one sentence, three weeks ago, said over someone’s shoulder in a kitchen at a party, and they’ve probably forgotten it. You haven’t. It plays again word for word, along with every clever thing you could have said back, and you’re tired of carrying it around without knowing how to put it down.

Everyone gets hurt, and everyone hurts other people, mostly without meaning to. This chapter looks at how hurt works and how relationships mend, and at how you can heal with or without the other person, for small hurts and bigger ones. If someone is hurting you on purpose, or you feel afraid, start with safety first: Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety)

  1. Hurt is real, and healing takes time.

    Being hurt by someone shows that something mattered, whether the person, your trust or your sense of being respected. The mind replays hurts because it’s trying to understand them, and to keep you safe from the next one. Healing rarely runs in a straight line. The feeling can come back on an anniversary, or when something reminds you, and that doesn’t mean you’ve failed.

    Months after a friend said something cruel at a party, Kwesi feels a jolt when the song that was playing comes on the radio. He tells himself it’s an old bruise being pressed. He turns the volume down and goes back to chopping onions. When a hurt replays for you, notice it, name it (“there’s that memory again”), and bring your attention to something in the room you can see or touch.

    Thoughts you could try “This hurts because it mattered.” “A feeling coming back doesn’t mean I’m back at the start.”

    Dig deeper: why hurt lingers

  2. Every close relationship has breaks. Repair is what counts.

    No relationship is smooth all the time. People snap and forget and misread each other, and let each other down. Research on parents and babies, on couples and on therapy all points the same way: breaks are normal, and what matters most is whether they get mended. A small repair, made soon, often leaves a relationship feeling safer than it did before the break.

    A dad snaps at his son for knocking a full glass of orange juice across the breakfast table. Twenty minutes later he sits down next to him on the sofa and says, “I was grumpy and I shouted. That wasn’t fair. Spills happen. Want to help me make a new one?” They go and do it together, and the boy pours, very carefully, with his tongue out. Think of a small break from this week, with anyone, and go back and mend it with one sentence.

    You could say “Can I have a do-over? That came out badly.” “I didn’t like how I spoke to you earlier. I’m sorry.”

    Dig deeper: breaks and repair

  3. Telling someone they hurt you.

    People can’t mend what they don’t know about. Saying “that hurt” is a risk, but it gives the relationship a chance, and it works best when you describe what happened and how it felt, leaving out what kind of person they are. Pick a calm moment, well away from the middle of an argument.

    Amara says to her friend, on a walk rather than over the phone, “When you told the group about my breakup before I was ready, I felt exposed. I’d like to be the one who shares my news.” She had a stronger word ready. She leaves it out and sticks to what happened and what she needs, and her friend, who had honestly thought she was helping, goes red and apologises.

    Words you could use “When… happened, I felt… What I’d like is…” “I’m telling you because I want us to be okay.”

    Before you say it, it helps to write it in three short lines: what happened, how you felt, what you’d like.

    Dig deeper: saying “that hurt”

  4. A real apology names it, owns it, and mends it.

    “Sorry if you were upset” doesn’t heal much. A real apology says what you did, takes responsibility without excuses, shows you understand how it affected the other person, and offers to put it right or do things differently. Research, such as a study led by Roy Lewicki (2016), suggests owning it and offering repair are the parts that matter most.

    Leila presented a shared idea at the Tuesday meeting as if it were hers, and saw her colleague’s face. The next day she tells him, “I presented our idea as mine. That wasn’t fair to you. I’ll email the team today and say it was joint work.”

    Ways to say it “I did… That was my doing. I can see it left you feeling… Here’s what I’ll do.”

    Next time you say sorry, check it has all four parts in it. Apology languages (spreadloveandacceptance.com/apology-languages) has more.

    Dig deeper: what makes an apology work

    Professor Puddles

    An apology lands best when it’s plain: what happened, that it was yours, and what you’ll do now. Rewind the talk can help you find those words.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  5. Forgiveness isn’t forgetting, excusing or going back.

    Forgiveness is usually described as letting go of resentment and the wish to get even, and it happens inside you. Forgiving someone doesn’t mean saying that what happened was okay, or forgetting it, or trusting the person again, or keeping them in your life. It’s a choice, often a slow one, and you never owe it on anyone else’s timetable.

    Danielle forgave her father for missing much of her childhood. She still keeps his visits short, and she still won’t leave her children alone with him when he has been drinking, and for her the forgiving and the protecting sit together without strain.

    Things to tell yourself “I can let go of wanting to get even, and still keep my limits.” “I don’t have to forgive today. I can just stop feeding the anger today.”

    If you’re weighing it up, write down what forgiving someone would mean to you, and what it wouldn’t. Seeing the difference can make it feel possible. It can also show you that you aren’t ready, which is fine.

    Dig deeper: what forgiveness is

  6. You can heal even if they never say sorry.

    Waiting for an apology that never comes can keep you stuck, because the person may be gone, or unwilling to understand. Your healing doesn’t have to depend on them. You can make sense of what happened, tell your story to someone safe and decide what it means for you now.

    After a hard breakup, Martha writes a letter she never sends, four pages in biro: what hurt, what she’d hoped for, what she’s taking with her. She folds it into the back of a notebook, and over the following weeks she reaches for it less and less, and then one day realises she hasn’t for a month.

    Things to tell yourself “I don’t need them to understand for my healing to count.”

    Writing works for a lot of people. Write about the hurt for fifteen minutes on three or four days in a row, the facts and the feelings both. If it ever makes you feel much worse, stop and talk to someone instead.

    Dig deeper: healing on your own

  7. Trust comes back in small, kept promises.

    After trust is broken, one big apology rarely rebuilds it. Trust grows back slowly, in many small moments where someone does what they said they would do. If you broke trust, being patient and consistent matters more than a grand gesture, and if you were let down, it is fair to watch what someone does as well as what they say.

    Declan hid a credit card debt from his partner for most of a year. After it came out, he started leaving his bank statement on the kitchen table on the first of each month, without being asked. Nobody made a speech about it. After a year of small, steady openness, his partner says, one evening, that she can breathe again.

    Words to try “I know my words aren’t enough. I want to show you, over time.” “I need to see it for a while before I can feel it.”

    Dig deeper: how trust is rebuilt

  8. Going back is a choice. Safety comes first.

    After a hurt, you can mend the relationship or change its shape. You can also step away. All three can be healthy. If someone keeps hurting you after you’ve told them, if you feel afraid of them, or if they control, threaten or put you down, the work is to protect yourself, not to repair. Counselling together isn’t advised when someone is afraid of their partner.

    Ellie’s housemate borrowed money twice and didn’t pay it back. Ellie let the first time go. The second time, forty pounds for a train ticket, she said, “I won’t lend money again. I still want us to get on in the house,” and they still share the Sunday roast most weeks.

    You could say “I’m not angry any more, and I’m not going back to how it was.” “I need some distance while I work out what I want.”

    Three questions can guide what comes next: is it safe, has the hurt stopped, and do you want this relationship in your life? If you feel unsafe, see signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#signs).

    Dig deeper: limits, distance and safety

  9. Look after the hurt part of you.

    Hurt lives in the body as well as the mind, as poor sleep or a jumpy feeling that won’t settle. Healing goes better with basic care, which means rest, food, movement, people who are kind to you, and talking to yourself the way you would talk to a hurting friend. Some people find they grow after something painful, and some don’t. Neither is a test you can fail.

    A man shouted at Idris on the top deck of the bus and called him names, and nobody else said a word. For days afterwards he felt shaky. He told a friend, went for long walks after work, and kept reminding himself that it was about the man on the bus and that he was safe now. Over a couple of weeks the shakiness faded, though he sat downstairs for a while.

    Things to tell yourself “This was hard. Anyone would be shaken. What do I need right now?”

    Pick one small act of care for today, an early night or a call to someone kind. Calm tools are in Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now)

    Dig deeper: healing in body and mind

Your part, and only your part. You can say what hurt, apologise for what you did, and look after your own healing. You can’t make someone apologise or change, and you don’t have to wait for them to start feeling better. Forgiveness, trust and going back are all yours to choose, in your own time.

Saturday, 11am

You’ve written it all down, every word of it. Then a much smaller version. “When you said that, I felt small. I’d like you to know.” You still haven’t decided whether to send it. It sits in your drafts, between a half-written email to the council and a shopping list. The two o’clock replays have gone a little quieter since it went onto paper.

In everyday life

Between partners, small breaks happen most days, and a quick “That came out wrong. Can I try again?” mends most of them (see How to apologise so it counts). Old family hurts often need a different kind of talk from new ones, and sometimes more time apart. A friend may not know they hurt you, and “Can I tell you something that stung? I’d rather say it than drift” keeps the door open. You can even heal a hurt with someone who has died, by writing to them or talking it through with someone you trust.

  • After an affair. The shock is real for both people. Couples can recover, and some decide to part; both can be done with care. Trust returns through kept promises over months, and a couples therapist can help. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-11-healing-in-depth).
  • If you decide to separate. Part as kindly as you can. Tell children together, without blame, and never ask them to choose. Write decisions down, and consider family mediation where it’s safe. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-11-healing-in-depth#separating).

If you want to help someone else with this

  • Listen before you advise. “That sounds really painful” helps more than “You should just let it go.”
  • Don’t rush forgiveness. Pushing someone to forgive can feel like being told their hurt doesn’t matter.
  • Don’t push them to cut someone off, either. It’s their relationship and their choice, unless they’re in danger.
  • If you caused the hurt, give a real apology and then give them time. Don’t ask them to make you feel better about it.
  • If they mention fear, threats or control, take it seriously and share Not safe at home?

Words you could use “Do you want to talk it through, or would it help more to take your mind off it?” “Whatever you decide about them, I’m on your side.”

When to get more help

Some hurts are too heavy to carry alone, and getting help takes some strength. Think about talking to a doctor, counsellor or therapist if:

  • More than a month after something frightening, you still have flashbacks, nightmares, feel constantly on edge, or avoid places and people that remind you of it. These can be signs of trauma, and there are well-tested treatments for it, such as trauma-focused talking therapies.
  • The hurt is taking over: you can’t sleep, work or enjoy anything, or you’re drinking or using more to cope.
  • The hurt came from abuse or violence, now or in the past. The page Free, private people to talk to (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#talk) includes specialist lines.
  • You’re having thoughts of hurting yourself or someone else. Please reach out today. In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number.

If you and someone else both want to mend things, a couples or family counsellor can help, as long as nobody is afraid of the other.

A limit to keep in mind: This chapter is for everyday hurts and for thinking about bigger ones. It isn’t therapy, and it isn’t a reason to stay somewhere unsafe. If you’re afraid of someone, the most healing step is getting safe. Not safe at home?

Part Three · Chapter 12

Helping others well: support without fixing, boundaries, and not burning out

How to help someone without taking over, by asking what they need, listening first, caring without drowning and keeping kind limits, with what to do in a crisis and how to keep going without burning out.

In this chapter

  1. Ask what kind of help they want
  2. Listening is a kind of help
  3. Fixing it for them can take away their power
  4. Care without drowning in their feelings
  5. Your limits make your help last
  6. Notice when you’re running on empty
  7. In a crisis, stay with them and bring in help
  8. Don’t wait for someone else to step in
  9. Let other people help you too
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. When to get more help
  14. Tools and reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

In short

  • Ask what kind of help they want. “Ideas, or just someone to listen?” saves a lot of misfires.
  • Listening is help. Fixing a problem for someone can take away their power.
  • Your limits make your help last, and caring from a steady place helps more than drowning in their feelings.
  • In a crisis, stay and bring in help. It’s okay to ask directly about suicide, and to call for help.

Wednesday, 7:15pm

Your friend is telling you about her awful week, and you have five good ideas before she’s finished her first sentence. You share all of them, in order, with reasons. She goes quiet and says, “Yeah, maybe.” You both hang up feeling a little worse, and neither of you could quite say why.

Most of us want to help the people around us, and helping well is a skill, because good intentions don’t always land. This chapter looks at how support works, why fixing can backfire and how to care for others in a way you can keep up. Two tools elsewhere grew out of it: One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, page 88), because carers burn out when everything counts as “just helping” and nobody else owns a job, and How much are you carrying? (Part Two, Chapter III, page 105), which helps you notice you’re running on empty before you snap or stop.

  1. Ask what kind of help they want.

    Help comes in different kinds. Some people want ideas, some want someone to listen, some want a practical hand such as a meal or a lift, and some just want company. Giving the wrong kind, however kindly, can leave someone feeling unheard, and the simplest fix is to ask.

    In the phone call above, a better start might have been, “That sounds like a rotten week. Do you want ideas, or do you just want to vent?” It feels slightly formal the first few times. People tend to love being asked.

    You could say “Would ideas help, or would you rather I just listened?” “What would help most right now?”

    Dig deeper: kinds of support

  2. Listening is a kind of help.

    Being truly heard helps people calm down and think, and quite often they find their own answer. Good listening means paying attention, letting them finish, checking you understood and showing that their feelings make sense, even if you would feel differently.

    Ravi comes home upset about his boss. His partner resists saying “Just quit” and says, “So he criticised you in front of everyone, after you stayed late all week. No wonder you’re furious.” Ravi’s shoulders drop. Ten minutes later he’s sketching out his own plan on the back of a takeaway menu, and it’s a better plan than “just quit”.

    Words you could use “So what happened was… Have I got that right?” “That makes sense. Anyone would feel that way.”

    In one conversation today, listen for two whole minutes without giving advice, then sum up what you heard. Two minutes is longer than you think.

    Dig deeper: how listening helps

    Sugarfoot

    Sometimes the best help is sitting close and listening, with no fixing. Listening takes energy too, so check your own tank now and then.

    Workpaper WP-02: How much are you carrying? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-02

  3. Fixing it for them can take away their power.

    When we love someone, we want to make the problem go away. Doing things for people that they could do themselves can leave them feeling less capable, though, so helping well often means helping someone do it themselves, which respects that it is their life and their choice.

    Rosalind’s twenty-four-year-old son is struggling with a job application for the council, and she is itching to rewrite it; she can see three things wrong with the first paragraph alone. She asks instead whether he’d like her to read it and say what stands out. He makes the changes himself, and when he gets the interview he’s quietly, enormously proud, and so is she, though she keeps that to herself.

    Things to tell yourself “Is this mine to fix, or theirs to solve with my support?” “What do they want to do here?”

    Dig deeper: support without taking over

  4. Care without drowning in their feelings.

    Feeling someone’s pain as if it were your own can wear you out fast. Researchers separate this “empathic distress” from compassion, which is warm concern from a steadier place, still caring deeply without sinking alongside the other person. A steady helper is more use than a second person drowning.

    When Abi’s housemate went through a breakup, Abi cried with her every night and stopped sleeping, and after a week she was wrecked. After that she stayed kind and present and also took breaks, a run in the mornings, an evening with her own friends, and kept reminding herself that this was her housemate’s pain to feel and hers to keep company with.

    Things to tell yourself “I can be with them in this without making it mine.” “I care, and I’m steady.”

    Dig deeper: empathy and compassion

  5. Your limits make your help last.

    Saying yes to everything leads in the long run to resentment, exhaustion and eventually to not being able to help at all. Limits tell people what you can give, so your yes means something, and a kind no that comes with an offer of what you can do is still help.

    Kojo’s sister keeps asking to borrow money, fifty here, eighty there, and none of it comes back. He loves her and he is running out. So he tells her, “I can’t lend money any more. I can help you go through your bills on Sunday, if you’d like.”

    Ways to say it “I can’t do that, but I can do this.” “I want to help, and I need to stop at nine tonight.”

    If there’s something you’re giving that you can’t keep giving, plan a smaller version you could offer instead.

    Dig deeper: boundaries in helping

    Professor Puddles

    Your limits keep your help going for longer. When you need to say “not this time”, Say no kindly helps you find the words, with something to offer instead.

    Tool: Say no kindly: make your scripts spreadloveandacceptance.com/refusals

  6. Notice when you’re running on empty.

    People who help a lot, such as carers, parents, nurses, teachers and the friend everyone calls, can burn out. The signs include feeling exhausted most of the time, or numb and cynical about the people you help, or dreading the next call. They mean that you need help too.

    Helen has looked after her husband since his stroke two years ago. She snaps at him over the remote control and then feels terrible for the rest of the day, and when she mentions it to her doctor, almost in passing, the doctor says it sounds like carer strain. A local carers’ group on Tuesday mornings and a few hours of respite each week give her back a little of herself.

    Thoughts you could try “Looking after myself is part of looking after them.”

    This week. Rate your energy from 1 to 10 each evening for a week. If it’s often 3 or lower, ask someone for one specific kind of help. See Caring for someone you love (spreadloveandacceptance.com/caregivers).

    Dig deeper: burnout and refilling

  7. In a crisis, stay with them and bring in help.

    If someone tells you they’re thinking of ending their life, or you’re worried they might be, it’s okay to ask them directly. Research, such as a review led by Dazzi and colleagues (2014), suggests asking about suicide doesn’t put the idea in someone’s head; it can bring relief. You don’t have to be their therapist. Your job is to listen, stay with them, and help them reach trained support.

    For example (a coworker): A colleague says, “Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me.” Kirsty says gently: “I’m really glad you told me. Are you thinking about ending your life?” She says she’s had thoughts. Kirsty stays with her and they call a crisis line together.

    Words to try “Are you thinking about suicide?” “I’m glad you told me. You don’t have to go through this alone. Let’s call someone together.”

    One small step. Save a crisis number in your phone now, so you have it if you ever need it. In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines. If someone is in immediate danger, call your local emergency number.

    Dig deeper: helping in a crisis

  8. Don’t wait for someone else to step in.

    When lots of people see something go wrong, each person can assume someone else will act. Psychologists call this the bystander effect, and knowing about it helps you break it. Small, safe actions count, such as asking “Are you okay?” or fetching a member of staff.

    On a train, a man is making a young woman uncomfortable, leaning in, asking where she’s getting off. Yvonne doesn’t confront him. She sits down next to the woman and asks brightly, “Hi! Is this the train to Leeds?” The woman joins in the chat with obvious relief, and at the next stop the man moves down the carriage.

    You could say “Are you okay? Do you need anything?” To someone else nearby: “Can you get the driver? I’ll stay here.”

    It helps to decide in advance what your safe move would be (distracting, getting help, checking in afterwards), because people with a plan act and people without one tend to freeze.

    Dig deeper: helping strangers and community

  9. Let other people help you too.

    Helping goes both ways, and people who are good at giving help are often bad at receiving it. Letting others help is a gift to them too, because most people like being useful to someone they care about, and relationships where only one person ever helps tend to feel uneven over time.

    Nkechi said “We’re fine, thanks” to every offer after the baby came, including several when she very much wasn’t. When she finally said yes to a neighbour’s offer of a lasagne, the neighbour was delighted. These days they walk their buggies round the park together on Thursday mornings. Say yes to the next small offer of help you get, even if you could manage without it.

    Words you could use “Yes, thank you. That would really help.” “Could you do one thing for me this week?”

    Dig deeper: receiving help

Your part, and only your part. You can offer help and listen well, and be honest about your limits. You can’t make someone accept help or get better on your timetable. Their life and their choices are theirs. If someone is in danger, your part is to bring in help, not to carry it alone.

The next Wednesday, 7:15pm

Your friend calls again, and this time you ask whether she wants ideas or just to talk it out. She laughs and says just talk, so you listen, through her manager and her landlord and the cat’s vet bill (£212, for a sock). At the end she says she thinks she knows what she’s going to do, and you realise you haven’t offered a single idea, and that it was a much better phone call.

In everyday life

Helping yourself counts too, and you can ask yourself the same question, whether you need ideas right now or just some rest. Caring for a parent or a child with extra needs is long-haul help, so share the load early (see Caring for someone you love). The friend everyone calls needs someone to call too. Covering for a struggling coworker is kind for a week, and after that it needs a real conversation with the team. In an emergency, point to one person, as in “You in the blue coat, please call for help,” because a crowd often waits for someone else. If you have ADHD, helping can feel interesting and urgent, so a fast yes comes easily, and “I’d like to help. Let me check my week and come back to you tonight” gives you time. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-12-helping-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

  • “Helping means solving the problem.” Often, helping means listening, being there or helping someone find their own answer.
  • “Good helpers never say no.” Good helpers last because they know their limits.
  • “Asking about suicide might give them the idea.” Research suggests it doesn’t, and asking can help someone open up.
  • “I’ll make it worse if I step in.” There are small, safe ways to help. Doing nothing often feels worse for the person in trouble.

If you want to help someone else with this

The helpers around you need looking after too.

  • Notice the helpers, such as the carer, the friend everyone calls and the coworker who always covers, and ask them how they are as if you mean it.
  • Offer specific help. “Can I take the kids on Saturday morning?” is easier to accept than “Let me know if you need anything.”
  • Give them permission to rest. “You’re allowed a night off. I’ve got this.”
  • If a helper seems burned out, share Caring for someone you love or suggest they talk to a doctor.

Ways to say it “You look after everyone. Who looks after you?” “I’d love to do something for you this week. What would help?”

When to get more help

  • If someone is in danger now, call your local emergency number.
  • If someone talks about suicide, stay with them and contact a crisis line together. In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines.
  • If someone tells you they’re being hurt or controlled at home, believe them, don’t confront the other person yourself, and share Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety)
  • If you’re burned out as a helper or carer, talk to your doctor, a carers’ organisation or a counsellor. Respite and support are not luxuries.
  • If helping someone is becoming unsafe for you, step back and bring in professionals. You can still care from a safer distance.

Tools and reading on the website

Tools helpers you use on the website

  • Library: empathic distress and compassion (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection) and social support (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection#social-support).
  • Library: burnout (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress) and caregiver strain (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress#caregiver-strain).
  • Library: saying no (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/communication#saying-no) and boundaries (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/communication#boundaries).

13

Part Three · Chapter 13

Anger: what it’s for and what to do with it

What anger is for, what to do in the hot minutes, how to repair afterwards, and how to tell when anger has turned into harm. For anyone, in any kind of relationship, or on your own.

In this chapter

  1. Anger is a signal about something that matters
  2. Anger often guards a softer feeling
  3. Anger rises in the body fast
  4. In the hot minutes: slow the body first
  5. Letting rip doesn’t empty it
  6. Step back and look from the outside
  7. Say it, don’t throw it
  8. After anger, repair
  9. When anger becomes harm
  10. If you’re a teenager
  11. In everyday life
  12. Common mix-ups
  13. If you want to help someone else with this
  14. When to get more help
  15. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  16. More for your situation

In short

  • Anger is a signal that something seems unfair, blocked or threatening. The feeling is allowed, and what you do with it is the part you choose.
  • The first minutes are about the body. Slow down, breathe out long, and step away with a time to come back.
  • Letting rip doesn’t empty anger. Shouting tends to feed it, while calming the body, putting it into words and repairing any sharp moments help more.
  • Anger that frightens, controls or hurts someone has become harm. That needs more help, and safety comes first.

Tuesday, 6:10pm

Your brother texts: “Can’t do Thursday after all, sorry!! Work thing.” Thursday is Mum’s hospital appointment, the one with the consultant, and this is the third time this month. Your jaw sets. Your face goes hot. Your thumbs are already typing “TYPICAL. You never…” and the message is one tap from sent.

Plenty of us were taught that anger was rude or dangerous, or grew up around anger that was frightening. Anger itself is a normal human feeling, though, and it very often points at something real. This chapter looks at how it works and then at what to do with it. It also sits under two tools elsewhere: the Calm-Down Kit (Part One, Now, page 35), which works because anger rises in the body first and slowing the body is what makes words possible, and letting a comment land before you react (Part Two, Chapter IV, page 120), which is the step back described further on.

  1. Anger is a signal about something that matters.

    Anger usually says that something is unfair, that someone is in your way, or that a line has been crossed. It pushes you towards a problem so you’ll change it. It can also land on the wrong person, or come out far bigger than the problem in front of it.

    Somebody keeps eating Shabnam’s lunch from the office fridge. Week one, she assumes a mistake. Week two, she writes her name on the box in marker pen. By week three her anger has told her clearly that a line has been crossed, and it’s the anger, frankly, that gets her to raise it at the Monday meeting. (It was the new starter. He thought the fridge was communal. He bought her a meal deal.) Next time you’re angry, finish this sentence privately: “I’m angry because something I care about, which is ___, seems ___.”

    Dig deeper: what anger is for

  2. Anger often guards a softer feeling.

    Anger can arrive first because it feels stronger and safer than what sits under it, whether that’s hurt or fear or shame or plain tiredness. Chapter 1 (page 152) calls this layers. The layer underneath usually tells you what you actually need.

    A father snaps at his sixteen-year-old for coming in an hour late. Under the anger is an hour spent at the front window, phone in hand, imagining the worst. When he tells her about that hour instead of the curfew, she hears it, and says sorry, and means it.

    You could say “I’m angry, and I think underneath I was really scared.” “I came across cross, but I think I’m actually hurt.”

    Dig deeper: what anger can cover

  3. Anger rises in the body fast.

    A hot face, a tight jaw, a pounding heart, a voice getting louder: that’s the body getting ready for a fight, and it can happen in seconds. When anger is high, careful thinking gets much harder, and so does listening. Chapter 2 (page 166) calls this being flooded, when you’re so stirred up that the thinking part of you goes quiet for a while.

    Halfway through an argument about whose turn it was to put the bins out, a woman notices her hands are shaking and realises she hasn’t heard a word her housemate has said for at least a minute. That’s her sign to stop. Learn your own early signs, two or three of them, like a tight jaw or talking faster, and treat them as your cue to slow down.

    Dig deeper: anger in the body

    Professor Puddles

    Anger moves faster than words. The Calm-Down Kit is a plan you make on a calm day, for the hot minutes.

    Workpaper WP-11: The Calm-Down Kit spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11

  4. In the hot minutes: slow the body first.

    When anger is high, settle your body before you try to sort anything out. Stop talking, or typing. Breathe out slowly, so the out-breath is longer than the in-breath. Unclench your hands, and if you can, move away for a while. A large review of 154 studies by Kjærvik and Bushman (2024) found that activities which calm the body, like slow breathing, relaxation and mindfulness, reduced anger, while ones that rev you up showed little or no benefit.

    A dad feels his temper going while he helps with fractions homework at the kitchen table. He says, “I’m getting frustrated, and that’s not your fault. I’m going to get a glass of water and come back in five minutes.” He comes back in five, and they finish the sheet together, and both of them get number six wrong.

    You could say “I’m too angry to talk well right now. I’ll come back at eight.” “I need ten minutes. I’m coming back to this conversation.”

    Make the plan on a calm day: your early sign, the words you’ll say, and where you’ll go for ten minutes. Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now) has steps for the hottest moments.

    Dig deeper: what to do in the moment

  5. Letting rip doesn’t empty it.

    A lot of people believe anger works like steam, so that shouting or slamming a door or hitting a pillow lets it out and leaves you calmer. It’s a lovely tidy idea, and the research doesn’t support it. In a well-known study by Bushman (2002), angry people who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who annoyed them ended up angrier than before.

    Going over what happened again and again in your head has a similar effect. In studies by Bushman and colleagues (2005), people who dwelt on a provocation were later more aggressive, even towards someone who only mildly annoyed them. Anger fades faster when the body is calmed and the mind has something else to do for a while.

    After a row with a colleague, a man spends his lunch break telling three different people how awful she is, and by the afternoon he’s angrier than he was at noon. The next time it happens he walks to the river and back instead, and by two o’clock he can think about the actual problem. If you catch yourself replaying an argument, set a timer for twenty minutes, do something absorbing, then come back to it.

    Dig deeper: venting and going over it

  6. Step back and look from the outside.

    Once your body has settled a bit, try looking at the moment as if you were watching from across the room. What happened? What might the other person have been dealing with? In experiments by Mischkowski, Kross and Bushman (2012), people who looked back on an annoying moment “like a fly on the wall”, instead of reliving it, felt less angry and acted less aggressively. Rethinking what happened, which psychologists call reappraisal (Gross, 1998), helps too.

    Furious that a friend has cancelled again, a woman imagines telling the whole story to a kind stranger on a train. Telling it that way, she remembers that her friend is caring for her dad, who has been in and out of hospital since June, and the anger turns slowly into worry. One way in is to write two lines about the moment with your own name instead of “I”: “Wes got angry because…” It feels odd. It also works.

    Dig deeper: stepping back

  7. Say it, don’t throw it.

    Anger is often a fair message sent in a hurtful way. Once you’re calmer you can still say you were angry, and why, without attacking anyone. A simple shape helps: what happened, how you felt, what you’re asking for.

    So instead of “You always let me down,” a woman says to her sister, “When you cancelled Mum’s appointment again, I felt really angry and alone with it. Can we make a plan for who takes her over the next three months?” It’s longer. It’s also the only version that ends with a plan. Write your angry message, then rewrite it in that shape before you send anything. Chapter 4 (page 195) has more on saying hard things.

    You could say “I was angry about what happened on Monday. Can I tell you why?” “When ___ happened, I felt ___, and what I’m asking for is ___.”

    Dig deeper: saying anger in words

    Sugarfoot

    Say it slowly, in one plain sentence. A soft start makes it far easier for the other person to hear you.

    Tool: Cool-down corner: soften a tense moment spreadloveandacceptance.com/tools/soften-a-tense-moment

  8. After anger, repair.

    Everyone gets angry, and most of us say something sharp now and then. What happens next matters a great deal. A short, real repair rebuilds trust, and it means naming what you did without a “but”, then saying what you’ll do differently.

    A grandmother shouts at her grandson when the blue vase from the hall table ends up in pieces, and he cries. An hour later she sits beside him on the stairs and says, “I shouted, and that was scary. You matter far more to me than the vase. I’m sorry.” He leans against her shoulder for a bit and then asks whether they can glue it. They try. It now has a visible crack and lives on the landing. Is there a recent moment when your anger landed on someone, and a short repair you could still make? Chapter 11 (page 292) has more on apologies that land.

    You could say “I was sharp with you earlier. That wasn’t fair, and I’m sorry.” “I’m still upset about what happened, and I also shouldn’t have spoken to you that way.”

    Dig deeper: repair after anger

  9. When anger becomes harm.

    Feeling angry is human. But some things done in anger are harm, whatever the feeling behind them: hitting, pushing, throwing things at or near someone, breaking their things, threatening, shouting so someone is scared, or using anger to control what another person does, wears, spends or who they see. People walking on eggshells around you is a sign too. Anger is never a reason someone deserves to be hurt.

    For example, a man realises his partner and children go quiet when he comes home in a bad mood. He doesn’t hit anyone, but they are afraid of him. He talks to his doctor and joins an anger course.

    You could say “I think my anger is scaring people I love. I want help with it.” (If it’s happening to you) “I’m frightened of how they get when they’re angry.”

    Try this. If this sounds like you, see Find a counsellor or therapist (spreadloveandacceptance.com/outside-help) and the Cool-down corner. If you’re afraid of someone else’s anger, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private help.

    Dig deeper: when anger becomes harm

Your part, and only your part. You can learn your early signs, settle your body, say what made you angry in words, and repair when you get it wrong. You can’t make someone else calm down, and you don’t have to accept being shouted at, threatened or controlled. If someone else’s anger frightens you, getting safe matters more than working it out. Not safe at home?

Tuesday, 6:40pm

You put the phone face down on the arm of the sofa and walk round the block, breathing out long. Somewhere near the postbox on the corner you notice what’s under the anger. You’re tired, and you’re frightened about Mum. Back home you delete the capitals and write, “I’m really frustrated. This is the third time and I feel alone with Mum’s care. Can we talk tonight and make a plan?”

He reads it at 6:52. By ten o’clock there’s still no reply, and you go to bed not knowing who’ll drive her on Thursday. You sent the message you can stand behind. That part is done, even if the rest of it isn’t.

zqaxunderstandingx13xangerxxteensqzIf you’re a teenager

Maisie is sixteen, and at ten o’clock her dad takes her phone, right in the middle of a group chat about Saturday. She shouts and slams her bedroom door hard enough to rattle the picture on the landing. The next morning, calmer, she tells him it felt as if he didn’t trust her, says sorry for the door, and asks for ten minutes’ warning next time. He agrees, and adds that he’d much rather hear this over breakfast than through a door.

Being angry with a parent is normal, and arguments often feel most intense in the middle teens. A rule given out of care is not control, even when it feels unfair, and a calm request the next day works more often than a slammed door.

You could say “I’m too angry to talk properly. Can we talk tomorrow?” “I don’t mind the rule so much as how it happened.” “Could we try it for two weeks and then check?”

Dig deeper: more worked examples

In everyday life

Anger at yourself counts too. “I’m so stupid” is anger turned inward, and it helps to talk to yourself the way you would to a friend who’d made the same mistake (Chapter 7, page 236, goes further). With a partner, agree a pause word on a calm day, and a time you’ll always come back. Children copy what we do with anger far more than anything we say about it. At work anger is common and rarely spoken, and “I’m frustrated about the deadline change. Can we talk about what’s realistic?” keeps it useful.

If you have ADHD, anger can arrive fast and big and then go just as quickly, so plan for the speed: a three-word pause line like “Back in ten”, and a rule to wait before you send anything. If you’re managing a clash between two other people, hear each of them alone first and then together, always about what happened and never about each other. The fight is often about the setup, two people who both believe they own the same job. The full chapter has a worked example (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-13-anger-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

Anger itself isn’t a bad feeling. It’s normal and it carries information; it’s some of the things done in anger that cause harm. Letting it out isn’t the healthy option it sounds like, because shouting or hitting things tends to keep anger going. “They made me angry, so it’s their fault I shouted” mixes up two things: someone can do something unfair, and what you do next is still yours. And holding it in isn’t as safe as it looks. Anger swallowed for years tends to come out sideways, as coldness or sarcasm or a sudden explosion over a teaspoon, so saying it calmly and early is the safer route.

If you want to help someone else with this

Keep yourself safe first. If someone’s anger scares you, step away; you don’t have to stay and calm them down. Otherwise speak lower and slower, and leave the argument until they’ve come down. Then listen for the message under it. There’s often something fair in there, and you can take that part seriously while still saying that the way it was said wasn’t okay.

You could say “I want to hear this, and I can’t while we’re both shouting. Can we try again at seven?” “I can tell this really matters to you.”

When to get more help

Everyone gets angry. It may be time to talk to a doctor, a counsellor or an anger management course if:

  • your anger feels out of control, or you often regret what you do or say when angry;
  • people close to you seem nervous or walk on eggshells around you;
  • you have hit, pushed, thrown things, broken things or threatened anyone;
  • anger is hurting your work, your friendships or your health;
  • you are using alcohol or drugs to cope with angry feelings.

Help for anger works for many people: a review of anger treatments by Del Vecchio and O’Leary (2004) found medium to large benefits. It is good for your health too: a review by Chida and Steptoe (2009) linked anger and hostility with a higher risk of heart disease. Asking for help is a responsible thing to do. Find a counsellor or therapist (spreadloveandacceptance.com/outside-help#counsellor) lists places to start, some of them free, and the Cool-down corner helps in the hot minutes.

If you are afraid of someone else’s anger, that fear is an important signal. Not safe at home? lists free, private help. If you or anyone is in danger right now, call your local emergency number.

This chapter is general education, not therapy.

zqunderstandingx14xpersonalityqz

14

Part Three · Chapter 14

Personality, temperament and change across life

What personality is, where temperament comes in, how people change across their lives, and how to live and work with people who are made differently from you, without putting anyone in a box.

In this chapter

  1. Traits work like dials
  2. Temperament is the starting point
  3. Situations matter too
  4. Introvert and extravert is about energy, not liking people
  5. People change across life
  6. You can change on purpose, a little at a time
  7. Every trait has gifts and costs
  8. Differences are usually about fit
  9. In everyday life
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. When to get more help
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In short

  • Traits work like dials. Everyone sits somewhere along each one, and most people are near the middle.
  • Temperament is a starting point. Babies already differ in how active, cautious or easily upset they are, and what happens next matters too.
  • People keep changing. On average people grow steadier and more organised as they get older, and you can change on purpose, slowly.
  • Most clashes between personalities are about fit, and nobody has to be at fault.

Saturday, 3:00pm

Your aunt’s seventieth, in the function room above the cricket club. You’re standing by the cake, minding your own business, when she tells the whole room, “Oh, she was always the shy one!”

Everybody laughs. You laugh. Something stings.

You’re forty-two. Every weekday at twenty to nine you stand in front of thirty eight-year-olds and get them to sit down, which takes some doing. So are you still the shy one? Were you ever?

We describe each other by personality all the time. Laid-back. A worrier. The organised one. And descriptions like those have a way of setting hard. This chapter is about how personality actually works, what stays put and what moves. Two tools elsewhere build on it. The “How to talk to me” card and the style quiz (Part One, Now, page 35) describe how you lean on a few dials, which is more use than knowing which box somebody once put you in. And One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, page 88) arranges the jobs round people’s differences, so nobody has to turn into someone else to share a house.

  1. Traits work like dials.

    Personality is the usual pattern in how you think and feel and act. Many psychologists describe it with five broad traits, often called the “Big Five”: openness (curious about new ideas and experiences), conscientiousness (organised and careful), extraversion (drawn to people and busy places), agreeableness (warm and cooperative) and emotional stability (how steady your moods are).

    The same five turned up in work such as McCrae and Costa (1987), whether people rated themselves or were rated by people who knew them well. Each runs from low to high, and most people sit near the middle of most of them. That’s the bit online quizzes leave out. Two friends did one on the train to Brighton and were told, very confidently, that one was an introvert and the other an extravert. Then they looked at the actual numbers. Four points apart, both bang in the middle. They spent the rest of the journey arguing about which of them was more middle.

    If you’re curious, mark where you think you sit on each dial from one to ten, and ask a close friend where they’d put you. The gap is often the interesting bit.

    Dig deeper: the five dials

  2. Temperament is the starting point.

    Temperament is the part of personality you can see very early on. Some babies are on the go from the moment they wake. Some are calm. Some take to a new routine straight away and some need a week. Some flinch at every loud noise. In their long-running study, Thomas and Chess (1977) described these early differences and the idea of “goodness of fit”, meaning how well a child’s temperament suits what the people and places round them expect.

    Isla is two and cried at every new playgroup. Her mum tried coaxing her into the circle, then bribing her, then (once, quietly) begging. In the end she just sat at the edge of the church hall with Isla on her lap, feeling a bit of a lemon, while everyone else did “The Wheels on the Bus”. It smelled of orange squash and floor polish. Week three, Isla climbed down on her own, walked to the sand table, and didn’t look back. Her mum, slightly put out, had a biscuit.

    You could say “You like to watch first. That’s fine. Join in when you’re ready.” (to yourself) “I need time to warm up. That’s how I’m made.”

    Dig deeper: temperament and fit

  3. Situations matter too.

    Personality describes a pattern, and patterns have exceptions. The same person can be loud with family and quiet at work, endlessly patient with toddlers and very short with call centres. A trait tells you what someone tends to do across lots of situations. It tells you much less about this one.

    Anita had decided her new colleague was cold. Polite, competent, cold. Then came the charity football match, and there he was in a borrowed bib two sizes too small, shouting encouragement at a goalkeeper who was letting in everything. On Monday Anita sat looking round the open-plan office with its grey partitions and humming lights and wondered how much of what she’d seen was the room.

    Dig deeper: person and situation

  4. Introvert and extravert is about energy, not liking people.

    People who are more introverted often like people a lot. What they find is that busy, noisy company uses energy up, and they need quiet afterwards to get it back. People who are more extraverted tend to be topped up by company. Most of us are a mix (sometimes called an ambivert), and every point on the dial just needs different things to be at its best.

    Eleven o’clock at a wedding in a barn outside Hexham. Fraser wants the after-party in the village pub. Luke wants bed and silence and possibly never to hear “Mr Brightside” again. They’ve had this exact standoff at four previous weddings. This time Fraser goes for an hour and Luke walks back to the hotel along the lane with his shoes in his hand, and they meet at breakfast, one of them hoarse and the other one smug, both of them happy.

    Words you could use “I loved tonight, and I’m out of social energy.” “Shall we go together, and I’ll head home at ten?”

    Dig deeper: introversion and extraversion

    Tidbit

    Some people recharge in a busy park and some under a quiet blanket. Both are fine. A short quiz can show you your own style.

    Tool: How you connect: the 2-minute style quiz spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength

  5. People change across life.

    Personality is fairly stable. It also moves. A large review by Roberts, Walton and Viechtbauer (2006) found that, on average, people become more organised, more emotionally steady and more confident with others as they move through adult life, with much of the change between 20 and 40. A later review by Bleidorn and colleagues (2022) found that emotional steadiness went on growing right across the lifespan. Big life events play a part, and so do the roles people take on and who they love.

    At school Tunde lost his keys about once a fortnight and once turned up to a maths exam on the wrong day. He’s a charge nurse now, forty-six, the calm one people look for when it goes wrong at three in the morning. At the reunion his old friends kept staring at him. “What happened to you?” one of them said. He thought about it. “Life kept asking me to cope,” he said, “and eventually I learned how. Also I have a key hook.”

    Thoughts you could try “Who I was at fifteen isn’t who I have to be now.” “People I knew years ago may have changed too.”

    Dig deeper: how personality changes with age

  6. You can change on purpose, a little at a time.

    If you want to change a trait you can, slowly, mostly by acting differently in small ways over and over. In a study by Hudson and Fraley (2015), people who set goals to change one of their traits tended to move in the direction they wanted over sixteen weeks. A review by Roberts and colleagues (2017) found that therapy was often linked to lasting change too, especially towards more emotional steadiness.

    Noor wanted to be less quiet at work. She made a rule. One thing in every team meeting, even if it was only “I agree with Neil”. The first fortnight her heart thudded so hard she was sure people could see it through her jumper. By the end of the second month it had become ordinary, and somewhere in the third month she forgot it had ever been a rule. Pick one small thing that fits who you’d like to be more of, and do it three times this week. Chapter 6 (page 223) has more on habits.

    Dig deeper: changing on purpose

  7. Every trait has gifts and costs.

    There’s no good personality. Every trait helps in some places and gets in the way in others. Very agreeable people are lovely to be around and may find “no” almost impossible to say. Very conscientious people are the ones you’d leave your keys with, and they can’t always stop. People high in openness love anything new and can be bored to tears by routine.

    For most of a year Alys was irritated by her housemate. His trainers in the hall. His “it’ll be fine”. Then the boiler died on the coldest night in January, and while Alys stood in the kitchen in her coat reading the manual, he rang round until he found a plumber who’d come out at ten o’clock, and then he filled everybody’s hot water bottles from the kettle. “It’ll be fine,” he said. It was, more or less.

    A one-page card, “How to talk to me” (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card), turns a trait people complain about into plain information about what helps.

    Dig deeper: gifts and costs

    Professor Puddles

    Every trait has gifts and costs. Writing down what helps you on a one-page card turns a “flaw” into useful information.

    Tool: How you connect: how I like to be spoken to spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card

  8. Differences are usually about fit.

    When two people with different personalities share a home or a family or a job, friction is normal. A tidy person and a relaxed one can both be right in their own way, and so can a planner and someone spontaneous, or a talker and someone who needs quiet. What helps is naming the difference and agreeing how to live with it, without either of you being the problem. Personality is also different from neurodivergence and from mental health conditions. If something feels bigger than personality, Chapter 9 (page 261) may help.

    A couple argue about every single holiday, because one wants every hour planned and the other wants to wander about and see what happens. This year they plan the mornings and leave the afternoons free. They still argue about the mornings. I’d count that as progress.

    Ways to say it “I think we’re just made differently here. What would work for both of us?” “I’m a planner and you’re not. Can we plan half and leave half?”

    Dig deeper: fit, not fault

Your part, and only your part. You can get to know your own mix, look after what you need, and practise one small change if you want to. You can’t change someone else’s personality, and you don’t have to change yours to be loved. If you’re always the one bending to fit, it’s fair to say so. Know your own wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself)

Saturday, 5:30pm

People are drifting off with slices of cake in kitchen roll. You think about sitting down next to your aunt and telling her about the thirty eight-year-olds. You don’t. You help stack the plates. On the drive home you’re still turning it over, half cross with her and half with yourself, and somewhere round the ring road you start drafting what you’ll say at Christmas if she does it again. It’s quite a good line, actually. You probably won’t use it.

In everyday life

On your own

Knowing your own mix helps you build a life that suits you, with about the right amount of company and quiet. “I’m just not a people person” might be true. It might also be an old label that deserves testing at least once. With a partner, a shared plan (one does the bills, the other does holidays) usually goes better than trying to change each other. A quiet friend who hardly texts may still care a great deal, so ask what kind of contact suits them. A child’s temperament says nothing about good or bad parenting, and adjusting to fit them is a skill you pick up. And family roles like “the clever one” or “the difficult one” can hang on long after they stop fitting. You’re allowed to grow out of them, whether or not your aunt has noticed.

Common mix-ups

You aren’t simply an introvert or an extravert. Most people are somewhere in the middle, and where you sit shifts with the setting and your mood. Personality isn’t set in stone by thirty, either. It keeps moving slowly all through life. Online type quizzes are good for fun and for starting a conversation, and that includes the website’s own Wave Code, which shows four leanings on four dials, but they sort people into a handful of types when real people are spread along each dial. “They’re just difficult” often means “they’re different from me”, and it can hide stress or illness or a need nobody has asked about. And practising something new isn’t being fake. It feels odd at first, like new shoes, and then it’s yours.

If you want to help someone else with this

Drop the old labels. Notice if you still describe someone the way they were twenty years ago. Ask instead of guessing. “What helps you recharge?” or “How do you like to plan things?” will tell you more than any theory. Say it when you see someone grow, because “You handled that so calmly” can show a person a change they hadn’t spotted. And describe what happened, not who someone is. “You’re so uptight” shuts doors that a plain description would leave open.

Words to try “I used to think of you as the shy one. I don’t think that fits any more.” “What do you need to be at your best this week?”

When to get more help

Personality differences are normal and don’t need fixing. It may be worth talking to a doctor, counsellor or psychologist if:

  • a pattern in how you feel, think or relate to people keeps causing you or others real distress, across many parts of life;
  • you feel very unsure who you are, or your moods swing so much it’s hard to cope;
  • worry, low mood or fear of people is stopping you from living the life you want.

Please don’t diagnose yourself or anyone else with a “personality disorder” from what you read online. Those are clinical terms that only a qualified professional can use, after a proper assessment.

A personality trait never excuses controlling, frightening or hurtful behaviour. If you’re afraid of someone close to you, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private help.

This chapter is general education, not a diagnosis or therapy.
