Part Three · Chapter 15

Closeness and love: being known, at every age

How closeness grows, what it means to feel truly known, how love changes over the years, and how it looks in every kind of relationship, at every age, including for people on their own.

In this chapter

  1. Love comes in many forms
  2. Closeness grows from being known
  3. Closeness is built a step at a time
  4. Feeling understood matters most
  5. Old maps show up in love
  6. Love changes over time
  7. Love at every age
  8. Love is something you do
  9. If you’re a teenager
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. When to get more help
  14. Reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

Friday, 10:30pm

You and Charlie have shared a home for eleven years. Tonight you’re both on the sofa and both on your phones, a cooking programme on in the background that neither of you is watching, and you realise you can’t remember the last time the two of you talked about anything except bills, the boiler and whose turn it is to cook. You love Charlie. You feel oddly alone in the same room.

This chapter is about closeness in all its forms, far beyond romance. It looks at what helps people feel near to each other, and why closeness fades and how it grows back, and it builds on Chapter 5 (page 210), on attachment and trust.

  1. Love comes in many forms.

    The ancient Greeks had several words for love, for friends, for family, for romantic partners and for strangers. People love in many ways today too. There are lifelong friendships, partners of any gender, people with more than one partner, chosen family, people who are asexual or aromantic and build deep closeness without romance or sex, and people on their own who pour love into friends, family, pets, work and community. A life can be full of love without a partner in it.

    A woman in her fifties who has never wanted a partner describes her best friend of thirty years as her great love story. They have been through two house moves, one cancer scare, a disastrous caravan holiday in Tenby and more Sunday phone calls than either of them could count. Try writing down three or more people you love, of any kind, and next to each one the way you show it. The list is usually longer than people expect.

    Dig deeper: the many forms of love

  2. Closeness grows from being known.

    Intimacy is about much more than touch or romance, and at its heart is being known. The psychologists Reis and Shaver described it as a back-and-forth, in which one person shares something real about themselves and the other responds in a way that leaves them feeling understood and cared for. In a diary study by Laurenceau, Barrett and Pietromonaco (1998), feeling that the other person really responded was a big part of what made everyday conversations feel intimate.

    Two brothers who mostly talk about football are driving to their dad’s care home when one admits that he finds the visits really hard. The other says he does too, and that he always feels guilty on the way home. It’s the longest conversation they’ve had in years, and it lasts all the way to the car park, where they sit with the engine off for another ten minutes. Sharing one small, true thing with someone you care about (a worry, a hope, something that made you happy this week) and noticing how they respond is the same thing on a smaller scale.

    Dig deeper: intimacy as being known

  3. Closeness is built a step at a time.

    People usually get close by sharing a little more, and then a little more, when it feels safe. In a well-known study by Aron and colleagues (1997), pairs of strangers who took turns asking gradually more personal questions, now known as the “36 questions”, felt closer after forty-five minutes than pairs who made small talk. The same idea works in friendships and long relationships, where closeness grows when both people take small, matched steps. Two new neighbours start with the weather and the parking, which in their street is a serious subject. A few months later one asks how the other’s mum is getting on. Some time after that, over the fence, one of them says, “Can I tell you what’s really been going on?”

    Next time you talk to someone you would like to know better, ask one question a little deeper than usual, such as what has been on their mind lately, and if they answer, share something of your own back.

    Dig deeper: building closeness step by step

    Professor Puddles

    Closeness grows when you know what feels like care to the other person, not just to you. A “What feels like care” card is a gentle way to find out.

    Tool: How you connect: what feels like care spreadloveandacceptance.com/love-languages

  4. Feeling understood matters most.

    What makes someone feel loved is often less about grand gestures and more about feeling understood. Researchers call this responsiveness, meaning noticing, understanding and caring about what matters to the other person, and it shows in small moments such as how you react to good news. Gable and colleagues (2004) found that people whose partners usually met their good news with real interest and warmth felt closer and more satisfied together. When a teenager announces that she’s been picked for the school band, her grandad puts the paper down, smiles, and asks which instrument and when the first concert is. She talks for twenty minutes, mostly about the trombone section. The next time someone shares good news with you, put your phone face down and ask two follow-up questions. That’s the whole method.

    Dig deeper: responsiveness

  5. Old maps show up in love.

    The patterns from Chapter 5 (page 210) often come out most strongly with the people we love most. Hazan and Shaver (1987) suggested that adult love uses the same attachment system as childhood bonds. When closeness feels shaky, some people reach harder for reassurance and others pull back to feel safe, and both are ways of protecting something precious. When his partner goes quiet, Leo texts five times in an hour, while his partner, who goes quiet in order to calm down, feels crowded. They agree that his partner will say, “I need an hour, and I’ll message you at eight,” and Leo finds, somewhat to his surprise, that he can wait for a known time. What he couldn’t bear was the not knowing. It’s worth noticing what you do when closeness feels shaky, and telling someone you trust what helps you feel safe again.

    Dig deeper: attachment in adult love

  6. Love changes over time.

    Early love is often intense, with racing thoughts and a lot of longing, and over the years it usually settles into something calmer and deeper. A review by Acevedo and Aron (2009) found that some people in long relationships still report strong romantic love, without the anxious, obsessive edge of early love, and that this was linked to being happier together.

    In experiments by Aron and colleagues (2000), couples who tried a new, mildly challenging activity together felt better about their relationship afterwards than couples given a dull task. After twenty-five years, one couple sign up for a pottery class at the community centre. They’re both terrible at it. They laugh all evening and bring home a bowl that won’t stand up, and on the way home one of them says it felt like a date. I’d take new over big: a new walk, a new recipe, a new café in the next town.

    Dig deeper: how love changes

    Sugarfoot

    Little rituals, like a Sunday walk or a goodnight text, keep love warm through the years. Look after the ones you already have.

    Workpaper WP-15: Keep your little rituals alive spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-15

  7. Love at every age.

    Love looks different across a life. Teenagers’ first loves can be huge and real, and adults juggle love with work and children and, often, ageing parents. Many older people choose to spend their time with fewer, closer people, which Carstensen and colleagues (1999) linked to feeling that time is more limited, so that the most meaningful relationships matter more. People find new love at seventy and eighty, and people lose great loves and carry them always. A widower of seventy-eight meets a woman at his walking group, and when his children are surprised he tells them, “I loved your mother for fifty years. I still do. And I’m allowed to be happy now.”

    If it feels right, ask someone from another generation about love in their life. Older relatives usually have stories nobody has asked for.

    Dig deeper: love across the lifespan

  8. Love is something you do.

    Feelings of love come and go, while the actions of love can be steady. They include turning towards someone when they speak, keeping small promises, saying thank you and sorry, and making room for who they are. Physical closeness, like a hug or holding hands, matters a lot to some people and less to others, and sex is part of closeness in some relationships and not in others. What matters is that both people feel comfortable and free to say yes or no. Love never includes fear, threats or control.

    A woman notices that her friend has gone quiet since his divorce. She has never once said she loves him. Every Thursday she texts the single word “Walk?” and turns up at his door at six, in her old wax jacket, whatever the weather. Ask someone you love what small thing makes them feel cared for, and do it this week.

    Dig deeper: love as action

Your part, and only your part. You can share a little of yourself, listen well, turn towards the people you love and keep small promises. You can’t make someone love you, or love you in the way you want. If closeness keeps hurting you, or you feel afraid, that is not a failure of love on your part. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety)

The next Friday, 10:30pm

This time you leave both phones on the kitchen counter, make two cups of tea and ask Charlie what they’ve been thinking about lately that they haven’t told you. Charlie is quiet for a moment and then talks about their dad getting older, and how they dread the phone ringing late at night. You listen, and then you talk about the restructure at work. The tea goes cold, and it is midnight before either of you looks at the clock.

If you’re a teenager

First love can be huge and real, and so can a first breakup. Ines is sixteen when she is dumped by message on a Tuesday night, and she cries until two in the morning. Being told by adults that she will get over it doesn’t help. Telling her cousin, who simply listens, does, along with muting the chat instead of rereading it and a rule of no checking his profile after ten. A few weeks later she notices that a whole day has gone by without her thinking about him.

You could say “I don’t need advice, I just need to tell someone.” “Can we reply when we can, rather than all day?” And if you are the one ending it, “I don’t want to go out any more. I’m sorry. It isn’t about something you did wrong.”

Dig deeper: more worked examples

In everyday life

On your own

Being single, widowed, divorced or happily alone doesn’t mean a life without love, because friendships, family, community and the way you treat yourself are all places where love lives. If you want a partner and don’t have one, that longing is real and worth being gentle with (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). Most partners drift into talking only about jobs and bills, and one real question a week can bring them back. Friendship needs tending like any other love, and families often love each other deeply and say it rarely, so a short “I’m glad you’re my sister” can mean a great deal.

  • Different levels of desire. This is very common in long relationships and is nobody’s fault. Talk at a calm time, keep some affection that doesn’t have to lead anywhere, and remember that a kind “no” is a no to the moment and never a rejection of the person. A qualified sex therapist or couples therapist can help. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-15-love-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

The spark fading doesn’t mean love is over; early intensity usually settles, and many long relationships stay warm and close and lively for decades. Nobody reads minds, either, however much they love you, so saying what helps is a gift and not a failure of romance.

  • “Jealousy proves love.” Feeling jealous is human, and asking for something out of care for the relationship is not control. Checking up without agreement, cutting someone off or punishing them is not love. See signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#signs).

If you want to help someone else with this

Respect their kind of love, without assuming that everyone wants a partner or children. Be a safe person to tell things to, which means listening without judging and keeping what they share private. After a loss or a breakup, keep showing up, because many people get plenty of support for two weeks and very little after that.

  • If you’re worried about someone’s relationship, stay close and kind rather than criticising their partner. If they seem afraid, gently share Not safe at home?

Words you could use “I’m always glad to hear from you.” “You don’t have to explain your relationship to me. I just want you to be happy and safe.”

When to get more help

  • If you feel very lonely or low most days for two weeks or more, talk to a doctor or counsellor.
  • If closeness feels frightening, or you keep ending up in relationships that hurt you, a counsellor or therapist can help you understand why.
  • Couples or family counselling can help when you feel stuck, or keep having the same fight.
  • If someone you love controls you, frightens you, checks your phone, cuts you off from friends or pressures you into anything you don’t want, that isn’t love. Not safe at home? lists free, private help.
  • If you’re in danger now, call your local emergency number. Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now) can help you take the first step.

This chapter is general education, not therapy.

  • The languages of connection (spreadloveandacceptance.com/languages-of-connection), on the different ways people show care.

Part Three · Chapter 16

Worry, low mood and trauma

How worry and anxiety work, the difference between a low patch and depression, what trauma is and isn’t, what helps day to day, how to support someone, and when and where to get more help. For anyone, in any kind of relationship, or on your own.

In this chapter

  1. Worry and anxiety are the body’s alarm
  2. Avoiding keeps fear going
  3. Give worry a time and a place
  4. Low mood is common. Depression is more than a bad week
  5. Doing often comes before feeling better
  6. Sleep, moving and people do a lot of the work
  7. Trauma is about what happened, and what it left behind
  8. After something frightening: safety, choice and no pressure
  9. Talking therapies help many people, and medicines can too
  10. If you’re a teenager
  11. In everyday life
  12. Common mix-ups
  13. If you want to help someone else with this
  14. When to get more help
  15. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  16. More for your situation

In short

  • Worry, low mood and the after-effects of trauma are common, human and treatable. They are not weakness, and they are not your fault.
  • They all run through the stress system from Chapter 2 (page 166). Small, steady things that settle the body and reconnect you with life help more than big pushes.
  • Avoiding and withdrawing feel safer but keep things going. Small steps back in, a little at a time, help most.
  • Talking therapies work for many people, and so can medicines. If it has lasted weeks, is getting in the way of life, or you feel unsafe, get help. If you might act on thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 (US) or call Samaritans on 116 123 (UK and Ireland) now.

Sunday, 10:50pm

The house is quiet. You’ve checked the front door twice and the back door once. Tomorrow is the hospital appointment, ten o’clock, and the same three thoughts keep going round: what if it’s bad, what if you can’t cope, what if there’s nobody to tell. Your chest is tight and your mind won’t stop. And if you’re honest, you haven’t really wanted to see anyone for a few weeks now. Even answering messages has started to feel like too much.

Almost everyone worries, feels low or goes through something frightening at some point. For some people the feelings settle by themselves. For others they stick, and grow, until they shape every day. This chapter explains how they work, what tends to help, and when it’s time to ask for more. It can’t diagnose anyone. If any of this is about you right now, you aren’t alone, and things can get better.

Some tools elsewhere in the books lean on this chapter. The daily check-in’s “low, medium or high” (Part Two, Chapter I, page 75) lets the people around you adjust when worry or low mood has shrunk the room you have. “A full tank means later, not never” (Part Two, Chapter III, page 105) names a time to come back, because avoiding a thing keeps fear going. And picking one small goal (Part One, Next, page 50) suits low mood, since doing very often comes before feeling better.

  1. Worry and anxiety are the body’s alarm.

    Fear is the body’s alarm for danger that is here now. Anxiety is the same alarm ringing about something that might happen, and worry is the thinking part, the “What if…?” on repeat. All three run through the stress system described in Chapter 2 (page 166): a racing heart, a tight chest, shallow breathing, a churning stomach, poor sleep. The alarm is trying to protect you. The trouble is that it can be set too sensitive, and it can’t tell a real tiger from a worrying email.

    A fifteen-year-old’s heart pounds before every presentation in class. Nothing bad has ever happened in one. Her alarm still treats a room of her own classmates, half of whom she’s known since primary school, as a dangerous place. When worry rises, breathe out slowly five times, each out-breath longer than the in-breath, then name three things you can see. It tells the body that the danger isn’t here right now.

    Things to tell yourself “This is my alarm talking, and alarms can be wrong.” “My body is getting ready to protect me. I can thank it and carry on.”

    Dig deeper: how anxiety works

  2. Avoiding keeps fear going.

    When something makes us anxious, stepping away brings quick relief, and the relief teaches the brain that escaping was a good idea. So next time the fear is a little bigger and the world a little smaller. What helps is going back towards the feared thing in small, chosen steps, and staying long enough to learn that you can cope. Therapists call this exposure. Craske and colleagues (2014) describe how it works best when each step tests what you expect to happen.

    After a panic attack on the number 42, a man starts walking everywhere, even in the rain, even the three miles to work. With his sister beside him he rides one stop, then two. Some weeks later he does the whole journey into town, and his brain has slowly learned that buses are survivable. Pick one small thing you’ve been avoiding, break it into three steps from easiest to hardest, and do the easiest one this week.

    Things to tell yourself “What do I think will happen? Let’s see what actually happens.” “Uncomfortable isn’t the same as dangerous.”

    Dig deeper: avoidance and small steps
  3. zqaxunderstandingx16xworryxxworryxtimeqz

    Give worry a time and a place.

    Trying hard not to worry rarely works. What helps a lot of people is postponing it: you notice a worry, write it down, and save it for a set “worry time” later in the day. In an early study by Borkovec and colleagues (1983), people who practised this for four weeks reported worrying less each day. In worry time, ask of each worry whether there’s something you can do about it. If there is, plan one step. If there isn’t, practise letting it go.

    A man caring for his own father keeps a worry notebook by the kettle, a small red one. At six in the evening he gives it fifteen minutes with a cup of tea, and by then many of the morning’s worries already look smaller, and a couple have sorted themselves out. Choose a fifteen-minute worry time well before bed.

    Thoughts you could try “Noted. I’ll think about that at six.” “Can I do anything about this today? If not, it can wait.”

    Dig deeper: worry time and problem-solving

  4. Low mood is common. Depression is more than a bad week.

    Everyone has low days, and sadness after a loss or a disappointment is normal. Depression is different. It means low mood, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy, for most of the day, nearly every day, for two weeks or more, often with poor sleep, tiredness, changes in appetite, feeling worthless or guilty, and finding it hard to think. It can look like sadness. It can also look like irritability, or simply running on empty. It is a health problem, and nobody gets it by being weak.

    A retired teacher notices he has stopped going to his Thursday walking group, isn’t reading, and wakes at four every morning. He tells himself he’s just getting old, until his daughter, on a visit, gently suggests it might be depression and that depression can be treated. If you’ve felt low or lost interest most days for two weeks or more, book a talk with a doctor this week, and write down what you’ve noticed to take with you.

    You could say “I’ve not been myself for a few weeks, and I don’t think it’s just tiredness.” “I don’t enjoy things I used to. Can I talk to you about it?”

    Dig deeper: low mood and depression

  5. Doing often comes before feeling better.

    Low mood tells you to wait until you feel like it. Withdrawing makes life emptier, though, and that deepens the low. A well-tested approach called behavioural activation turns this round: you plan small, doable things that bring a bit of pleasure or a sense of having done something, and you do them whether you feel like it or not. A review of 26 trials by Ekers and colleagues (2014) found it helped with depression, though many of the studies were small.

    A woman living alone after her divorce plans three small things a day: a ten-minute walk to the postbox and back, one call or message, and one job she can finish, like wiping the hob. Some days they feel pointless. She does them anyway. Over a few weeks the days begin to feel less flat, though she couldn’t tell you which day it changed. Tomorrow, try three tiny things of your own, one for pleasure, one for connection and one you can finish.

    Things to tell yourself “I don’t have to feel like it to do it.” “Small counts.”

    Dig deeper: behavioural activation

  6. Sleep, moving and people do a lot of the work.

    These sound too simple to matter. The evidence for them is solid. Improving sleep can lift mood: in a large trial with university students, Freeman and colleagues (2017) found that an online sleep course reduced insomnia, and with it some other mental health difficulties.

    Exercise helps depression too. A review of 218 trials by Noetel and colleagues (2024) found walking or jogging, yoga and strength training all helped. Belonging to groups protects as well. Cruwys and colleagues (2013) found that people with depression who joined groups were less likely to relapse. A new dad who is exhausted and flat agrees with his partner on one protected long sleep each at the weekend, a pram walk every morning, and his old Wednesday five-a-side. Pick whichever of the three is most off for you right now and make one small change to it.

    Words you could use “I need help protecting my sleep for a while.” “Would you come for a short walk with me? I find it hard to go on my own.”

    Dig deeper: sleep, exercise and connection

    Professor Puddles

    Small, steady things help: a walk, a regular bedtime, time with someone kind. Calm sounds can be a soft way to wind down at night.

    Tool: Cool-down corner: calm sounds and music spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes

  7. Trauma is about what happened, and what it left behind.

    Trauma usually means going through, or seeing, something that threatened life or safety, such as violence, abuse, a serious accident, war, or the sudden death of someone close. It is very common. In surveys across 24 countries, Kessler and colleagues (2017) found about 7 in 10 adults had been through at least one.

    Most people recover over time. A smaller number develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), with memories that come back vividly, avoiding reminders, feeling on high alert, and sleep problems. Ordinary hard times and stress hurt too, even when they aren’t trauma in this sense.

    Months after a car crash on a wet roundabout, a woman still jumps at screeching brakes and won’t drive after dark. Her alarm learned that cars can mean danger and hasn’t yet unlearned it, which is a long way from overreacting. If something frightening happened more than a month ago and it still shapes your days, talk to a doctor. Trauma-focused talking therapies help many people.

    Things to tell yourself “My reactions make sense after what happened.” “It’s in the past, even if my body doesn’t feel that yet.”

    Dig deeper: what trauma is and isn’t

  8. After something frightening: safety, choice and no pressure.

    After a frightening event, people need safety, practical help, warmth and choice. They don’t need to be made to talk. A review of single-session “debriefing” after trauma by Rose and colleagues (2002) found it did not prevent PTSD, and might make things worse for some. Services that are “trauma-informed” (SAMHSA, 2014) put safety, trust, choice and working together first, and the same ideas help in families, friendships and workplaces.

    After a break-in, a grandmother doesn’t want to talk about it. Her grandson doesn’t push. He fixes the back-door lock, stays the night on her sofa, and says, “If you ever want to talk about it, I’m here.” A week later, over the phone, she does.

    Ways to say it “You don’t have to tell me anything. What would help right now?” “You’re safe now. I’m staying.”

    Dig deeper: trauma-informed care

  9. Talking therapies help many people, and medicines can too.

    Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) teaches practical ways to notice and change patterns of thinking and doing. It’s one of the most studied talking therapies, and a review of over a hundred meta-analyses by Hofmann and colleagues (2012) found the strongest support for anxiety problems and stress, and support for many other problems too.

    Guidelines such as NICE (2022) also recommend guided self-help, behavioural activation, exercise groups and, for some people, antidepressants. Questions about medicine, including starting, changing or stopping it, are for a doctor or prescriber. Please don’t stop a medicine suddenly without advice.

    A young man is too embarrassed to ask for help with panic attacks, until one stops him getting on the 7.40 for the second week running. His GP refers him to a short course of CBT, and after eight sessions he’s taking the train to work again, with a book and a bottle of water for the bad days. Before an appointment, it helps to write three lines: what you’ve noticed, how long it has lasted, and what it’s stopping you doing.

    Words to try “I’d like to talk about my mood. It’s been going on for a while.” “What are my options, and what do you recommend for someone like me?”

    Dig deeper: what treatment involves

Your part, and only your part. You can learn how your alarm works, keep the basics going, take small steps back towards life, and ask for help when it’s more than you can carry. You can’t think your way out of depression by trying harder, and you can’t fix someone else’s. Being kind to yourself, and getting the right help, are part of the work. If you feel unsafe, reaching out today matters more than anything in this book.

Monday, 7:30am

Last night you wrote the three worries on the back of an envelope from the gas board and told them they could wait until today, and you slept a little. This morning you breathe out long at the kitchen window, then text your neighbour: “Hospital at ten. A bit scared. Fancy a cuppa after?”

She replies with three hearts and says of course. The appointment is still the appointment. You won’t be facing it on your own, though. Looking at the envelope again, you notice how many weeks it’s been since you felt like yourself, and you add one more line at the bottom, to ask the doctor about your mood as well.

If you’re a teenager

Exams, friends, group chats and the future can all pile up at once, usually at about one in the morning. Tolu is seventeen and can’t sleep the night before a chemistry exam. She writes the worry down for tomorrow’s ten-minute worry time, plans one small step (ask Mr Okafor about question types) and puts her phone on the landing. The next day she tells her mum, and it helps more than she expected it to.

If worry or low mood is stopping you sleeping or going to school most days for a few weeks, tell someone you trust or your doctor. Under 19 in the UK, you can call Childline free on 0800 1111.

You could say “I keep worrying at night. Can I talk it through?” “I don’t need you to fix it. I just need to say it.”

Dig deeper: give worry a time and a place

In everyday life

Living alone can make worry louder at night and low mood quieter and easier to miss, so one small contact a day is worth protecting, even a two-minute call (see On your own: when it’s lonely, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). With a partner, low mood can look like not caring and anxiety can look like nagging, so name it plainly: “I’m low today, and I’m not cross with you.” Children and teenagers get anxious and low too, and calm, routine and listening help them more than reassurance on repeat. A friend who keeps cancelling may be struggling. Keep inviting them, with no pressure to say yes.

Grief and depression overlap without being the same thing, and Chapter 8 (page 248) looks at grief on its own terms. At work, a short, honest line to a manager often opens up more support than people expect. If you have ADHD, avoidance often looks like putting things off, so make the first step almost silly (“open the envelope”), set a ten-minute timer, or do it with someone else in the room. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-16-worry-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

Anxiety doesn’t mean something is wrong with you. It’s a normal alarm, and it only becomes a problem when it rings too loud or too often, or starts shrinking your life. Depression isn’t just sadness, and nobody snaps out of it; it affects sleep, energy, thinking and the body as well as mood, and many people recover with the right help. Not everything bad that happens is trauma in the clinical sense, which usually means a threat to life or safety, but other hard things still hurt and still deserve care, and the word doesn’t need to fit for help to be fair. Talking about trauma straight away doesn’t help everyone. Some people want to and some don’t, forcing it can make things worse, and safety and choice come first.

And asking someone about suicide does not put the idea in their head. A review by Dazzi and colleagues (2014) found no evidence that asking increases suicidal thoughts, and it may help.

If you want to help someone else with this

Notice, and ask. “You’ve seemed low lately. How are you doing, really?” opens the door, and after that it helps to listen more than you talk. Leave the feeling alone rather than arguing with it; “Cheer up” and “It could be worse” push people away, while “That sounds really hard” keeps them close. Offer something specific, like a walk, a meal, a lift to the doctor or an evening on the sofa together, because a small practical offer is much easier to accept than a big vague one.

Ask directly about safety if you’re worried. “Are you having thoughts of ending your life?” If yes, stay with them, and get help together today. And look after yourself too, because supporting someone who is struggling is tiring (see Chapter 12, page 305).

Words you could use “I’m not trying to fix it. I just want you to know I’m here.” “Would it help if I came with you to the doctor?”

zqaxunderstandingx16xworryxxmorexhelpqzWhen to get more help

Talk to a doctor, a counsellor or a mental health service if:

  • you’ve felt low, empty or hopeless, or lost interest in things, most days for two weeks or more;
  • worry or panic is stopping you doing things, or you’re avoiding more and more;
  • something frightening happened over a month ago and still shapes your days and nights;
  • you’re using alcohol, drugs, food or anything else to cope;
  • you’re not sleeping, eating or looking after yourself;
  • you have thoughts of harming yourself.

If you might act on thoughts of ending your life, or you are in danger, get help now. Call your local emergency number (911 in the US and Canada, 999 in the UK, 112 in most of Europe). In the US, call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or text HOME to 741741. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123, or text SHOUT to 85258.

In Canada, call or text 988. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Under 19 in the UK? Childline is free on 0800 1111. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines in your country. More are on Someone to talk to, free (spreadloveandacceptance.com/outside-help).

In England you can usually refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies without seeing a GP first. Find a counsellor or therapist (spreadloveandacceptance.com/outside-help#counsellor) has more places to start. If someone at home is hurting or frightening you, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private help.

This chapter is general education. It isn’t a diagnosis or a substitute for care from a professional.

Part Three · Chapter 17

Fitting in: groups, influence and culture

Why fitting in pulls so hard, how groups shape what we say and do, how culture and family set the unwritten rules, and how to stay yourself, and disagree kindly, without losing your place, whether the group is a family, a friendship, a team, a faith, a neighbourhood or a group chat.

In this chapter

  1. The pull to fit in is old and strong
  2. We go along more than we think
  3. Authority can lead people a long way
  4. “Us and them” forms fast
  5. Norms are the rules nobody wrote down
  6. Cultures differ, and so do people inside them
  7. Every family is a small culture
  8. Online groups pull harder and faster
  9. You can belong and still be yourself
  10. Disagree kindly, and early
  11. If you’re a teenager
  12. In everyday life
  13. If you want to help someone else with this
  14. When to get more help
  15. Reading on this site
  16. More for your situation

Thursday, 9:20pm

The family group chat is buzzing. Someone has posted a joke about your cousin’s new partner, and the laughing faces are piling up underneath it. You don’t find it funny, and you also don’t want to be the one who can’t take a joke. Everyone else seems fine with it, and your thumb is already hovering over the laughing face.

We all belong to groups, and we need them. Chapter 5 (page 210) looks at belonging, at why we need each other and how trust grows. This chapter looks at the other side, at how groups pull on us, why we go along and how to stay true to yourself while staying connected.

  1. The pull to fit in is old and strong.

    For most of human history, being part of a group meant survival, and being left out still feels alarming. In studies by Williams and colleagues (2000), people who were simply left out of an online ball-throwing game, by strangers they would never meet, felt worse and less as if they belonged. So we bend to stay in, by laughing at jokes, keeping quiet and going along. A new starter at a warehouse gets called “Prof” because he wears glasses and once used the word “ostensibly”. He hates it. He laughs anyway, every time, because more than anything that first month he wants to be one of the team.

    This week, notice one moment when you went along with something to fit in. Wanting to fit in is normal. You still get to choose what you go along with.

    Dig deeper: why being left out hurts

  2. We go along more than we think.

    In Solomon Asch’s famous experiments (Asch, 1956), people judged which of three lines matched another line. When the actors around them all gave the same wrong answer, people went along with the group on about a third of the answers, even though the right answer was obvious.

    Many people never went along at all. Later research, such as a review by Bond and Smith (1996), found the effect is real but varies, smaller in more recent studies and larger in cultures that put the group first. In a meeting where everyone praises a new rota, one woman sees a big problem with the Friday cover and stays quiet. Afterwards, by the lifts, two colleagues tell her they had doubts too. Writing down your own view before a group decision, and only then listening to the group, makes it easier to say what you actually think.

    Dig deeper: Asch and what came after

  3. Authority can lead people a long way.

    In Stanley Milgram’s experiments (Milgram, 1963), many ordinary people kept giving what they believed were painful electric shocks to a stranger because a man in a lab coat told them to, although no shocks were real. Burger (2009) repeated part of the study safely and found similar results. The studies are also debated. Later researchers, such as Haslam and Reicher (2012), argue that people went along when they believed in the cause, and many people refused.

    A nurse is told by a senior doctor to give a dose that looks wrong to her. She checks, speaks up and turns out to be right, and checking was the loyal thing to do. Think of one person whose word you tend to follow without question, and whether there is anything you would want to check next time, perhaps with “Before I do this, can I check one thing?”

    Dig deeper: Milgram and its critics

  4. “Us and them” forms fast.

    Part of how we see ourselves comes from our groups, whether that is a family, a town, a team, a faith or a job. Tajfel and Turner (1979) called this social identity. It brings pride and loyalty, and it also makes us quick to favour “us” and to see “them” as all the same, even when the groups are formed on almost nothing. Two branches of one family always sit apart at weddings, and nobody can quite remember why. One year a cousin quietly swaps the seating plan, and the two sides discover a shared weakness for terrible music.

    Think of a “them” in your life and name one person from that group as an individual, with something they like and something they worry about.

    Dig deeper: social identity

  5. Norms are the rules nobody wrote down.

    Every group has norms about what you wear, how you speak, what you laugh at and what you never mention, and we often guess them wrong. In studies at one university, Prentice and Miller (1993) found that most students were privately less comfortable with heavy drinking than they thought everyone else was. Each person thought they were the odd one out, so everyone kept going along. In one office everyone answers emails at midnight because they think it’s expected, until a manager says, quite casually, that she doesn’t expect replies after six, and the relief is almost audible. In my years as a government auditor I heard “we have always done it this way” constantly, and it usually meant a norm nobody had checked in years.

    Pick one unwritten rule in a group you belong to and ask one person, privately, what they really think of it.

    Dig deeper: norms and wrong guesses

  6. Cultures differ, and so do people inside them.

    Cultures differ in how much they put the individual or the group first, which researchers call individualism and collectivism (Hofstede, 1980). In some, standing out is admired, and in others fitting in and keeping harmony are signs of maturity. Labels need care, though. A large review by Oyserman and colleagues (2002) found the differences were smaller and less tidy than often claimed, and individuals vary hugely within every culture. A woman raised in a close-knit family moves in with a partner who grew up being told to do his own thing. He sees her daily calls home as clingy and she sees his rare calls as cold, while each is following the rules they learned.

    Name one thing you think of as simply how people should behave, then ask where you learned it and whether someone else might have learned the opposite.

    Dig deeper: culture, with care

  7. Every family is a small culture.

    Families have their own norms about how loud people are and how feelings are shown. Some things get talked about and some never do, and there are rules about how you say sorry, if you do. We often only notice our family’s rules when we live with someone from a different family, and Where your lens came from (page 22) looks at the rules you grew up with. Two housemates clash over the kitchen because in one’s family you wash up straight after eating and in the other’s you leave it to soak and do it in the morning. Neither of them is lazy or fussy. Each is following a rule from a kitchen two hundred miles away.

    Write down three rules from the family you grew up in. Keep one you value, and question one you don’t, perhaps by asking, “What did yours do? Shall we make our own rule?”

    Dig deeper: family cultures
  8. zqaxunderstandingx17xgroupsxxonlineqz

    Online groups pull harder and faster.

    Group chats, forums and social media make group pressure quicker and more public, because likes and replies show the norm instantly. In a study of over half a million posts, Brady and colleagues (2017) found that messages with more moral and emotional words spread further, mostly among people who already agreed. Outrage travels fast while quiet doubts stay put. A parents’ group chat turns against a teacher after one angry post about a detention, forty messages in an hour. A dad who knows the teacher a little sends a calm message saying he’d want to hear her side before anyone decides anything. Two other parents agree with him. The thread goes quiet, and stays quiet.

    Before you react to a heated post, wait ten minutes, then decide whether to reply in public, in private, or not at all.

    Dig deeper: groups online

    Tidbit

    Group chats move fast. Before you send a reply, a helper on the website can read the room with you.

    Tool: Chat analyzer spreadloveandacceptance.com/signal-translator

  9. You can belong and still be yourself.

    Belonging means being accepted as you are, while fitting in means changing in order to be accepted (Chapter 5, page 210, says more). Good groups have room for difference. It helps to know your own values, to have more than one group and to have at least one ally, and in Asch’s experiments, when just one other person gave the right answer, going along with the group dropped sharply. A teenager who loves chess gets teased about it by his mates. He doesn’t drop chess and he doesn’t drop his mates. He joins the club that meets in the library on Wednesdays as well, and with two groups, neither one gets to decide who he is.

    Write down three things you value, and the next time a group pulls on you, check whether the pull is in line with them.

    Dig deeper: staying yourself
  10. zqaxunderstandingx17xgroupsxxdissentqz

    Disagree kindly, and early.

    You don’t have to choose between going along and starting a war. A kind disagreement is short and calm, it is about the issue rather than the people, and it leaves room for others. Speaking early is easier than speaking late, and a private word often works better than speaking in front of everyone. Some people keep a sentence ready, such as “I see it a bit differently. Can I say why?”, “I’m not comfortable with that joke” or “Can we hear from people who haven’t spoken yet?”

    Choose the sentence that sounds most like you and say it out loud a few times, so it is ready when you need it.

    Dig deeper: kind dissent

    Professor Puddles

    Disagreeing early and kindly is easier with the words ready. This workpaper helps you say it so it lands.

    Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

Your part, and only your part. You can notice the pull to fit in, check what you actually think, choose your groups, and say “I see it differently” kindly.

You can’t control what a group does, and you don’t have to stay in a group that keeps asking you to hide who you are or go against what’s right. If a group, a family or a partner uses pressure, fear or threats to control you, that’s not belonging. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has free, private help.

Thursday, 9:40pm

You delete the laughing face and message your aunt privately instead. “I know it was meant to be funny, but it might hurt if they see it. Could we leave it?” A few minutes later the joke disappears, followed by a message to you saying it was only a bit of fun and people are too sensitive these days. Later your cousin messages you to say thank you, because she saw it before it went. Your aunt is noticeably short with you at Sunday lunch, and you still don’t know whether that will pass.

If you’re a teenager

Group chats are where a lot of friendship happens, and a lot of hurt. Rhys is fifteen when he finds a photo of himself from PE being joked about in his class chat. He doesn’t answer back.

He screenshots it and mutes the chat. Then he tells his sister, and together they tell his form tutor. Then a girl in his class messages him privately to say it wasn’t funny and that she is sorry she didn’t say anything. Most people in a group chat don’t like what is happening, and each of them thinks everyone else does.

You could say “I’m not okay with this. Please delete it.” To a friend, “That wasn’t okay. Are you alright?” To an adult, “Something’s happening online and I need help with it.”

Dig deeper: groups online

In everyday life

Having no group can be as hard as having a pushy one, and groups built around something you enjoy bring belonging along with the activity. Partners bring two families and two sets of rules, which are worth talking about openly before you make your own. Children and teenagers feel peer pressure strongly, and practising a “no” that saves face helps them. Old family roles, the peacekeeper or the black sheep, can be hard to step out of. At work, when everyone agrees too fast, it helps if whoever leads shares their view last and asks each person to name one risk before deciding (more in the full chapter, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-17-groups-in-depth). And online, you are allowed to mute, leave or take a break from groups that leave you feeling worse.

If you want to help someone else with this

If someone speaks up, back them up, even quietly with “I think that’s a fair point,” because one ally makes a big difference. In any group you lead, invite quieter people and different views by asking what nobody has thought of yet. If someone seems to be going along against their wishes, ask gently, away from the group, and keep an eye on who gets left out of the chats and the plans, so you can bring them in.

Words you could use “I noticed you went quiet when they said that. Are you okay?” “I’d like to hear what you think, even if it’s different.”

When to get more help

Group pressure is part of life. It may be time for more help if:

  • a group, family or partner controls who you see, what you wear, what you spend or what you believe, or punishes you for disagreeing;
  • you feel you can’t leave a group without being threatened, shamed or cut off from everyone you know;
  • you’re being bullied, at school, at work or online;
  • being left out or pressured is leaving you very low, anxious or hopeless.

Talk to someone you trust, a counsellor or a doctor. Not safe at home? lists free, private help if someone at home controls or frightens you. For low mood or worry, see Chapter 16 (page 371). If you are thinking about ending your life, please tell someone today.

In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines.

This chapter is general education, not therapy.

Afterword

Afterword

What the book adds up to

A short look back at the whole book: what each part was for, the few ideas that run through all of it, and where to go next. For anyone who has read some or all of it, in any kind of relationship, or on your own.

In this chapter

  1. Three parts, one idea
  2. Six threads that run through the book
  3. Notice before you judge
  4. Settle before you speak
  5. Say it plainly and kindly
  6. Small steps beat big pushes
  7. Repair is normal
  8. Your part, and only your part. Safety first
  9. Where to go from here

In short

  • Part One was about you: where your lens came from, how you work now, and where you want to go.
  • Part Two was about sharing a life: seeing the work, sharing it fairly, and talking about it kindly.
  • Part Three was about people: how feelings, stress, trust, change, loss, minds and groups work.
  • The thread through all of it: notice before you judge, settle before you speak, say it plainly and kindly, take small steps, repair, and keep everyone safe.

You don’t need to have read every page to get something from this one. If you skipped around, that’s how most people read. The book was written so you could start anywhere, stop anywhere and pick it up again.

Three parts, one idea

Part One: Yourself (page 22) looked at the lens you see through: what life taught you, how your mind and body work now, and what matters to you next. It came first because everything else depends on it. You can’t share a life well if you don’t know how you work.

Part Two: Between us (page 62) looked at the quiet work of running a shared life, a home, a family, a team, and how to see it, share it fairly and talk about it without blame. Each chapter came with a worksheet, because ideas only help when they turn into something you do.

Part Three: Understanding people (page 152) looked at how people work: feelings, stress, how we see each other, how we talk, why we need each other, how we change, our worth, loss, different minds, values, healing, helping, anger, personality, love, worry and low mood, and the pull of groups.

Underneath all three is one idea: most of what goes wrong between people is understandable, and much of it can be put right. Mostly by seeing a little more clearly and acting a little more kindly, which is easier than trying to be perfect.

Six threads that run through the book

The book rests on five big ideas, set out at the front: see the whole load; fix the setup, not the person; read your state first; tune how you send and receive; and notice the quiet incentives. The six threads below are the same ideas said as everyday habits, plus one rule that sits around all of them: safety first. The table after the list shows how they match.

  1. Notice before you judge.

    A sharp word, a forgotten job or a quiet evening usually has a reason: tiredness, a full stress tank, a different family rule, a different kind of mind. Asking “What might be going on?” before “What’s wrong with them?” changes most conversations. See Chapter 3 (page 182).

  2. Settle before you speak.

    When the body is flooded, nobody listens well. Slow the breath, step away with a time to come back, then talk. See Chapter 2 (page 166) and Chapter 13 (page 319).

  3. Say it plainly and kindly.

    What happened, how it felt, what you’re asking for. Clear is kind, for everyone. See Chapter 4 (page 195).

  4. Small steps beat big pushes.

    One job with one owner. One walk. One message. One step on the ladder. Change that lasts is usually small and repeated. See Chapter 6 (page 223).

    Tidbit

    That’s the end. Pick one small thing from the book and try it this week, and leave the rest for later.

    Tool: Ten-minute start spreadloveandacceptance.com/start-in-10-minutes

  5. Repair is normal.

    Everyone gets it wrong. What keeps relationships going is coming back: a short, real apology and a plan for next time. See Chapter 11 (page 292).

  6. Your part, and only your part. Safety first.

    You can change what you do. You can’t make anyone else change, and you never have to accept being frightened, controlled or hurt. If that’s happening, getting safe comes before working it out. See Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety)

Where to go from here

  • On your own: The self path (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) turns Part One into a few steps you can take at your own pace.
  • With someone: The six-week program (spreadloveandacceptance.com/prog-01) turns Part Two into one small step a week, for a home, a family or a team. Miss a week? Pick up anywhere.
  • With a question: Ask Professor Puddles (spreadloveandacceptance.com/ask), the site’s private helper, about anything in the book.
  • Want the evidence? The research behind this book lists every study the book draws on, in plain words, with how strong the evidence is.
  • Read it again, differently: every chapter has a fuller version, and the contents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/) lists them all.
  • When it’s more than a book can help with: Help beyond this book (spreadloveandacceptance.com/outside-help) lists counsellors, helplines and support groups.

Any day, any time

You close the book. Nothing at home has changed yet. But maybe next time a sharp word lands, you’ll wonder what’s under it. Maybe you’ll breathe out before you answer. Maybe you’ll say the thing plainly, or say sorry sooner. That’s all this book was ever asking for: a little more understanding, a little more often. Thank you for reading.

This book is general education, not therapy. If you are struggling, please reach out: someone to talk to, free (spreadloveandacceptance.com/outside-help#talk).

How the numbers work

Every number in this book is arithmetic you can do with a pencil. None of them is a test, a diagnosis or a verdict on anyone: they describe a week, a load or a way of sharing work. The weights and cut-offs are this book’s own rules of thumb, not research findings, and you are free to disagree with them. The worked examples are the book’s own, so you can check them against the chapters.

Two habits run through all of them. Scores are rounded to two decimal places before their band is read, so the number you see and the words you see always agree. And nobody’s score is ever worked out for them: if someone’s own answer is missing, the total waits.

The stress tank: How much are you carrying?

You score five things from 0 (not at all) to 4 (very true), about the last day or two: sleep debt, workload elsewhere, unresolved conflict, your physical state, and time pressure today.

tank = (sleep + workload + conflict + body + time) ÷ 20

The answer runs from 0 to 1, and higher means fuller. Under 0.30 is light, 0.30 up to 0.60 medium, and 0.60 or more high. (The worksheet splits each band in two for its words: very light under 0.15, light, medium on the lighter side under 0.45, medium on the heavier side, high under 0.80, and very high from 0.80.) Your battery is the other side of the same thing, the energy you have left, so a full tank means a low battery. The battery is a picture in words, not a second score.

Worked example Rosa, from Part Two, Chapter III, page 105, scores sleep 3, workload 4, conflict 1, body 2 and time 3.

3 + 4 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 13; 13 ÷ 20 = 0.65, which is in the high band.

Two or more of you: each person scores only themselves, and the shared figure is the plain average of everyone’s own scores. If any one person is at 0.60 or more, treat that as the headline, whatever the average says.

Coming back after a pause (the Calm-Down Kit): if you like numbers, take the score again after a calming round. Under 0.50, go back at the time you named. From 0.50 to 0.59, take another round. At 0.60 or more after two rounds, put it off to a named time. The kit’s line sits at 0.50 on purpose: you don’t need an empty tank to come back, just one less than half full.

My weather today: the room in your day

My weather today shows words, not numbers: a sky (clear, gusty or fogged in) and how much room you have today. Behind the words sits a rough tally from 0 to 100, where higher means a heavier day. You only see it if you tick “Show the numbers behind this”.

What you pickedAdds
The sky: clear, gusty, fogged in0, 26, 34
The pressure: light, building, heavy (skipped: 6)0, 10, 20
Last night’s sleep: properly rested, about enough, short night, barely slept (skipped: 6)0, 2, 10, 18
People load: barely any, a normal amount, a lot, nonstop (skipped: 4)0, 3, 9, 14
Ground conditions (hungry, thirsty, in pain and so on)4 each, up to 14
What’s blowing in (work, money, health and so on)3 each, up to 10

Under 45 reads as lots of room today, 45 to 64 as some room, and 65 or more as very little room.

Worked example Joel, from Part One, Now, page 35, picks gusty, building pressure, a short night, a lot of people time, one ground condition (hungry) and one thing blowing in (work).

26 + 10 + 10 + 9 + 4 + 3 = 62: some room today, with less than usual, so the forecast says to go gently and settle first.

Workload balance: how evenly the hours are shared

Two people. Work out each person’s share of the logged hours as a percentage.

balance = 1 − (the difference between the two percentages ÷ 100)

50/50 scores 1.00; one person doing everything scores 0.00. It doesn’t matter which of you does more. Balance ignores the total, which is one reason the stress tank sits beside it.

Worked example Rosemary logs 14 hours and Ken 10 (Part Two, Chapter II, page 88). Out of 24 hours, that is 58.3% and 41.7%.

1 − (58.3 − 41.7) ÷ 100 = 1 − 0.167 = 0.83

Three or more people, or an agreed split. The same idea, said more generally: how much of the week would have to change hands to reach the target, compared with the most that ever could.

each share = that person’s hours ÷ everyone’s hours target = an even share (1 ÷ number of people), or the split you agreed moved = ½ × the sum of every |share − target| most = 1 − the smallest target share balance = 1 − moved ÷ most

Worked example Three partners log 15, 9 and 6 hours (Chapter II, page 88): shares 0.50, 0.30 and 0.20, against a third each.

moved = ½ × (0.167 + 0.033 + 0.133) = 0.167; most = 1 − 0.333 = 0.667; balance = 1 − 0.167 ÷ 0.667 = 0.75. In hours, 0.167 × 30 = 5 hours a week would change hands for an even split.

With an agreed split, use it as the target: co-parents who agreed 60/40 and log 12 and 8 hours score 1.00.

Ownership: does every job have a name?

ownership = jobs with a named owner ÷ all the jobs on the list

The calculator counts a job as owned when it has one named owner. A backstop, the person who notices if it slipped, is a good habit and has its own column, but the score only needs the owner. The starter jobs on the worksheet don’t count until you give them an owner or change them. Never raise the score by deleting the jobs nobody owns: they are exactly what the score is there to show.

Worked example Rosemary and Ken list 12 regular jobs, and 9 have an owner: 9 ÷ 12 = 0.75.

Who carries more of the list. A score of 1.00 can still mean one person owns everything, so One owner per job also shows each person’s share of the list, with each job weighted by how often it comes round and how big it is:

weight of a job = how often × size how often: daily 5, weekly 1, ongoing 1, monthly 0.25, as needed 0.1 size: small 0.5, medium 1 (the default), big 2 (or, where you gave the hours each time: hours ÷ 0.5) share = the weights of that person’s jobs ÷ the weights of all the jobs

A job you decide together counts the same for each of you; on a list for two homes it shows as “Together” instead.

Worked example One person owns the cooking (daily, medium: 5) and the bills (monthly, medium: 0.25). The other owns the laundry (weekly, big: 2) and the car (as needed, medium: 0.1). Each owns two jobs, but 5.25 ÷ 7.35 = 71% of the list’s weight sits with the first person, and 29% with the second.

Who’s carrying more right now. Who did what flags the busiest person when their share of the logged minutes (or of the work done without being asked) is at least half, and at least 20 points over an even share: 70% or more for two people, 53% or more for three. In the example in the Preface, page 62, one partner did 105 of the 115 minutes that were noticed and handled without anyone asking: 91%, so the sheet says so.

The setup score: can the way you share the work last?

setup score = balance × 0.40 + ownership × 0.35 + (1 − the average tank score) × 0.25

The weights add up to 1, so the score runs from 0 to 1, and here higher means the setup is working better, the opposite of the tank score. The tank is the only part that counts against the score, which is why it enters as 1 − tank. 0.70 or more reads as working well (the “Who does what?” page says “holding”); 0.40 up to 0.70 as needs a look (“drifting”); below 0.40 as needs a rethink, together. It is a snapshot of the setup, never a probability and never a verdict on anyone.

Worked example Rosemary and Ken (Chapter II, page 88): balance 0.83, ownership 0.75, and their own tank scores are 0.45 and 0.30, an average of 0.375.

0.83 × 0.40 + 0.75 × 0.35 + (1 − 0.375) × 0.25 = 0.333 + 0.263 + 0.156 = 0.75: working well.

The shortfall is what each part could have earned minus what it did earn: balance 0.40 − 0.333 = 0.067; ownership 0.35 − 0.263 = 0.088; tank 0.25 − 0.156 = 0.094. The biggest shortfall is the tank, which usually eases outside the chore list (more sleep, a lighter week elsewhere). The calculator’s “what would help most” is the single change with the biggest gain: handing about 2 hours a week from Rosemary to Ken would take balance from 0.83 to 1.00, worth 0.067. Naming one more job’s owner would be worth 0.029, and a tank score lower by 0.10 on average 0.025.

The overall score adds a fourth part, retuning: of the moments that landed badly this week, how many you retuned before answering.

overall = balance × 0.35 + ownership × 0.30 + (1 − tank) × 0.20 + retuning × 0.15 (no rough moments this week: leave retuning out, and divide the first three parts by 0.85)

In Chapter II’s first worked example (balance 0.60, ownership 0.80, an average tank score of 0.40, and 3 of 5 rough moments retuned): 0.21 + 0.24 + 0.12 + 0.09 = 0.66.

The 30-day look-back: what shifted this month?

The look-back splits the last 30 days into four weeks (the first takes the first ten days). For each part you filled in (balance, ownership, the stress tank, and last-minute rescues), it compares the start of the month with the end:

start = the average of weeks 1 and 2 end = the average of weeks 3 and 4 it shifted if end − start is 0.10 or more (balance, ownership, tank), or 1 a week or more (rescues); anything smaller didn’t shift

One next step: a part that moved the wrong way comes first (the biggest move for its size). Otherwise, the first of these that is still true at the end: ownership under 0.70, balance under 0.70, 2 or more rescues a week, or anyone’s tank at 0.60 or more. If none is, keep the same rhythm and look again in 30 days.

Hours to change hands over the month: for each person, the hours they did minus their share of everyone’s hours, added up week by week. Half the sum of those gaps (ignoring the minus signs) is how many hours would change hands to make the month even.

Worked example Suppose Rosemary and Ken keep going for a month (made up, like them). Their four weeks: hours 14 and 10, 15 and 9, 13 and 11, 12 and 12; jobs with an owner 9, 9, 11 and 11 of 12; Rosemary’s tank 0.45, 0.50, 0.40, 0.35 and Ken’s 0.30 every week; rescues 3, 2, 1, 1.

PartStart (weeks 1–2)End (weeks 3–4)ChangeReads as
Balance(0.83 + 0.75) ÷ 2 = 0.79(0.92 + 1.00) ÷ 2 = 0.96+0.17Better
Ownership0.750.92+0.17Better
Average tank score0.390.34−0.05About the same
Rosemary’s own tank0.480.38−0.10Lighter
Rescues a week2.51−1.5Fewer

Three of the four parts shifted, all for the better, and nothing is left on the watch list, so the next step is to keep the rhythm. The setup score went from 0.73 to 0.87. Over the month Rosemary did 54 hours and Ken 42, so 6 hours would have changed hands for an even month.

On your own: is your week sustainable?

The “Who does what?” page’s “just me” view adds up the hours your week is spoken for (jobs, the thinking work, care and so on) and compares them with a waking week of about 112 hours (16 waking hours, 7 days).

share = the hours spoken for ÷ 112

Under 50% reads as sustainable, 50% up to 70% as full but workable, and 70% or more as stretched. For example, 50 hours spoken for is 45%, which leaves real room; 80 hours is 71%, a lot to keep up week after week.

All of these are this book’s own ways of putting things into numbers. They have not been tested in research studies, and they shouldn’t be quoted as findings. The free calculators on the website do the arithmetic for you, and each one has a “How is this worked out?” note.

zqglossaryqz

Words used in this book

The book’s own words, each in one plain sentence. More at spreadloveandacceptance.com/glossary.

Alexithymia
Finding it hard to notice, name or describe your own feelings. It is a trait on a scale, not an illness, and it is more common in some autistic people. Naming body signals first can help.
Backstop
The second name on a job: someone who notices if it slipped and checks in kindly. Not a supervisor. A job counts as owned once it has an owner; the backstop is a good habit on top.
Battery
Your battery is how much energy you have left today. Full means you have room to spare; low means you’re running on empty. “How much are you carrying?” measures the other side of it, how full your stress tank is: a fuller tank means a lower battery. For example: After a poor night and a long workday, your stress tank is nearly full and your battery is low, so a small request feels big.
A bid
A bid is any small reach for attention or connection, like “look at this,” a sigh or a joke. For example: They show you a photo of a dog. Looking and smiling back is turning towards it.
Calm-down plan
Your calm-down plan (once called the Calm-Down Kit) is your own short list of what settles your body, chosen ahead of time so you don’t have to think when you’re wound up. For example: A glass of cold water, a walk to the corner, and three long breaths out.
Carrier wave
The carrier wave is the feeling that travels underneath the words: the tone that arrives before the meaning does. For example: “Fine.” can carry calm, hurt or tiredness. The carrier wave tells you which.
Check-in
A check-in is a short, planned talk that keeps small things small. The daily one takes about ninety seconds, with no debating. For example: “Load today: heavy. Thank you for the dishes. One small thing: the car. My ask: could you fill it up?”
Complacency
Complacency is what happens when something has worked for a long time and you stop checking on it. It isn’t laziness or a lack of love. It’s a setup nobody has looked at lately. For example: “How was your day?” “Fine.” Months go by and nobody has asked a real question.
Double empathy
The idea, from the autistic researcher Damian Milton, that misunderstandings between autistic and non-autistic people run both ways: each finds the other hard to read, so neither side is simply “missing” something.
Drift
Drift is how two people slowly fall out of step when nobody checks in, even when nothing is wrong. For example: Three busy weeks, no real talk, and small things start to feel big.
Flooded
Flooded means being so wound up that listening stops working for a while. The kind thing is a short pause with a time to come back. For example: “I need twenty minutes. Can we talk again at eight?”
Frequency
Your frequency is your natural pace: how fast you decide, talk, reply and recover. For example: One person answers a text in a minute; the other answers at the end of the day. Neither is wrong.
Gatekeeping
Holding on to how a home or child-care job must be done, so the other person steps back. Researchers first described it in mothers (“maternal gatekeeping”), but anyone can do it.
If-then plan
A small plan written as “If this happens, then I will do that”, which makes a new habit easier to start (Peter Gollwitzer).
A kind no
A kind no says what you can and can’t do right now, without blaming anyone. For example: “I can’t take that on this week. I could help on Saturday.”
Kinship care
When a grandparent, aunt, older sibling or family friend raises a child whose parents can’t.
The ladder
Three everyday states: calm and connected, revved up, running on empty. My weather today calls them clear, gusty and fogged in. A best guess about your state, not a measurement.
Ledger
A notebook where you write down what happened, so you can look at it calmly later. The book works the same way: see what is really going on, without blame, then change one small thing.
The load
The load is all the work of a shared life, including the thinking, planning and remembering that nobody sees. For example: Buying the gift is one job. Remembering the birthday, picking the gift and wrapping it are three more.
Masking
Masking is hiding the way you’re wired to fit in, which can be very tiring over time. For example: Forcing eye contact and rehearsing small talk all day, then needing the evening to recover.
Mental load
The noticing, planning and remembering behind running a shared life: knowing the shoes are too small, booking the appointment, keeping the list. It is real work, even though nobody sees it.
Monotropism
A theory of autistic attention: attention gathers deeply on a few things at a time, rather than spreading thinly across many. Switching away can take real effort.
My weather today
My weather today is a one-minute check on your own conditions today, like sleep, stress and energy: Clear means calm and connected, Gusty means revved up, and Fogged in means running on empty. For example: Short night, busy day: the forecast says to keep big talks for tomorrow.
Owner (one owner per job)
The owner of a job is the one person who makes sure it gets done from start to finish, so nobody has to keep asking. For example: Sam owns the recycling: noticing it’s full, taking it out and buying the bags.
Parallel parenting
Co-parenting with as little direct contact as possible: each home runs its own way, and messages stay short, polite and about the children.
Person A and Person B
Person A and Person B are simply the two people on a two-person worksheet or tool. They are labels, not a ranking. For example: In the Chat analyzer, Person A sends the message and Person B receives it.
Pressure
Pressure, in My weather today, is how much you were already carrying today: light, building or heavy. Behind the forecast sits a rough tally from 0 to 100; under 45 leaves room in the day, 65 or more means go gently. It is a reading of what you told it, not a score or a grade. For example: A pressure of 40 leaves room in the day; 75 means go gently and leave big things for later.
Prolonged grief
Grief that stays intense and gets in the way of daily life for a long time after a death (6 to 12 months or more, depending on the guideline). It is treatable; a GP or doctor is a good first step.
Psychological safety
A shared sense in a group or team that you can speak up, ask a question or admit a mistake without being punished or embarrassed (Amy Edmondson).
Repair
A repair is anything that stops a tense moment from getting worse, like a joke, a softer tone or “Can we start over?” For example: “I said that badly. What I meant was…”
Retune
To retune is to notice you’ve fallen out of step with someone and adjust together: slower, softer, or at a better time. For example: “Can we start that again? I came in too fast.”
The rulebook from home
The rulebook from home is the unwritten set of rules you grew up with, about love, upset, chores and rest, that you may still expect others to follow. For example: “Whoever notices the mess cleans it” was the rule at home, so a messy kitchen feels like “It’s always me.”
Rumination
Going over the same worry or regret again and again without getting closer to an answer.
Second arrow
The extra pain we add on top of a hard moment, such as being angry at ourselves for being sad. The first arrow is the event; the second is what we tell ourselves about it (a Buddhist image).
Setup score
The one number from Is the setup working for everyone?: balance, ownership and stress added up with weights (0.40, 0.35 and 0.25), from 0 to 1. 0.70 and up is working well, 0.40 to 0.69 needs a look, under 0.40 needs a rethink, together. It judges the setup, never a person.
Static
Static is the crackle between two people when the words are fine but the tone, pace or timing doesn’t match. For example: You ask “When will you do it?” calmly. They hear pressure. Nobody meant harm, but it crackles.
Stress tank
How much stress you are already carrying, from How much are you carrying?, scored from 0 (empty) to 1 (full). Under 0.30 is light, 0.30 to 0.59 medium, 0.60 and up high. A fuller tank means less room to take more on. (Your battery is the other side of it: energy left.)
Talk window
The talk window says whether now is a good time for a big conversation: open, wait a little, or closed for today. For example: Your window says “wait,” so you ask to talk after dinner instead of right now.
Unbilled debt
Unbilled debt is the work of a shared life that got done but was never noticed or thanked. For example: You remembered the dentist appointment, and nobody knew there was anything to remember.
Wave Code
Four letters from the style quiz in How you connect, one for each of four preferences about how you take in and send words. Each letter shows where you lean on a dial today: a shorthand for preferences, not a personality type.
Window of tolerance
The range in which you can feel strong feelings and still think and talk. Above it you are flooded or revved up; below it you shut down. A phrase from the psychiatrist Dan Siegel.
Wired differently
Being wired differently means your brain works in a less common way, such as being autistic, ADHD, dyslexic or highly sensitive, which changes how words land. For example: A hint like “the bins are full” may be heard as a plain fact, not a request.
Wiring
Your wiring is the way your brain and senses take in words, sound, change and people. It stays the same from day to day. For example: Some people need a plan in writing. Others think best out loud.
Workpaper
A page you fill in, on your own or with someone, about your own week or your own side. Every workpaper is free to print or to fill in on the website. For example: “Who did what” is a week’s log of who did what.
Your lens
Your lens is the set of understandings about yourself, other people and what they owe you that you picked up growing up and still use without noticing. For example: “Rest is earned” can feel like plain fact, until you notice it was your family’s rule.

zqnotesqz

Research notes

The 445 studies and books the chapters mention, chapter by chapter, each with what it found in plain words and where to read it. Each entry was looked up and checked: most against the paper itself or its abstract, some (mostly older books) against a publisher’s or library’s record. Unchecked works are left out. The full list, with notes on how strong each finding is, is at spreadloveandacceptance.com/research.

Reading research: a few words in plain English

The chapters often say how sure the research is: “a small study”, “linked with”, “didn’t replicate”. Here is what those words mean, so every note in the book is something you can weigh for yourself.

Correlational (“linked with”)
Two things tend to go together: people who sleep less tend to argue more. It doesn’t show which causes which, or whether a third thing, like a new baby, causes both.
Experiment
Researchers change one thing on purpose, ideally deciding by chance who gets it, and compare. Better at showing cause, though often in a lab, for a short time, with a small group.
Meta-analysis
A study of studies: it pools many studies of the same question. Usually more trustworthy than any one study, but only as good as the studies in it.
Replication
Doing a study again to see if the result holds. When a large team re-ran 100 published psychology studies in 2015, only about a third gave a clear result again, and the effects were on average about half as big. So one study is a start, not the end.
Effect size
How big a difference is, not just whether there is one. A result can be real (“significant”) and still tiny. The book says “small” or “modest” when that is the case.
Who was studied
Much of psychology studies students in Western, educated, well-off countries. A finding may not fit every age, culture or kind of family, and many studies of couples looked only at a mother and a father.
Self-report
People answered questions about themselves. That is often the only way to ask about feelings, but memory and wanting to look good both creep in.

How the book labels things: a Research note describes published findings in plain words and says where the evidence is thin. This site’s idea marks the book’s own ways of putting things into practice, such as the worksheets and the setup score, which have not been tested in studies. The full list at spreadloveandacceptance.com/research also says how strong each finding is: strong, moderate or early.

Part One · Then Where your lens came from

  • Ainsworth, M. D. S., Blehar, M. C., Waters, E., & Wall, S. (1978). Patterns of Attachment: A Psychological Study of the Strange Situation. Lawrence Erlbaum Associates (Hillsdale, NJ). Reported the Strange Situation studies of infants and mothers and described secure and insecure attachment patterns. search.worldcat.org/title/4194069
  • Bowlby, J. (1969). Attachment and Loss, Vol. 1: Attachment. Hogarth Press and the Institute of Psycho-Analysis (London) / Basic Books (New York). The first volume of Bowlby's trilogy, setting out attachment theory: children's bond with caregivers is an evolved system for seeking safety and comfort. vufind.lboro.ac.uk/Record/194760
